plans.title: Growing in Gratitude
plans.subtitle: See God's goodness daily.
plans.description: See God's goodness every day and grow a heart of gratitude.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants to grow in gratitude and joy
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May your heart continue to grow in gratitude as you walk with God each day.

days.title: Grateful for Today
days.devotion: Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving. It opens and closes with the same call to thank the LORD because He is good (vv. 1, 29). Just before our verse, the psalmist sings of a stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone (v. 22), and the New Testament applies this to Jesus (Matthew 21:42; Acts 4:11). So the day God has made in verse 24 is first a day of God's rescue and victory. Because God has acted for us in Christ, every ordinary day we are given carries that same reason for joy. Gladness here is not a mood we wait for; rejoicing is a choice made in response to what God has done. Today did not happen by chance. It came from His hand. Begin it by thanking Him.
days.reflection: What is one gift in today, however small, that you can thank God for right now?
days.prayer: Lord, this is the day You have made. Thank You for waking me to it, and for the greater gift of Jesus, the stone the builders rejected, who is now my sure foundation. Teach me to rejoice in You, not only in how the day goes. Open my eyes to Your goodness in the hours ahead, and let my first words today be words of thanks. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You began today by noticing God's goodness.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 118:24

days.title: God's Goodness
days.devotion: Lamentations was written over the ruins of Jerusalem. The writer has just poured out deep sorrow (3:1–20). Then, in the middle of that darkness, he calls something to mind and finds hope (v. 21). He does not deny the pain. He sees that it could have been worse: God's people have not been wiped out. That we still stand is itself mercy. And God's compassion is not a store that runs low; like the morning light, it arrives fresh each day. Gratitude often starts here, not when everything is right, but when we notice God's faithfulness holding us in what is wrong. His goodness does not depend on our circumstances. It rests on His character: His faithfulness is great.
days.reflection: Looking back over a hard season, where can you now see that God's mercy kept you from being destroyed?
days.prayer: Faithful God, thank You that Your mercies are new this morning. When I remember my troubles, help me also to remember You. Thank You that I have not been destroyed, and that Your compassion has never failed me. Be my portion today, and let my hope rest on Your faithfulness, not on my feelings. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that His mercies are new every morning, including this one.

days.title: Remember His Blessings
days.devotion: In Psalm 103, David speaks to his own soul, calling it to praise the LORD. He knows his heart can grow dull and forgetful, so he stirs it up. His call not to forget any of God's benefits is a command to remember. He then counts those benefits: God forgives all our sins, heals our diseases, rescues our life from ruin, crowns us with steadfast love and compassion, and fills our life with good things (vv. 3–5). Notice that the first is forgiveness. The greatest gift is not only what God gives us, but that He receives us. Ingratitude is often not open rebellion but simple forgetfulness. Thankfulness grows when we take time to remember, one mercy at a time.
days.reflection: Using verses 3–5 as a guide, name one way God has forgiven, kept, crowned or satisfied you.
days.prayer: With all my soul I will praise You, Lord. Father, my heart forgets so quickly. Today I remember: You have forgiven my sins, You have kept my life, and You have crowned me with steadfast love and compassion. Stir up my soul to praise You with all that is within me, and let me not forget even one of Your benefits. Amen.
days.completion_message: You took time to remember His benefits instead of forgetting them.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 103:2

days.title: Thankful in All Things
days.devotion: Paul gives three short commands together: rejoice always, keep on praying, and give thanks in every circumstance (vv. 16–18). They belong together and describe a life lived in God's presence. Paul says to give thanks in every circumstance, not for every circumstance. We are not asked to thank God for evil, but to see that in every situation there is still reason to thank Him: His presence, His promises, His purpose. Paul wrote this to young believers who had received the word in the midst of great suffering (1:6), so it is not naive advice. And he adds that this is God's will for them in Christ Jesus. If you have ever wondered what God's will is for your life today, here is a clear part of the answer.
days.reflection: What situation are you facing right now in which you can thank God, even if not for it?
days.prayer: Lord, You have made Your will plain: give thanks in every circumstance. In the situation that weighs on me most today, I thank You that You are with me, that Your promises still stand, and that You are working even here. Help me to rejoice, to pray, and to give thanks, not only today but always. In Christ Jesus, Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked for reason to thank God right where you are.

days.title: Gratitude in Trials
days.devotion: James is speaking here of trials of every kind, hardships that test our faith (compare v. 12). James does not tell us to enjoy pain or pretend it does not hurt. He tells us to consider it joy, to judge it rightly, because of what God does through it: the testing of our faith builds steady endurance. Verse 4 says that endurance makes us mature and whole, lacking nothing. A trial is not proof that God has left you. In His hands it becomes a tool for growing a faith that lasts. And if you lack wisdom in the middle of it, James says simply: ask God, who gives generously to everyone (v. 5).
days.reflection: How might God be using a present difficulty to grow patience and trust in you?
days.prayer: Father, I do not always feel joy in hard times, but I choose to trust what Your word says. Thank You that no trial is wasted in Your hands. Use this season to strengthen my faith and teach me endurance. When I do not know what to do, give me wisdom, as You have promised to all who ask. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your trials to God and trusted Him to grow your faith through them.

days.title: A Heart of Praise
days.devotion: Psalm 95 is a call to worship: come, it says, let us sing to the LORD (v. 1). Our verse shows how we draw near: we come into His presence with thanksgiving. Thanksgiving is the way in. Before we ask God for anything, we thank Him for who He is and what He has done. The psalm gives the reasons: He is the great King over all gods, the Maker of the sea and the dry land (vv. 3–5), and, most tenderly, we are the people He shepherds, the flock under His care (v. 7). Praise is not only for Sunday. Thanksgiving helps us draw near to God with our attention fixed on who He is. Gratitude turns our eyes from ourselves to Him.
days.reflection: Before asking God for anything today, what can you thank Him for about who He is?
days.prayer: Great King and good Shepherd, I come into Your presence with thanksgiving. You made the earth and the sea, and You made me. Thank You that I belong to Your flock and that You lead me. Let my heart sing to You today, and let my thanks rise before my requests. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came before God today with thanksgiving.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 95:2

days.title: Rooted in Thankfulness
days.devotion: Paul reminds the Colossians how their life with Christ began: they received Christ Jesus as Lord. Now, he says, keep going the same way: continue to live in Him. Then he gives two pictures: a tree "rooted" deep in the soil, and a building "built up" on a firm foundation. Our growth comes from staying connected to Christ. The final phrase is the fruit of that connection: overflowing with thanksgiving. Gratitude is not a seven-day exercise that ends today. It is the natural overflow of a life rooted in Jesus. As you finish this Connection Path, the invitation is to keep walking in Him and to let thanks become the habit of your heart.
days.reflection: What one practice of thanksgiving from this week will you carry into your daily walk with Christ?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I received You by faith; now help me to walk in You every day. Root me deep in Your love and build me up in the faith I have been taught. Let my life overflow with thanksgiving, not just this week but always. Keep me close to You. In Your name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You ended this Connection Path by choosing to stay rooted in Christ. Keep walking in Him with a thankful heart.

plans.title: Closer to God
plans.subtitle: Reconnect with God every day.
plans.description: Discover how God has drawn near to you, and learn to draw near to Him each day.
plans.best_for: Anyone who feels distant from God or longs for a closer daily walk with Him
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep drawing near to God each day, knowing He has already drawn near to you in Christ.

days.title: He Loved You First
days.devotion: John writes to believers so they can be sure of God's love. In this chapter he says it plainly: "God is love" (v. 8). Then he shows where that love is seen most clearly. Love did not begin with us reaching up to God; it began with His love for us, shown when He sent His Son. The word many English Bibles render "propitiation" or "atoning sacrifice" means a sacrifice that fully deals with sin, so that nothing is left standing between us and God. This is the starting point for any closer walk with Him. You do not have to earn your way near or prove that you are worthy. God moved toward you first, at the cost of His own Son. Every step you take toward Him this week is a response to a love that was already there. As verse 19 puts it, our love is a response to the fact that He loved us first.
days.reflection: Where do you most need to remember that God loved you before you did anything for Him?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that You loved me first. Before I ever looked for You, You sent Your Son for me. Forgive me for the times I have tried to earn Your love or felt I had to prove myself to You. Help me to rest in what Jesus has done, and let my love for You grow as an answer to Yours. Draw my heart closer to You this week. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You began by remembering the love that reached you first.

days.title: Brought Near in Christ
days.devotion: Paul reminds the Ephesian believers of where they once stood. Before Christ they lived in the world without God and without hope (v. 12). They were outsiders, far from God and from His people. Then come the words "But now," and everything changes. In Christ Jesus, those who were far off have been brought near to God by Christ's blood. Notice who does the work: they are brought near. Their closeness to God is not a feeling they must create; it is a new place that Christ's death has given them. Verse 18 adds that through Him all of us, together, can approach the Father by the one Spirit. On days when God feels distant, your feelings are not the final word. If you belong to Christ, the distance has already been closed.
days.reflection: When God feels far away, what truth from today's verse can you hold on to instead of your feelings?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I was far off, and You brought me near by Your own blood. Thank You that my place with the Father does not rest on how I feel today, but on what You have done. When You seem distant, remind me that the way to God is open. Give me confidence to come to the Father through You, with a grateful and trusting heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that in Christ the distance has already been closed.

days.title: Draw Near to Him
days.devotion: James is writing to believers whose hearts had become divided. They wanted God and the world at the same time, and it was leaving them restless and quarrelling (vv. 1–4). His answer is a call to return: submit to God (v. 7), and come near to Him. This is not a way of earning God's attention; in Christ He has already brought us near. It is an invitation to live out that closeness. Drawing near means turning our hearts back toward Him: being honest about sin (what James calls cleansing our hands), and letting go of divided loyalties (his call to the double-minded to purify their hearts). And the promise is sure: He will come near to you. When we turn toward God, we find Him ready to meet us.
days.reflection: What is one thing that divides your heart right now, and how can you bring it honestly to God today?
days.prayer: Holy God, I want to draw near to You. You know the places where my heart is divided and the things I have let crowd You out. I bring them to You honestly now. Cleanse my hands and give me an undivided heart. Thank You for Your promise that as I turn toward You, You meet me. Make my heart clean, O God. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned your heart toward God and responded to His invitation to draw near.

days.title: Seek Him With All Your Heart
days.devotion: Jeremiah sent this letter to God's people in exile in Babylon (v. 1). They were far from home because of their sin, and they would wait seventy years before returning (v. 10). Yet even there God spoke of a future with Him: they would call on Him and come and pray to Him, and He would listen (v. 12). Our verse follows: they would seek Him and find Him when they searched for Him with all their heart. Seeking God is not a half-hearted glance in His direction. It is turning to Him with everything, even in a hard place you did not choose. This passage reminds us that God desires wholehearted seeking, not a divided pursuit of Him. Israel was called to seek Him from within exile, not only after it ended. In the same way, we can turn to Him with our whole heart in whatever place we find ourselves today.
days.reflection: What would seeking God with all your heart look like in your ordinary routine this week?
days.prayer: Lord, through Jeremiah You called Your people to seek You with all their heart. I do not want to seek You half-heartedly. In the place where I am today, even if it is not where I hoped to be, I turn to You. Let me seek Your face above everything else, and hear me as I call upon You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to seek God with your whole heart, right where you are.

days.title: Be Still Before Him
days.devotion: Psalm 46 is a song sung in the middle of upheaval. The earth gives way, the mountains are carried into the sea, the waters roar, and the nations rage (vv. 2–3, 6). Yet God is our shelter and our strength, a help who is always close at hand in trouble (v. 1). The psalm shows the LORD bringing wars to an end (v. 9), and then God Himself speaks. He calls for stillness and for the knowledge that He is God, and He declares that He will be exalted among the nations and in all the earth. In this setting, "be still" is first a command to stop: to cease the striving and raging, and to recognize that God rules over the nations and over history. It is less about a quiet room and more about yielding to His sovereign rule. For us, this means laying down our own anxious striving, and making space, even a few quiet minutes, to acknowledge that He is God and we are not. The psalm's refrain holds true: the LORD of hosts stands with us (v. 11).
days.reflection: What are you striving hardest to control right now, and how can you pause today to acknowledge that God, not you, rules over it?
days.prayer: Lord of hosts, my world can feel noisy and unsteady. You rule over the nations, and You rule over my life too. Today I stop my striving and lay down my need to control everything. You are God, and I am not. Be my refuge and strength, my help that is always near, and quiet my heart so that I can know You better. Amen.
days.completion_message: You laid down your striving and acknowledged that He is God.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 46:10

days.title: Near to the Brokenhearted
days.devotion: David wrote Psalm 34 after a frightening time, when he fled from Saul and had to pretend to be mad before a foreign king (see the psalm's title and 1 Samuel 21). He knew what it was to be afraid and alone. Yet the psalm is full of praise, because when he, a poor man, cried out, the LORD heard him (v. 6). In our verse David tells us something about God's heart: the LORD is close to those whose hearts are broken. We often think our pain pushes God away. Scripture says the opposite. When your heart is broken and your spirit crushed, God is not standing at a distance. He comes close, and He saves those whose spirits are crushed. You can bring Him your brokenness just as it is.
days.reflection: What pain or disappointment do you need to bring to God today, trusting that He is near to you in it?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that You are near to the brokenhearted. You know the hurts I carry, even the ones I rarely speak about. I bring them to You now, just as they are. Heal what is broken in me and hold me close. Like David, I cry to You; hear me, and deliver me from all my fears. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your pain to the God who is near to the brokenhearted.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 34:18

days.title: Good to Be Near God
days.devotion: Psalm 73 is Asaph's honest story. He nearly lost his footing when he saw the wicked prospering and felt that his own faithfulness had been in vain (vv. 2–3, 13). Everything changed when he entered God's sanctuary (v. 17) and began to see things from God's point of view. Then he discovered what he truly had: he was always with God, and God was holding him by his right hand (v. 23). His conclusion is simple: being near God is good for him. Nearness to God is not only a duty; it is our deepest good. As this Connection Path ends, Asaph shows the way forward: keep choosing closeness to God, keep trusting Him, and let your life tell others of all His works.
days.reflection: What one habit will help you keep drawing near to God after this Connection Path is finished?
days.prayer: Lord God, being near You is good for me. I have no one in heaven but You, and there is nothing on earth I desire besides You. Thank You for holding me by my right hand, even when I have stumbled. Keep me close to You in the days ahead, help me to trust You, and let my life declare Your works. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path affirming that it is good to be near God. Keep drawing near.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 73:28

plans.title: Build a Prayer Habit
plans.subtitle: Learn to pray, day by day.
plans.description: Learn from Jesus and the people of Scripture how to build a steady, grace-filled life of prayer.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants to pray more regularly but struggles to know how to begin or keep going
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May prayer keep growing in you, not as a duty to earn God's favour, but as the daily conversation of a child with a Father who welcomes you in Christ.

days.title: Lord, Teach Us to Pray
days.devotion: The disciples had watched Jesus heal the sick, calm storms and teach the crowds. Yet the one thing Luke records them asking Him to teach them was prayer. They saw Him praying in a certain place, and when He finished, one of them asked Him to teach them to pray. Prayer was a normal part of Jewish life, and John the Baptist had taught his own disciples to pray. But something in the way Jesus prayed made them want to learn. Jesus did not scold them for not knowing already. He answered at once, giving them words to pray and teaching them about the Father's goodness (vv. 2–13). This is where a prayer habit begins: not with pressure to perform, but with a humble request. You do not need to be good at prayer to start. You can come as a learner to the best Teacher there is.
days.reflection: What do you most want Jesus to teach you about prayer as you begin this Connection Path?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, like Your first disciples, I want to learn to pray. I often do not know what to say, and my prayers can feel weak or scattered. Thank You that You welcome learners and do not turn me away. Teach me to pray. Shape my heart as I spend time with You over these days, and help me to know the Father as You do. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to Jesus as a learner and asked Him to teach you to pray.

commentary: Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer, Lesson 1 ("Lord, teach us to pray" – Luke 11:1)

days.title: Welcomed Before the Throne
days.devotion: Before we build any habit, we need to know why we can pray at all. The writer of Hebrews has just described Jesus as our "great high priest" who is not distant from us, but faced every kind of temptation we face, yet never sinned (vv. 14–15). Because of Him, we are invited to come boldly to the throne of grace. Notice what kind of throne it is. It is a throne of grace, where we come to receive mercy and to find grace that helps us when we need it. Our boldness does not come from how well we pray or how often. It comes from Jesus, who has opened the way. A prayer habit does not earn you a place before God. In Christ, that place is already yours. Regular prayer is simply learning to come, again and again, to where you are already welcome.
days.reflection: What makes you hesitate to come to God in prayer, and how does knowing it is a throne of grace speak to that?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that I can come to You because of Jesus, my great high priest. He knows my weakness, and He has opened the way for me. Forgive me for thinking I have to earn my place before You. I come boldly today, not in my own worthiness, but in Your grace. Give me mercy and help for what I need right now. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to God boldly, trusting in Christ rather than your own performance.

days.title: Jesus Made Room to Pray
days.devotion: In Luke 5, news about Jesus was spreading fast, and huge crowds gathered to hear Him and to be healed (v. 15). The needs were real and the crowds were endless. Yet Luke tells us that He would slip away to lonely places and pray. This was not a single event. Luke shows it as Jesus' pattern: He prayed at His baptism (3:21), prayed all night before choosing the Twelve (6:12), and prayed alone before asking His disciples who He was (9:18). If the Son of God made room to be with the Father, we can be sure we need it too. Jesus did not withdraw because He did not care about people. He withdrew because His life and work flowed from His relationship with the Father. A prayer habit often begins with the same simple step: choosing a time and place to step away, even briefly, from what is pressing on us.
days.reflection: What time and place in your day could you set aside to step away and pray, even for a few minutes?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, even when the crowds pressed in, You made room to be with the Father. My days are full, and I often let prayer be crowded out. Help me to step away from the noise, even for a few minutes, and spend time with You. Show me the time and place that fit my life, and meet me there. Amen.
days.completion_message: You made room in your day to step away and pray.

commentary: E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer, ch. 7 ("Much Time Should Be Given to Prayer")

days.title: Your Father Sees in Secret
days.devotion: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus warns against people who like to stand and pray in the synagogues and on street corners so that others will see them (v. 5). Their prayer was really a performance for an audience. Jesus offers something different: go into your inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. The point is not that praying with others is wrong, but that the heart of prayer is being with our Father, not being seen. He sees what is done in secret. Nothing about you is hidden from Him, and He is not waiting to be impressed. Jesus adds that your Father knows what you need before you ask Him (v. 8). A private place of prayer is where you can simply be honest with a Father who already knows you and loves you.
days.reflection: Is there anything you tend to say or do in prayer to sound right rather than to be honest with God?
days.prayer: Father in secret, thank You that I do not need an audience or the right words to come to You. You see me and You know what I need before I ask. Free me from praying to impress, whether others or myself. As I shut the door today, let me simply be honest with You, and rest in Your love for me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You made time to pray to your Father in secret and spoke to Him honestly.

commentary: Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer, Lesson 3 ("Pray to thy Father, which is in secret" – Matthew 6:6)

days.title: As He Did Before
days.devotion: Daniel was an old man serving in Persia when his jealous rivals persuaded King Darius to sign a decree: for thirty days, no one could pray to any god or man except the king, on pain of the lions' den (v. 7). Daniel knew about it. Yet he went home, opened his windows toward Jerusalem, and knelt three times a day to pray and give thanks to his God, just as he had always done. Those last words matter most. Daniel was not starting something new for a crisis. He simply kept a rhythm he had followed for years. His steady habit of prayer was already in place when the test came. The number of times is not a rule for us. The lesson is that faithfulness in hard days often grows from ordinary, regular prayer in easier ones. Notice too that his prayer included giving thanks, even under threat.
days.reflection: What regular rhythm of prayer, however small, could you begin to build into your ordinary days?
days.prayer: God of Daniel, thank You for his example of steady prayer, kept up long before the lions' den. I want my life with You to have that kind of rhythm. Help me to come to You regularly, not to earn Your favour, but because I need You every day. Build in me a habit of prayer and thanksgiving that will hold me when hard days come. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose a steady rhythm of prayer for your ordinary days.

days.title: Pray About Everything
days.devotion: Paul wrote to the Philippians while he was in prison (1:13), not knowing whether he would live or die. Yet he tells them not to be anxious about anything. His answer to anxiety is not to ignore it, but to bring it to God: in everything, through prayer and pleading with thanksgiving, they are to make their requests known to Him. Everything means the small worries as well as the large ones. And he adds thanksgiving, which turns our eyes back to what God has already done. The promise that follows is not that every request will be granted as we ask. It is that the peace of God, which is beyond all understanding, will guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. The Greek word Paul uses for guarding was used of soldiers keeping watch over a place. A daily habit of prayer includes turning our worries into requests, one by one.
days.reflection: What worry have you been carrying that you have not yet turned into a prayer?
days.prayer: Father, You tell me not to be anxious but to bring everything to You. So I bring You what is weighing on me today, both the small things and the big ones. Thank You for all You have already done for me. I leave my requests with You, and I ask that Your peace, which passes all understanding, would guard my heart and mind in Christ Jesus. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned your worries into prayer and left them with God.

days.title: Praying God's Word Back
days.devotion: Psalm 119 is a long love song about God's word, and much of it is prayer. Here the psalmist is in affliction, and he asks God to remember His word to His servant, the word that has given him hope. God does not forget His promises, but the psalmist takes what God has said and brings it back to Him in prayer. He adds that his comfort in suffering is this: God's word has given him life. One of the best ways to grow in prayer is to let Scripture give us words. When we do not know what to say, we can read a passage slowly and turn it into prayer: thanking God for what it shows of Him, confessing what it reveals in us, and asking for what it promises. We should pray His words in their true sense, not bend them to our wishes, but they will teach us to pray.
days.reflection: What verse or passage could you take this week and turn into your own prayer?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for Your word, which gives me hope and comfort. When I do not know how to pray, help me to open the Scriptures and let them teach me. Remember Your word to Your servant. Let it bring life to me in my struggles, and let my prayers be shaped more and more by what You have said, not only by what I want. Amen.
days.completion_message: You took God's word and began to pray it back to Him.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 119:49

days.title: Honest Confession
days.devotion: John writes to believers who needed to walk honestly with God. Some were claiming they had no sin at all, and John says plainly that anyone who claims to be without sin is only fooling themselves (v. 8). Instead he offers a better way: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, and He will forgive our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness. To confess is to agree with God about what is true. Notice that God forgives because He is "faithful and just." Forgiveness is not a reward for how sorry we feel. It rests on the blood of Jesus, God's Son, which cleanses us from every sin (v. 7). Honest confession belongs in a healthy prayer life. It is not a way of earning our way back to God, but of keeping nothing hidden from the One who has already made a way for us to be clean.
days.reflection: Is there something you have been avoiding bringing honestly to God that you can confess to Him today?
days.prayer: Faithful and just God, I do not want to pretend before You. You already know my sin, so I bring it to You honestly now. Thank You that Your forgiveness rests on the blood of Jesus, not on my feelings or efforts. Forgive me and cleanse me from all unrighteousness. Help me to walk in the light with You, keeping nothing hidden. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your sin honestly to God and trusted His forgiveness in Christ.

days.title: The Spirit Helps Us
days.devotion: Romans 8 speaks honestly about life in a groaning world. Creation groans, and we ourselves groan inwardly as we wait for all that God has promised (vv. 22–23). In that setting Paul admits something freeing: we do not know what we ought to pray for. Even the apostle did not always know how to pray. But he adds that the Spirit helps us in our weakness. The Holy Spirit does not stand back waiting for us to get prayer right. He comes alongside, and He intercedes for us in ways deeper than words. And God, who searches the heart, knows the mind of the Spirit, who prays in line with God's will. This means your weak, wordless or confused prayers are not failures. When you do not know what to say, you are not praying alone. You can simply come, and trust the Spirit to help you.
days.reflection: When your prayers feel weak or you do not know what to say, how could you rely on the Spirit's help instead of giving up?
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, thank You that You help me in my weakness. So often I do not know what I should pray for. Some days I have only sighs and no words at all. Thank You that You pray for me in line with God's will. Help me to keep coming, even when my prayers feel small, and to trust that You are at work in them. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to pray trusting the Spirit to help you in your weakness.

days.title: Praying for Others
days.devotion: Paul wrote to Timothy, who was leading the church in Ephesus, about how believers should live and worship together. "First of all," he says, the church should pray, bringing requests, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving, and pray for all people. He even names kings and all who are in authority, rulers who in that day were often pagan and sometimes hostile to Christians. The reason he gives is God's own heart: He desires everyone to be saved and to know the truth (v. 4). Intercession simply means praying on behalf of someone else. It is one of the ways a prayer habit grows beyond our own needs. It stretches our love to family, friends, neighbours, leaders, and even people we find difficult. Keeping a few names before God each day is a quiet way of loving them well.
days.reflection: Who are two or three people, including someone in authority, you can begin praying for regularly?
days.prayer: God our Saviour, You desire all people to be saved and to know the truth. Forgive me for praying so often only about myself. Widen my heart. I lift up to You the people You have placed in my life, and those who lead in my community and my nation. Give them wisdom, draw them to Yourself, and teach me to love them through prayer. Amen.
days.completion_message: You began carrying other people to God in prayer.

days.title: Speak, Lord
days.devotion: Samuel was a boy serving in the tabernacle at a time when a word from the LORD was rare (v. 1). He had not yet come to know the LORD (v. 7), so when God called him in the night, he ran to Eli, thinking the old priest had called. At last Eli understood and told him how to answer. When the LORD called again, Samuel answered by asking the LORD to speak, for His servant was listening. Samuel was being called as a prophet, and God spoke to him in a special way. But his answer shows an attitude every believer can share. Prayer is not only speaking to God; it is also being ready to listen. Today God speaks to us above all through His written word. When we come to prayer with Scripture open and a quiet, willing heart, we can take Samuel's words as our own, ready to hear and to obey.
days.reflection: How could you make more room to listen to God through His word, rather than only speaking in prayer?
days.prayer: Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening. I confess that I often come to You full of words and in a hurry, with little room to hear. Quiet my heart as I open Your word. Show me what You want me to see, and give me a willing heart to obey what You say. Make me a listener as well as a speaker in prayer. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to God ready to listen as well as to speak.

days.title: Praying Together
days.devotion: Acts 12 opens with grief. King Herod had put James, John's brother, to death with the sword (v. 2), and now he arrested Peter too, guarded by four squads of soldiers (v. 4). The church could not open the prison. But they could pray: while Peter was held in prison, the church kept praying earnestly to God for him. God sent His angel and set Peter free, and Peter went straight to a house where many had gathered to pray (v. 12). At first they could hardly believe it was him (v. 15). This passage does not promise that prayer always brings the rescue we ask for; James was not delivered. What it shows is a church that brought its fear to God together, and kept at it. Private prayer matters, but it was never meant to be our only prayer. We need others to pray with us, and they need us.
days.reflection: Who is one believer you could pray with regularly, or what burden could you invite others to pray about with you?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for the church that prayed together for Peter, even while they grieved for James. You know the burdens I carry, and the ones my brothers and sisters carry too. Help me not to pray only alone. Lead me to others I can pray with, and make me faithful in praying for them. Whatever answer You give, keep us coming to You together. Amen.
days.completion_message: You took a step toward praying together with other believers.

days.title: Pray Without Ceasing
days.devotion: Paul wrote to a young church in Thessalonica that had received the gospel in the midst of great suffering (1:6). Near the end of his letter he gives a string of short commands: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in every circumstance (v. 18). To pray without ceasing does not mean saying words every minute. It means that prayer never shuts down. It becomes a constant conversation we keep returning to, in set times and throughout the day. Paul lived this way himself, praying for them earnestly night and day (3:10). Rejoicing and thanksgiving sit right beside prayer here, because an ongoing life with God is not only asking. It is noticing His kindness and thanking Him for it along the way. A few set times of prayer can grow into a whole day that is turned toward Him.
days.reflection: What ordinary moment in your day could become a reminder to turn your heart to God in a brief prayer?
days.prayer: Father, I want my whole day to be turned toward You, not only a few minutes of it. Teach me to pray without ceasing, to talk with You in ordinary moments, and to notice Your kindness as it comes. Give me a rejoicing and thankful heart in everything. Let my set times of prayer spill over into the rest of my day. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to keep turning your heart to God throughout your day.

days.title: Keep Praying, Don't Lose Heart
days.devotion: Jesus told a parable to show that His followers should always pray and not lose heart. A widow kept coming to an unjust judge until he finally helped her, only to stop her troubling him (vv. 2–5). Jesus is not saying God is like that judge. He is showing the contrast: if even an unjust judge will act, how much more will God act for His chosen ones who cry out to Him day and night (v. 7). To lose heart is to become discouraged and give up. Every prayer habit will have gaps and dry seasons. You will miss days. Answers may seem slow. None of that cancels your welcome before God. His love for you in Christ has not changed. The call is simply to keep coming back. As this Connection Path ends, do not measure your prayer life by a perfect record. Keep praying, trust your Father, and do not lose heart.
days.reflection: When your prayer habit slips or answers seem slow, what will help you come back to God instead of giving up?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that my welcome before You does not depend on a perfect record. You know how easily I grow tired and discouraged in prayer. When I miss days or answers seem slow, help me not to lose heart. Draw me back to You again and again. Grow in me a faith that keeps praying, because You are good and You hear Your children. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to keep praying and not lose heart.

commentary: Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer, Lesson 16 ("Speedily, through bearing long" – Luke 18:1–8)

plans.title: Trust God More
plans.subtitle: Strengthen your trust through His Word.
plans.description: Grow in trusting God by seeing who He is and how faithfully He keeps His word.
plans.best_for: Anyone who finds it hard to trust God, or who wants their trust in Him to grow deeper and steadier
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep resting your weight on God Himself, who is faithful, whose word stands, and who holds your times in His hand.

days.title: With All Your Heart
days.devotion: Proverbs 3 is a father teaching his son how to live wisely before God (v. 1). At its centre is a call to trust the LORD wholeheartedly and not to rely on your own understanding. To lean is to put your whole weight on something. The father is not telling his son to stop thinking, but to stop treating his own understanding as the thing that holds him up. Verse 7 adds a warning not to be wise in your own eyes. Trust means resting your full weight on the LORD, and acknowledging Him in every area of life, not only in the religious parts of life. The promise is that He will make your paths straight: God guides those who look to Him. This Connection Path begins here, because trust is not a feeling we work up. It is a choice about where we lean.
days.reflection: Where are you leaning most heavily on your own understanding right now, and what would it look like to lean on God there instead?
days.prayer: Lord, You call me to trust You with all my heart. So often I lean on my own understanding and try to hold everything up by myself. Today I choose to put my weight on You. I want to acknowledge You in every part of my life, not only the parts I think of as spiritual. Direct my paths, and teach me to trust You more. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to lean on God rather than on your own understanding.

days.title: Knowing His Name
days.devotion: In Psalm 9 David praises God for judging justly and defending the weak. He has seen that the LORD is a safe stronghold for the oppressed, a place of refuge when trouble comes (v. 9). Then he says that those who know God's name will trust in Him. In Scripture, God's name stands for His character: who He has shown Himself to be. Trust grows out of knowing Him. We find it hard to trust someone we barely know, but easy to trust someone whose faithfulness we have seen again and again. David adds the reason: the LORD has never abandoned those who seek Him. If your trust feels thin, the answer is not to try harder to feel confident. It is to get to know God better, through His Word, through remembering what He has done, and through time spent with Him.
days.reflection: What do you already know about God's character that could help you trust Him with something you are facing this week?
days.prayer: LORD, I want to know Your name, not just words about You, but who You truly are. Thank You that You are a refuge when trouble comes and that You have not forsaken those who seek You. Where my trust is weak, show me more of Your faithful character through Your Word. As I come to know You better, let my trust in You grow. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked to God's character as the ground of your trust.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 9:10

days.title: He Keeps His Word
days.devotion: These words come from a surprising speaker. Balak, king of Moab, had hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. But every time Balaam opened his mouth, God made him bless them instead. Here Balaam explains why he cannot change the message: God is not a human being who lies, nor a mortal who changes his mind. People make promises and break them, or change their minds when things get hard. God does not. Balaam asks: when God has said something, will He not do it? When He has spoken, will He not carry it through? This is why trusting God is not wishful thinking. Our trust rests on His truthfulness, not on our strength of feeling. When you hold on to what God has actually said in His Word, you are standing on the one word that will never be taken back.
days.reflection: Is there a promise of God that you find hard to believe right now, and what would change if you took Him at His word today?
days.prayer: Faithful God, You are not like us. You do not lie, and You do not go back on what You have said. Forgive me for the times I have doubted Your word because I was measuring You by people who let me down. Help me to hold on to what You have spoken in Scripture, and to rest my trust on Your faithfulness rather than on my feelings. Amen.
days.completion_message: You rested your trust on the God who keeps His word.

days.title: Like Mount Zion
days.devotion: Psalm 125 is one of the songs of ascent, which are traditionally understood as songs for worshippers travelling up to Jerusalem for the feasts, a city set among hills. The psalmist turns that view into a picture of trust: those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be shaken but stands firm forever. Then he looks at the hills surrounding the city: just as the mountains encircle Jerusalem, so the LORD encircles His people, now and forever. Notice where the stability comes from. The one who trusts is steady, not because their feelings never shake, but because the LORD Himself surrounds them. The psalm does not pretend there are no wicked people or hard days (v. 3). It shows that those who trust God are held by Someone who does not move.
days.reflection: What is shaking you right now, and what would change if you pictured the LORD surrounding you in it?
days.prayer: LORD, You surround Your people as the mountains surround Jerusalem. When I feel shaken, remind me that my steadiness comes from You, not from my own strength or feelings. I choose to trust You today. Make me like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, because You surround me now and forever. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to trust the LORD who surrounds His people.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 125:1–2

days.title: Commit Your Way
days.devotion: Psalm 37 was written by David in his old age (v. 25) to people troubled by a hard question: why do the wicked seem to prosper? His answer is repeated three times: do not fret (vv. 1, 7, 8). Instead of fretting, he calls us to trust. Our verse calls us to commit our way to the LORD and trust in Him, with the promise that He will act. The Hebrew word behind "commit" means to roll, like rolling a heavy load off your own shoulders and onto someone else. We are to roll our whole path, our plans, worries and unfinished situations, onto the LORD. The promise that He will act is not that God will do everything we want in the way we picture it. Verse 6 shows its meaning: God will bring out the rightness of those who trust Him, in His own time.
days.reflection: What situation have you been carrying on your own shoulders that you need to roll onto the LORD today?
days.prayer: Lord, I have been carrying things that were never mine to carry alone. Right now I roll my way onto You: my plans, my worries, and the situations I cannot fix. Help me to stop fretting and to trust You instead. I leave the outcome in Your hands, knowing You will act rightly and in Your time. Amen.
days.completion_message: You rolled your burden onto the LORD instead of fretting over it.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 37:5

days.title: Roots by the River
days.devotion: Jeremiah spoke to Judah at a time when the nation was looking to political allies for security instead of to God. Just before our verses, the LORD pronounces a curse on the one who trusts in mere people and relies on human strength (v. 5). Such a person is like a dry shrub in a salt desert. Then comes the contrast: blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD and whose confidence is in Him. That person is like a tree planted by water, sending its roots out toward the stream. Notice that the heat still comes and the drought still comes. The tree is not spared hard seasons. But its roots reach a hidden source, so its leaves stay green and it never stops bearing fruit. Trust in God does not remove every dry season; it gives us roots that reach Him in it.
days.reflection: What have you been relying on for security instead of God, and how can you send your roots toward Him this week?
days.prayer: LORD, I confess that I often look to people, plans or money to hold me up. Forgive me for relying on human strength. I want to be like a tree planted by water, with roots that reach down to You. When the heat and dry seasons come, keep me green and fruitful because my hope is in You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to put your roots down in the LORD rather than in lesser things.

days.title: My Times Are in His Hand
days.devotion: David wrote Psalm 31 under real threat. He heard slander, terror surrounded him, and his enemies were plotting to take his life (v. 13). He does not pretend the danger is small. Yet in the middle of it he turns: but I trust in You, LORD; I say, You are my God. That little word "but" marks a choice. His circumstances had not changed yet, but he decided where to look. Then he says that his times are in God's hand. The seasons, events and length of his life were not in the hands of his enemies, but in God's. David still asks to be delivered; trust does not stop us from praying for help. It changes how we pray, from panic to confidence that our days are held by a faithful God.
days.reflection: What part of your future feels most out of your control, and how can you place it in God's hand today?
days.prayer: O LORD, You are my God. There are things ahead of me that I cannot control, and some of them frighten me. But I trust in You. My times are in Your hand, not in the hands of people or circumstances. I ask You to help me and deliver me, and I rest in knowing that my days are held by You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You placed your future in God's hand and declared that He is your God.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 31:15

days.title: Fully Persuaded
days.devotion: Paul uses Abraham to show that God counts people righteous through faith, not works. God had promised Abraham a son when he was about a hundred years old and Sarah was far past childbearing (v. 19). Abraham did not ignore those facts. He did not treat his own body as the final word, because he looked beyond it to God. He did not waver in unbelief at God's promise, but grew strong in faith and gave glory to God. What made his faith strong? Not his own spiritual effort, but his view of God: he was fully convinced that God had the power to do what He had promised. Abraham was not perfect; Genesis records his doubts and mistakes. But his trust rested on God's power and faithfulness. The strength of faith lies in the One it looks to.
days.reflection: What fact in your life seems to argue against trusting God, and what do you know about His power that is bigger than it?
days.prayer: God of Abraham, You are able to do what You have promised. When I look at my circumstances, I often stagger and doubt. Turn my eyes from the size of my problem to the greatness of Your power and faithfulness. Make me fully persuaded that You will keep Your word, and let my trust give glory to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked past what you can see to the God who keeps His promises.

days.title: Coming to God
days.devotion: Hebrews 11 was written to believers tempted to give up under pressure. The writer reminds them of men and women who trusted God before them. Here, speaking of Enoch who "pleased God" (v. 5), he says that without faith no one can please God. Then he explains what that faith looks like: anyone who draws near to God has to believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him. Faith, at its heart, is coming to God. It trusts two things: that God is real, and that He is good to those who seek Him. The "reward" here is not wealth or an easy life; many in this chapter suffered greatly (vv. 36–38). The greatest reward is God Himself and the promises He keeps. Trust begins by coming to Him, believing He welcomes you.
days.reflection: What would it look like for you to come to God this week believing that He is good to those who seek Him?
days.prayer: Father, I come to You believing that You are, and that You are good to those who seek You. Sometimes I hold back, unsure if You really want me near. Thank You that You welcome those who come to You through Jesus. I want to seek You diligently, not for what You can give me, but because You are my true reward. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to God believing that He exists and that He is good.

days.title: Not by Sight
days.devotion: Paul wrote this while facing hardship and knowing his body was wearing out (4:16). In chapter 5 he calls the body a tent, in which we groan under a heavy burden (v. 4). He longs to be at home with the Lord (v. 8). But for now, he says, we live by faith, not by sight. In context, this does not mean ignoring reality or guessing blindly. It means that the most important realities, the Lord Himself and the future He has promised, are not yet visible to us. We live now by trusting what God has said about what we cannot yet see. Paul adds that God has given the Spirit as a deposit (v. 5), a down payment guaranteeing the rest. Walking by faith is living each day in step with promises that are sure, even when they are unseen.
days.reflection: What unseen promise of God do you most need to live by this week, instead of by what you can see?
days.prayer: Lord, so much of what matters most I cannot yet see. My body grows tired and my circumstances can discourage me. Thank You for the Holy Spirit, Your pledge that everything You promised will come. Help me to walk by faith and not by sight, living today in light of what You have said. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to walk by God's promises and not only by what you see.

days.title: Working for Good
days.devotion: This verse is often quoted as if everything will turn out the way we hope. Its setting is deeper. Paul has just spoken of creation groaning and believers groaning as they wait (vv. 22–23), and of the Spirit helping us when we do not know what to pray for (v. 26). Then he says that we know God works all things together for the good of those who love Him. The next verse tells us what this "good" is: to be shaped into the likeness of His Son (v. 29). God does not call evil good, and not every event feels good. But for His people, He is at work in all things, even pain, to make us like Christ and bring us safely home (v. 30). Trust does not need to explain every event. It rests on God's purpose, which cannot fail.
days.reflection: What painful situation in your life do you need to trust God to use for His good purpose of shaping you to be like Christ?
days.prayer: Father, I do not understand everything that happens in my life, and some of it hurts. But I trust that You are at work in all things for those who love You. I will not call evil good, but I believe You can use even this to make me more like Jesus. Help me to trust Your purpose when I cannot see the whole picture. Amen.
days.completion_message: You trusted God's good purpose even in what you do not understand.

days.title: Pour Out Your Heart
days.devotion: David wrote Psalm 62 while people were trying to bring him down, speaking kindly to his face but cursing him inwardly (v. 4). In that pressure he tells his own soul to rest quietly in God alone (v. 5), for God alone is his rock and his salvation (v. 6). Then he turns to others: they should trust Him at all times and pour out their hearts before Him, for God is our refuge. Trusting God does not mean hiding what we feel. It includes pouring out our hearts to Him, our fears, disappointments and questions, as water is emptied from a jar. The Psalms are full of honest prayers like this. We can be honest with God because He is a safe refuge. Trust "at all times" includes the times when our hearts are heavy and confused.
days.reflection: What have you been holding back from God that you could honestly pour out before Him today?
days.prayer: God, You are my rock and my refuge. I do not need to pretend with You. Right now I pour out my heart before You, the things I feel, fear and do not understand. Thank You that You are safe and that You listen. Teach me to trust You at all times, including the times when my heart is heavy. Amen.
days.completion_message: You poured out your heart honestly before God, your refuge.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 62:8

days.title: He Will Never Leave You
days.devotion: At the end of Hebrews the writer gives practical guidance, and here he addresses money, calling believers to be content with what they have. Why can believers be free from the grip of wanting more? Not because they have enough saved, but because of a promise: God Himself has said that He will never leave them or abandon them. These words echo God's promises to Jacob, to Israel and to Joshua (Genesis 28:15; Deuteronomy 31:6; Joshua 1:5), now applied to all who belong to Him through Christ. Trust grows when our security rests on God's presence rather than our possessions. Because He has said this, we can say with confidence that the Lord is our helper. Contentment and courage both grow from the same root: God will not abandon His people.
days.reflection: What are you tempted to rely on for security instead of God's promise to never leave you?
days.prayer: Lord, You have said that You will never leave me nor forsake me. Forgive me for looking to money and possessions to make me feel safe. Teach me to be content with what I have, because I have You. You are my helper, and I will trust You with my needs and my future. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to rest your security on God's promise to never leave you.

days.title: I Know the One I Trust
days.devotion: Paul wrote these words from prison, near the end of his life, to his young friend Timothy. He was suffering for the gospel and many had turned away from him (v. 15). Yet he writes that he is not ashamed. His confidence did not come from his circumstances. It came from a Person: Paul knows the One he has believed, and he is convinced that Christ is able to guard what Paul has entrusted to Him until that day. Notice that Paul does not say "what" he believed but "whom." Trust in the end is not about having every answer; it is about knowing the One you trust. Paul had placed his life in Christ's hands, and he was sure Christ would keep it safe until the day of His return. As this Connection Path ends, you can say the same.
days.reflection: What will you commit into God's keeping as you finish this Connection Path, trusting Him to hold it safe?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I know the One I have believed in. You are faithful and able to keep everything I entrust to You. I place my life, my future and the people I love into Your hands again today. When I do not understand, help me to remember who You are. Keep me trusting You until that day. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by committing your life into the keeping of the One you trust.

plans.title: Morning With God
plans.subtitle: Start your day with God's presence.
plans.description: Begin each morning with God in praise, surrender, Scripture and prayer, and carry your day into His hands.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants to turn to God first thing each morning, before the busyness of the day begins
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May each new morning find you turning first to the Lord, offering Him your day, and walking through it with Him.

days.title: Long Before Daylight
days.devotion: Mark 1 describes a full day in Capernaum. Jesus taught in the synagogue, healed Peter's mother-in-law, and then that evening, after sunset, the whole city gathered at the door with the sick and troubled (vv. 32–33). The next morning, long before daylight, He rose, went out to a quiet, deserted place, and prayed there (v. 35). Before the crowds returned, Jesus sought time alone with His Father. When the disciples found Him and told Him that everyone was looking for Him (v. 37), He already knew where He must go next (v. 38). The Son of God did not treat prayer as optional, even after a demanding day. His example is not a rule about the hour on the clock. It is an invitation: before the day's demands reach us, we can turn first to the Father who loves us.
days.reflection: What usually fills the first minutes of your morning, and what would it take to give some of them to God?
days.prayer: Father, thank You for the example of Jesus, who rose early to be alone with You before the crowds came. My mornings are often rushed, and my mind runs ahead to everything I must do. Help me to make room for You first. Meet me in a quiet place, and let my day flow from time spent with You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You began this Connection Path by making room for God at the start of your day.

days.title: Prayer Set in Order
days.devotion: Psalm 5 is David's prayer as he faces people who speak lies and plot against him (vv. 6, 9). He begins by asking the LORD to listen to his words (v. 1), and he calls Him his King and his God (v. 2). Then he makes a settled choice: in the morning he will lay his prayer before God and look up (v. 3). The Hebrew word for laying his prayer before God means to set in order, and it is used elsewhere for laying out an offering. The word for looking up is used elsewhere of a watchman keeping watch, so it suggests waiting expectantly. For David, morning prayer was not a hurried wish but an ordered, hopeful act of trust. We can do the same. We can bring God our day with its pressures, lay it out before Him, and then live the hours ahead watching with hope for His answer.
days.reflection: What do you most need to lay out before God this morning, and how will you watch for His answer today?
days.prayer: My King and my God, I come to You this morning. Hear my voice. I lay before You the day ahead: the tasks, the people, and the worries I carry. I set them in order before You and leave them in Your hands. Help me to look up through this day, watching with hope for Your answer and Your leading. Amen.
days.completion_message: You set your prayer before God and chose to look up for His answer.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 5:3

days.title: I Will Seek You Early
days.devotion: The heading of Psalm 63 tells us David wrote it in the wilderness of Judah. Cut off from the sanctuary and from home, he could have filled his prayer with complaint. Instead he begins by calling God his own God and resolving to seek Him early (v. 1). The dry land around him became a picture of his own soul: his soul thirsts for God, he says, in a land that is dry, worn out and without water. David's deepest need was not water or safety, but God Himself, because God's faithful love is better than life (v. 3). To seek God early means to seek Him first and earnestly, before other things claim our hearts. Our mornings can find us thirsty in many ways: tired, anxious or empty. This psalm invites us to bring that thirst to God first, and to look to Him for what nothing else can supply.
days.reflection: What are you thirsty for this morning, and how can you bring that longing to God before anything else?
days.prayer: O God, You are my God; I will seek You early. You know the dry places in my life and the thirst in my soul that nothing else satisfies. I do not want to run first to my phone, my worries or my plans. I come to You. Your faithful love is better than life, so let my lips praise You today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your thirst to God and sought Him first this morning.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 63:1

days.title: His Faithful Love in the Morning
days.devotion: Psalm 143 is a prayer from a hard place. David's enemy has crushed his life to the ground (v. 3), and he confesses that his spirit is overwhelmed within him (v. 4). Yet in verse 8 he asks for two things in the morning. First, he asks God to let him hear of His faithful love in the morning, because his trust is in Him. Before he asks for direction, he asks to hear again of God's steadfast, covenant love. Second, he asks God to make known to him the path he should walk. Assurance of God's love comes first; guidance follows. This is a healthy order for our mornings too. We often rush to ask God what to do, but David first asks to be reminded of who God is toward him. When we begin the day resting in His faithful love, we can lift up our soul to Him and ask for the way to walk.
days.reflection: Before you ask God for direction today, what do you need to hear again about His love for you?
days.prayer: Lord, let me hear of Your faithful love this morning, for I trust in You. Some days my spirit feels overwhelmed before the day has even begun. Remind me first that Your love for me is faithful and steady. Then show me the way I should walk today, because I lift up my soul to You. Teach me to do Your will. Amen.
days.completion_message: You started your morning by listening for God's love before asking for His direction.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 143:8

days.title: Satisfied Early With His Mercy
days.devotion: Psalm 90 is a prayer of Moses. He reflects on how short human life is: our years pass like a story that is quickly finished (v. 9), and our strength is soon gone (v. 10). He does not stop at sadness. He asks God to teach His people to number their days (v. 12), and then prays that God would satisfy them early with His mercy, so that they can sing for joy and be glad through all their days (v. 14). The Hebrew word here may mean at the start of the day, or soon, before life slips by. Either way, Moses knew that only God's mercy, His steadfast love, could give lasting gladness to lives so brief. We often look for satisfaction later: after the task, after the weekend, after the next success. This prayer asks to be satisfied now, at the beginning, with the mercy of God, so that the whole of life can be lived with joy.
days.reflection: Where are you waiting to be satisfied "later," and how can you ask God to satisfy you with His mercy today?
days.prayer: Eternal God, my days are short and pass so quickly. Teach me to number them wisely. Satisfy me early with Your mercy, so that I do not spend my life chasing what cannot fill me. Let Your steadfast love be enough for me this morning, and give me a gladness that lasts through all my days. Establish the work of my hands today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked God to satisfy you with His mercy at the start of your day.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 90:14

days.title: Joy Comes in the Morning
days.devotion: David wrote Psalm 30 looking back on a time when God rescued him from severe trouble. He cried to the LORD his God for help, and God healed him (v. 2). Then he calls God's people to praise, because of what he has learned about God's ways: God's anger is brief, but His favour brings life (v. 5). Sorrow is real. David does not deny the night of weeping, but he knows it is not God's last word for His people: tears may linger through the night, yet morning brings joy. This verse is not a promise that every trouble will lift by tomorrow. It describes the shape of God's dealings with those who belong to Him: sorrow is temporary, while His favour lasts. Each new morning can remind us that the night does not go on forever, and that God's favour is the deeper reality we wake into.
days.reflection: What sorrow or heaviness are you carrying into this morning, and how can you hand it to God with hope?
days.prayer: O LORD my God, You know the weeping I have known in the night. Thank You that sorrow is not Your final word and that in Your favour is life. This morning I bring You what is heavy in my heart. I do not ask to pretend it away, but to trust You with it. Turn my mourning into praise in Your time. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your sorrow to God this morning and chose to hope in His favour.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 30:5

days.title: Awake, My Soul
days.devotion: The heading of Psalm 57 links it to the time David hid from Saul in a cave. His soul is "among lions" (v. 4), and his enemies have set a trap for his feet (v. 6). Yet in the middle of danger he declares, twice over, that his heart is steadfast and fixed on God, and that he will sing and give praise (v. 7). A fixed heart is steady and settled, anchored on God rather than on circumstances. Then David speaks to himself, calling his soul, and his harp and lyre, to wake, for he himself will rise at dawn (v. 8). He would wake the dawn with praise rather than let fear wake him. His confidence did not rest on the cave becoming safe, but on God, whose mercy reaches as high as the heavens (v. 10). As this first week ends, we can choose the same: to fix our hearts on God and make praise one of the first things we say each day.
days.reflection: What is one thing you could do tomorrow morning to make praise one of the first things you say?
days.prayer: O God, my heart is set on You. When fears crowd in and my circumstances feel unsafe, steady my heart in Your mercy. Wake me with praise instead of worry. Tomorrow morning, let one of my first words be thanks to You. Be exalted above the heavens, and let Your glory be over all the earth and above everything in my life. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to fix your heart on God and to wake with praise.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 57:7–8

days.title: Sing of His Mercy in the Morning
days.devotion: The heading of Psalm 59 links it to the night Saul sent men to watch David's house and kill him (1 Samuel 19:11). Through the night his enemies prowled the city and growled like dogs (v. 14). David could have spent the morning counting threats. Instead he resolves to sing of God's power, and to sing aloud of His mercy when morning comes (v. 16). Notice his reason: God has been his fortress and his refuge whenever trouble came. His praise was rooted in what God had already shown Himself to be. Morning praise is not pretending that everything is fine. It is a deliberate turning of attention from the night's fears to the character of God, His power and His mercy. When we begin the day that way, we carry into the hours ahead a truer picture of who holds them.
days.reflection: As your day begins, do you most need to praise God for His power or for His mercy, and why?
days.prayer: O my strength, I will sing to You this morning. You have been my defence and my refuge, even in days of trouble. I turn my attention from the fears of the night to Your power and Your mercy. Let praise be the first thing on my lips today, and let it shape how I see everything that follows. Amen.
days.completion_message: You started your day by praising God for His power and mercy.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 59:16

days.title: Hoping in His Word
days.devotion: Psalm 119 is a long, careful meditation on God's word. In verses 145–152 the writer cries to God with all his heart (v. 145) while people who pursue wicked schemes draw near (v. 150). He tells us when he prayed: he was up before the dawn, crying for help, with his hope set on God's word (v. 147). He adds that his eyes were awake before each watch of the night, so that he could meditate on God's word (v. 148). For this believer, early prayer and God's word belonged together. He did not only pour out his needs; he anchored his hope in what God had said. Our mornings can follow the same pattern: speaking to God in prayer and listening to Him in Scripture, letting His promises, not our fears, set the tone for the day.
days.reflection: What would help you read even a few verses of Scripture before the rest of your day begins?
days.prayer: Lord, I cry to You with my whole heart this morning. Before my day fills with other voices, let me hear Yours. My hope is in Your word. Open it to me as I read, and let Your promises steady me more than my fears or my plans. You are near, O Lord, and all Your commandments are truth. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to anchor your morning hope in God's word.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 119:147

days.title: An Ear Awakened Each Morning
days.devotion: Isaiah 50:4–9 is one of the passages where the Servant of the LORD speaks. Christians have long seen these words fulfilled in Jesus, the one who offered his back to those who struck him (v. 6) and set his face like flint (v. 7). Here the Servant describes the secret of his ministry: the Lord wakes him morning after morning, rousing his ear to listen as a learner listens. Before He spoke a timely word to sustain the weary, He first listened. Morning by morning the Lord GOD opened His ear, and He did not rebel or turn back (v. 5). This is first a picture of Christ's perfect obedience. Yet it also gives His followers a pattern. A morning with God is not only speaking; it is listening. As we let God speak to us through His word, we are better prepared to bring a kind and timely word to the weary people we meet.
days.reflection: Who is one weary person you will meet today, and what might God want you to hear before you speak to them?
days.prayer: Lord God, thank You for Jesus, who listened to You morning by morning and never turned away. Waken my ear today. Quiet my own noise so that I can hear You in Your word. Then give me a timely word for the weary people I will meet, words that come from You and not only from me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You made room to listen to God before speaking to others.

days.title: Bread for Each Morning
days.devotion: Soon after leaving Egypt, Israel murmured in the wilderness, afraid they would die of hunger (vv. 2–3). God answered with grace: He would rain down bread from heaven for them (v. 4). Each morning manna lay on the ground, and the people were told to gather what they needed for that day. Some tried to keep it until the next morning, and it swarmed with worms and smelled foul (v. 20). So each morning they gathered it, each one as much as he would eat (v. 21). God was teaching His people to trust Him one day at a time; He said He would test them this way (v. 4). The manna was a unique provision for Israel in the wilderness, not a formula for how God will meet every need. But its lesson reaches us: life with God is lived daily. We come back to Him each morning for fresh grace. Jesus later called Himself the bread of life (John 6:35).
days.reflection: In what area of your life are you trying to live on yesterday's strength instead of coming to God fresh today?
days.prayer: Faithful God, You fed Your people in the wilderness morning by morning. I confess that I often try to store up strength for tomorrow or lean on yesterday's faith. Teach me to come to You each day. Give me what I need for today, and help me trust You with tomorrow. Thank You for Jesus, the bread of life. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to God for today's grace instead of leaning on yesterday's.

days.title: Seek First His Kingdom
days.devotion: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus speaks to ordinary people worried about food, drink and clothing (v. 31). He points them to the birds and the lilies, and reminds them that their heavenly Father knows they need all these things (v. 32). Then He gives them a better focus: to seek first God's kingdom and His righteousness (v. 33). To seek His kingdom is to put God's rule and His ways first in our desires and choices. Jesus is not promising wealth; He is assuring His disciples that the Father cares for His children's real needs. He adds that they should not worry about tomorrow (v. 34). Each day has enough trouble of its own. A morning with God is a good moment to decide again what comes first, and to leave tomorrow in the Father's hands while we live faithfully today.
days.reflection: What worry about tomorrow is competing with seeking God first today?
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, You know what I need before I ask. Forgive me for the way my worries so easily take first place. Today I choose to seek Your kingdom and Your righteousness first. I leave tomorrow with You. Help me live this one day faithfully, trusting that You will care for me as Your child. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to put God's kingdom first and to leave tomorrow with Him.

days.title: An Undivided Heart
days.devotion: Psalm 86 is a prayer of David from a day of trouble (v. 7). He is "poor and needy" (v. 1) and cries to God daily (v. 3). His confidence rests on who God is: the Lord is good and ready to forgive, rich in mercy (v. 5). Out of that trust comes a prayer of surrender: he asks the LORD to teach him His way, promises to walk in His truth, and asks God to unite his heart to fear His name (v. 11). He asks to be taught before he promises to walk, and he asks God to make his scattered heart one. He does not offer God a perfect heart; he offers a willing one and asks God to unite it. This is a fitting way to give Him the day ahead. Each morning we can place our divided hearts and our plans in His hands, ask Him to teach us, and choose to walk in His truth.
days.reflection: Where is your heart most divided as this day begins, and what would it look like to give that part of your day to God?
days.prayer: Lord, You are good, ready to forgive, and rich in mercy. This morning I give You my day. Teach me Your way, and I will walk in Your truth. You know how easily my heart is pulled in many directions. Unite my heart to fear Your name, so that my choices today come from one desire: to honour You. I will praise You with all my heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You offered God your day and asked Him to unite your heart.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 86:11

days.title: Commit Your Works to Him
days.devotion: Proverbs 16 opens with reminders that God is sovereign over our plans: people make plans in their hearts, but the fitting reply on their tongue comes from the LORD (v. 1). And the LORD weighs the spirit (v. 2); He sees our motives. Then comes the counsel: commit what you do to the LORD, and your plans will be made firm (v. 3). The Hebrew word for "commit" pictures rolling a heavy load off your own shoulders onto someone else. Wisdom does not mean refusing to plan, but placing our plans and work in God's hands. When we do, our purposes are made steady, because they rest on Him rather than on our own strength. This proverb is a general truth about life with God, not a promise that every plan will succeed as we hope. Morning is a good time to roll the day's work onto the Lord before we begin it.
days.reflection: Which task or plan for today do you most need to roll onto the Lord before you begin?
days.prayer: Lord, You see my heart and weigh my motives. Before I start today's work, I commit it to You. I roll off my shoulders the tasks I am anxious about and the plans I cannot control. Make my thoughts steady by resting them on You. Where my plans are not Yours, redirect them, and let my work honour You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You committed your day's work into God's hands.

days.title: Words and Thoughts That Please Him
days.devotion: Psalm 19 begins with the heavens declaring God's glory (v. 1), and then praises God's law, which is perfect and revives the soul (v. 7). Seeing God's glory and holiness, David becomes aware of his own heart: no one can fully discern his own errors, so he asks God to cleanse him from hidden faults (v. 12). He ends with a prayer that what he says and what he ponders in his heart would be pleasing in the LORD's sight (v. 14). David knows that words spring from the heart, and that both matter to God. He also knows he cannot manage this alone, so he calls on the LORD as his rock and his redeemer. As we step into a day full of conversations, messages and inner thoughts, this prayer is a simple way to invite God into all of it.
days.reflection: Which conversation or situation today will most test your words, and what would words that please God look like there?
