days.prayer: O LORD, my rock and my redeemer, I give You my words and my thoughts today. Cleanse me from faults I cannot even see. In the conversations ahead, guard my tongue from careless or harsh words. Let what I say, and what I dwell on in my heart, be acceptable in Your sight. Amen.
days.completion_message: You invited God into your words and thoughts for the day ahead.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 19:14

days.title: Known in Every Moment
days.devotion: In Psalm 139 David marvels at how completely God knows him: the LORD has searched him and knows him (v. 1). God knows when he sits down to rest and when he gets up, the ordinary moments of each day. He understands David's thoughts from far away, before they are spoken, and is familiar with all his ways (vv. 2–3). This is not the watching of a harsh inspector. As the psalm goes on, David finds comfort in it: wherever he goes, God's hand will lead him and His right hand will hold him (v. 10). As you rise this morning, you are already known. Every place you will go today, every task and conversation, is already familiar to God. You do not walk into this day unseen. You can go into it honestly, knowing that the One who knows you best also leads you and holds you.
days.reflection: Which part of your ordinary day do you tend to forget that God sees and cares about?
days.prayer: O LORD, You have searched me and You know me. You know when I sit down to rest and when I get up, and You understand my thoughts before I speak them. Thank You that I am not unseen today. Lead me with Your hand through every ordinary moment, and hold me with Your right hand when I feel weak. Amen.
days.completion_message: You began your day remembering that God knows you and leads you.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 139:2–3

days.title: The Lord Always Before Me
days.devotion: Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust. David asks God to keep him safe, because he has put his trust in Him (v. 1), and rejoices that the LORD Himself is his portion and inheritance (v. 5). Then he says that he has set the LORD always before him; because the LORD is at his right hand, he will not be shaken (v. 8). To set the LORD before us is a deliberate act of attention, keeping Him in view as we go through the day. The confidence that follows rests on God being at our right hand, the place of a helper and protector. Peter later quoted this psalm about the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 2:25–28), so its fullest meaning is found in Christ. Yet it also shapes our days. We cannot always change what happens, but we can choose each morning to set the Lord before us, and to turn our attention back to Him again and again.
days.reflection: What simple reminder could help you turn your attention back to the Lord several times today?
days.prayer: Lord, I set You before me today. You are my portion and my trust. When I get busy and forget You, draw my attention back to You. Because You are at my right hand, keep me steady when things shake around me. Show me the path of life, and let me find joy in Your presence. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to keep the Lord before you through the day.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 16:8

days.title: Everything in Jesus' Name
days.devotion: Paul writes to believers in Colossae who have been raised with Christ (v. 1). Because their life is now hidden with Christ in God (v. 3), everything about how they live is changing. Here he gives a wide-reaching principle: whatever they say or do, they are to do it all in Jesus' name, thanking God the Father through Him (v. 17). To do something in Jesus' name is to do it as one who belongs to Him, in a way that fits His character and honours Him. No part of the day is left out: speech and action, work and rest, the big and the small. And thanksgiving runs through it all. We do not live this way to become His; we live this way because we already are His. Carrying His name into the day turns ordinary tasks into acts of devotion.
days.reflection: What ordinary task today could you do consciously in Jesus' name, with thanks to God?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I belong to You. Today I want everything I say and do to fit Your name. Remind me of You in the small moments as well as the big ones. Keep a thankful heart in me as I work, speak and rest. Let my ordinary tasks honour You, and let me give thanks to the Father through You in all of it. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to carry the name of Jesus into everything you do today.

days.title: Working for the Lord
days.devotion: This verse was first written to servants, people with little control over their work or their masters (v. 22). Paul does not pretend their situation was easy. But he tells them they can bring a new purpose to their work: whatever their task, they can put their whole heart into it, serving the Lord rather than people. The Greek phrase Paul uses here means from the soul, with the whole heart. Their work was not only for an earthly master who might never notice, but for the Lord who sees everything: it is the Lord Christ they are serving (v. 24). The same truth reaches into our days, whether our work is paid or unpaid, noticed or unnoticed: caring for children, studying, office work, cleaning, or looking after a relative. Doing our work for the Lord does not make hard work easy, but it gives it meaning and frees us from living only for people's approval.
days.reflection: Which part of your work today feels unnoticed, and how would doing it for the Lord change the way you approach it?
days.prayer: Lord Christ, You see the work I will do today, even the parts no one else notices. Help me to do it heartily, as for You and not only for people. When I feel unappreciated, remind me that I serve You. Free me from needing the approval of others, and let my work today be an offering to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You offered your work to the Lord, whether or not anyone else notices it.

days.title: If the Lord Wills
days.devotion: James pictures traders confidently planning their year: which city they will go to, how long they will stay, and how much they will gain (v. 13). Planning itself is not wrong. The problem is planning as though God had no part in it. James reminds them that they do not know what tomorrow will bring, and asks what their life really is. It is like a mist, visible for a little while and then gone (v. 14). Instead, they should say that if it is the Lord's will, they will live and carry out this Connection Path or that one (v. 15). This is not a phrase to attach mechanically to every sentence. It is a humble posture of the heart: holding our plans with open hands, trusting that our days belong to God. Beginning the morning this way frees us to plan wisely and work hard, while leaving the outcome with Him.
days.reflection: Which plan for today or this week do you need to hold with open hands, entrusting it to the Lord's will?
days.prayer: Lord, my life is in Your hands. I have plans for today and for the days ahead, but I do not know what tomorrow holds. Forgive me for the times I have planned as if You had no part in my life. I hold my plans with open hands. If it is Your will, I will live and do what I have planned. Let Your will be done in my day. Amen.
days.completion_message: You placed your plans for the day under God's will.

days.title: Your Going Out and Coming In
days.devotion: Psalm 121 is one of the Songs of Ascents, likely sung by pilgrims travelling up to Jerusalem. The road was long and could be dangerous, and the traveller asks where his help will come from (v. 1). The answer: his help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth (v. 2). The LORD "will not slumber" (v. 3). The psalm closes by saying that the LORD will keep him from all evil and keep his soul; the LORD will keep his going out and his coming in, from now on and forever (vv. 7–8). This does not mean believers will never face hardship; God's people in Scripture often suffered. It means the LORD keeps watch over our lives and souls, and nothing can finally undo what He keeps. Every morning we go out, and every evening we come in. As this Connection Path ends, you can begin each new day under the care of the One who keeps you.
days.reflection: As this Connection Path ends, what will help you keep beginning your mornings with God in the weeks ahead?
days.prayer: LORD, my help comes from You, the Maker of heaven and earth. Thank You that You never slumber or sleep. As I go out today and come in tonight, keep my soul. Thank You for these mornings spent with You. Help me keep turning to You at the start of each day, and keep my going out and my coming in, now and always. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by entrusting your going out and coming in to the Lord.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 121:7–8

plans.title: A Month With God
plans.subtitle: Build a lasting connection.
plans.description: Walk through the Bible's big story of God pursuing people, and see your own connection with Him inside it.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants to see the whole Bible story and build a lasting daily connection with God
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep walking with the God who has pursued you from the beginning, and who will one day dwell with His people forever.

days.title: Made in His Image
days.devotion: The Bible's story opens with God creating. After light, land, seas, plants and animals, God does something different, saying, Let us make humankind in our image, to be like us (v. 26). Then comes our verse: God created humanity in His own image; in God's image He created them, male and female. Chapter 2 adds a tender picture. The LORD God shaped the man from the dust of the ground and breathed life into his nostrils (2:7). Of all creation, only people are said to bear God's image. We were made to reflect Him and to live in relationship with Him. This is where your story with God begins too. You are not an accident or an afterthought. Before you ever looked for God, He made you, and He made you to know Him.
days.reflection: How would your day look different if you truly believed you were made on purpose to know God?
days.prayer: Creator God, thank You that You made me in Your image. I did not make myself, and I am not here by accident. You formed me and gave me breath so that I could know You. Forgive me for the times I have lived as if I belonged only to myself. As I begin this month with You, open my eyes to see that I was made for You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You began this month by remembering that God made you to know Him.

days.title: Where Are You?
days.devotion: Genesis 3 tells how the first man and woman listened to the serpent and ate what God had forbidden. The result was immediate: shame, fear and hiding. When they heard the sound of God moving through the garden in the evening breeze, they hid from Him among the trees (v. 8). Then God called out: "Where are you?" The all-knowing God did not need information. His question was a call, inviting Adam to come out and face what had happened. Sin had broken the relationship, but God did not wait for Adam to come looking. He came looking for him. That call echoes through the whole Bible. When we hide from God, through shame, busyness or silence, He is the one who calls first. You can answer Him honestly today, just as you are.
days.reflection: In what area of your life have you been hiding from God, and what would it look like to answer His call honestly today?
days.prayer: Lord God, like Adam I have sometimes hidden from You. Sometimes it is shame, sometimes it is fear, and sometimes I simply stay busy so I do not have to face You. Thank You that You still call to me. Here I am, Lord. I come out from hiding and bring You my heart as it really is. Amen.
days.completion_message: You answered God's call and came out of hiding.

days.title: The First Promise
days.devotion: Before God described the painful results of sin to Adam and Eve, He spoke to the serpent. He announced a lasting conflict between the serpent and the woman, and between the serpent's offspring and hers. Then comes a surprising word: her offspring would strike the serpent's head, while the serpent would strike his heel. The serpent would wound, but the woman's offspring would deal the crushing blow. Christians have long seen here the first hint of the gospel. The New Testament shows it fulfilled in Jesus, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who came to destroy what the devil had done (1 John 3:8). Notice when this promise was given: on the very day of humanity's failure. God did not wait for people to put themselves right. From the start, His answer to our sin was a promise of rescue, and He kept it.
days.reflection: What failure makes you feel furthest from God right now, and how does His promise on the day of the first failure speak to it?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that on the day sin entered the world You already spoke a promise of rescue. You did not give up on us. Thank You for sending Jesus to defeat the enemy and break the power of sin. When my failures make me feel far from You, remind me that Your answer to sin is grace. I trust Your promise today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You held on to God's first promise of rescue.

days.title: Called to Be a Blessing
days.devotion: After the flood and the tower of Babel, the story narrows to one man. God told Abram to leave his country, his relatives and his father's household, and go to a land God would show him. With the call came a string of promises: God would make him into a great nation and bless him. God took the initiative. He chose Abram by grace and gave him a future he could not yet see. And the blessing was never meant to stop with him: through him all the families of the earth would be blessed. Paul later saw the gospel announced here beforehand (Galatians 3:8), reaching the nations through Christ. If you know God today, you share in that promise. God's call still involves trust and sometimes leaving things behind, but it always begins with His grace.
days.reflection: What is God asking you to trust Him with, even though you cannot yet see where it leads?
days.prayer: Lord, You called Abram by grace and promised to bless the nations through him. Thank You that Your blessing has reached me in Christ. Give me Abram's willingness to trust You when I cannot see the whole road. Help me let go of what holds me back, and make my life a blessing to the people around me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to trust God's call, even without seeing the whole road.

days.title: Taking God at His Word
days.devotion: Years had passed since God's promise, and Abram was still childless. In Genesis 15 he told God so honestly, asking what God could give him while he remained childless (v. 2). God took him outside and told him to look up at the sky and count the stars, if he could, and then promised that his offspring would be just as many (v. 5). Nothing in Abram's circumstances had changed, yet Abram trusted the LORD, and the LORD counted his faith as righteousness. Abram was not declared right with God because of a perfect record, but because he trusted God's word. Paul uses this very verse to show that we are made right with God through faith, not by our works (Romans 4:3–5). A relationship with God rests on trusting Him, not on proving ourselves. Like Abram, you can bring God your honest questions and still take Him at His word.
days.reflection: What promise of God do you find hardest to believe right now, and what would it mean to take Him at His word today?
days.prayer: Lord God, like Abram I sometimes look at my circumstances and wonder how Your word can be true. Thank You that You welcome my honest questions. Thank You that I am made right with You by trusting You, not by proving myself. Today I choose to believe what You have said. Lord, I believe; help my unbelief. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to take God at His word today.

days.title: God in This Place
days.devotion: Jacob was running for his life. He had deceived his father and taken his brother Esau's blessing, and now Esau wanted to kill him (27:41–43). Alone on the road, with a stone for a pillow, he dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, with the LORD standing above it. God did not reject him. He renewed the promise given to Abraham and said that He was with Jacob and would watch over him wherever he went. This promise was spoken to Jacob about his own journey and his return to the land. Yet it shows God's heart: He meets people who do not deserve it, in places they do not expect. Jacob awoke and said that the LORD was truly in this place, and he had not known it (v. 16). Jesus gives His followers a similar assurance, promising to be with them always (Matthew 28:20).
days.reflection: Where in your everyday life do you most need to recognize that God is with you?
days.prayer: Lord, You met Jacob when he was running and alone, and You spoke grace instead of rejection. Thank You that You meet people in places they do not expect. Open my eyes to see You in my ordinary days and in my hard places. Like Jacob, I want to recognize that You are truly in this place. Thank You that You are with me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked for God's presence in your own ordinary place.

days.title: God Meant It for Good
days.devotion: Joseph's brothers had sold him into slavery out of jealousy. Years of suffering followed, including false accusation and prison. Yet God raised Joseph to power in Egypt, where he saved many lives during a severe famine, his own family among them. After their father Jacob died, the brothers feared Joseph would finally take revenge. Instead he wept and told them that they had planned evil against him, but God had planned it for good, in order to do what was now happening: keeping many people alive. Joseph did not pretend the wrong was small. He called it evil. But he had come to see that God had been at work through the long, painful years, keeping His promise to Abraham's family. This is Joseph's testimony, not a formula that explains every sorrow. Still, it shows that God does not abandon His people in their darkest chapters, even when His purpose is hidden for a time.
days.reflection: What painful chapter of your story do you need to entrust to God, even if you cannot yet see His purpose in it?
days.prayer: Faithful God, Joseph's story reminds me that You were at work even when he was betrayed and forgotten. I bring You the painful parts of my own story. I do not understand them all, but I trust that You have not left me. Help me, like Joseph, to let go of bitterness and to answer wrong with kindness. Amen.
days.completion_message: You entrusted a painful chapter of your story to God.

days.title: I AM
days.devotion: Centuries later, Abraham's descendants were slaves in Egypt. God told Moses He had seen their affliction and heard their cry (3:7). From a burning bush He sent Moses to lead His people out. Moses asked what he should say if the people asked God's name. God answered by calling Himself I AM WHO I AM, and told Moses to say that "I AM" had sent him to them. This name speaks of a God who simply is: He depends on nothing, does not change, and is always present. In the next verse He ties it to His covenant name, the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (v. 15). The God who stands above all things is the same God who keeps His promises to people. Jesus later spoke of Himself in these terms, declaring that before Abraham came to be, "I am" (John 8:58). This unchanging God invites you to know Him personally.
days.reflection: Which part of your life feels most unsteady right now, and how does knowing God as the unchanging I AM change how you face it?
days.prayer: LORD, You are the great I AM. You never change, You depend on nothing, and You are always present. Yet You heard the cry of Your people and came to rescue them. Thank You that the God above all things wants to be known by me. Steady my heart in the unsteady places of my life, and help me rest in who You are. Amen.
days.completion_message: You fixed your trust on the unchanging God who is.

days.title: I Will Be Your God
days.devotion: Moses' first visit to Pharaoh made things worse. The slaves' work became harder, and even Moses complained to God (5:22–23). In reply, God repeated His promises. He would bring them out, rid them of bondage, and redeem them with His arm stretched out in power (v. 6). Then He revealed the goal of it all: He would take them as His own people and be their God. Freedom from Egypt was not the final aim; belonging to God was. The people were too discouraged to listen at first (v. 9), but God's purpose did not depend on their feelings. This promise, that God will be their God and they will be His people, echoes through the whole Bible. God does not rescue people only to leave them on their own. He rescues them to bring them to Himself, and that is still His purpose in Christ.
days.reflection: When you think about what God has saved you from, how might it change your day to remember that He also saved you for Himself?
days.prayer: Lord, You rescued Your people from slavery so that they would belong to You. Thank You that You have not only saved me from something, but for Yourself. When I am discouraged, like Israel, and find it hard to listen, keep speaking Your promises to me. Help me to live today as one who belongs to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that God has saved you for Himself.

days.title: God Among His People
days.devotion: At Mount Sinai, after bringing Israel out of Egypt, God gave Moses detailed instructions for the tabernacle, the tent at the center of the camp. Page after page describes its curtains, altar and priests. Then God tells us why it mattered: He would live among the Israelites and be their God. He adds that He brought them out of Egypt so that He might dwell among them. The rescue from Egypt had a destination. The holy God who had come down on the mountain wanted to live in the middle of His people. Yet the tabernacle also showed that sin had to be dealt with before sinners could draw near, through sacrifices, priests and a veil. God's desire to dwell with His people runs through Scripture and finds its answer in Jesus. The God you are getting to know this month is a God who wants to be near.
days.reflection: Knowing that God desires to dwell with His people, what part of your daily life do you most want to bring before Him?
days.prayer: Holy God, You brought Israel out of Egypt so that You could dwell among them. Thank You that You are not a distant God, but One who desires to be near His people. Thank You that through Jesus the way to You has been opened. I bring my daily life before You, the ordinary parts and the hidden ones. Be my God in all of it. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your daily life before the God who desires to dwell with His people.

days.title: With All Your Heart
days.devotion: Before Israel entered the promised land, Moses gathered them to remind them of all God had done and to prepare them to live as His people. At the center of his words stands this call: Israel must listen, because the LORD their God is the one and only LORD. Surrounded by nations that worshipped many gods, Israel was to know that there is only one God, and He had made Himself their God. Then comes the response: they are to love the LORD their God with their whole heart, their whole soul and all their strength. Notice the order. God first rescued them; then He called for their love. Jesus named this the first and most important commandment (Matthew 22:38). Loving God is not a duty we perform to be accepted. It is the wholehearted answer to a God who has already made us His own. He wants all of us, not just a part.
days.reflection: Which part of your life, whether your heart, your soul or your strength, have you been keeping back from God?
days.prayer: LORD our God, You alone are God. You have loved me and made me Your own, and I want to love You in return with all my heart, soul and strength. Show me the parts of my life that I have been keeping back from You. Unite my heart to love You fully, not out of fear or duty, but as an answer to Your love. Amen.
days.completion_message: You offered God your whole heart in answer to His love.

days.title: Choose This Day
days.devotion: Israel had crossed the Jordan and settled in the land God promised. Near the end of his life, Joshua gathered the tribes at Shechem and retold their story: God called Abraham, rescued them from Egypt, and gave them the land (vv. 2–13). Then he called for a response: they must choose that very day whom they would serve. Some still held on to the gods of their ancestors or of the nations around them (v. 14). Joshua made his own choice clear: he and his household would serve the LORD. A relationship with God is not something we simply inherit or drift into. It is a choice we renew, grounded in what He has already done for us. Every day, other things quietly compete for our trust and devotion. Joshua's words invite us to decide again who will have our loyalty.
days.reflection: What is quietly competing with God for your loyalty, and what will you choose about it today?
days.prayer: Lord, You have done so much for me, just as You did for Israel. Today I choose again to serve You. Show me the things that quietly compete for my trust and devotion, and help me put them away. As for me and my household, we will serve You, LORD. Give me a faithful heart to follow You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose again whom you will serve.

days.title: Your God, My God
days.devotion: In the days of the judges, a famine drove an Israelite family to Moab. There Naomi lost her husband and both sons. Returning home, she urged her Moabite daughters-in-law to go back to their own people. Orpah went back to her people and her gods (v. 15). But Ruth clung to Naomi. Wherever Naomi went, Ruth said, she would go; Naomi's people would be her people, and Naomi's God her God. Ruth was a foreigner with no claim on Israel's God, yet she chose to trust Him. Boaz later spoke of her as one who had come to take refuge under the wings of the LORD (2:12). And God welcomed her. She became the great-grandmother of King David and is named in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Ruth's story shows that God's family is open to outsiders who turn to Him.
days.reflection: What part of your background or past makes you feel like an outsider with God, and how does Ruth's story speak to it?
days.prayer: God of Israel, thank You for welcoming Ruth, a foreigner who chose to trust You. Thank You that Your family is open to all who turn to You, including me. Where I feel like an outsider, remind me that I am welcome under Your wings. I say with Ruth that Your people will be my people, and You will be my God. Amen.
days.completion_message: You claimed God as your God, just as Ruth did.

days.title: After His Own Heart
days.devotion: Saul, Israel's first king, had been told to wait for Samuel before the sacrifice was offered at Gilgal. Under pressure, with his army slipping away, he went ahead without him (vv. 8–12). Samuel told him plainly that he had not kept the command the LORD his God had given him (v. 13). Then came a sobering word: the LORD had already sought out someone after His own heart. Notice who was seeking. God was looking for a king whose heart would be turned toward Him. When Samuel later went to anoint that king, God reminded him that people judge by what they see on the outside, while the LORD sees the heart (16:7). He chose David, the youngest son, who was out keeping the sheep. David was far from perfect, as tomorrow's reading shows, but his heart kept turning back to God. God is not impressed by outward show. He sees your heart completely, and He values a heart honestly turned toward Him.
days.reflection: Where are you more concerned with how things look than with whether your heart is turned toward God?
days.prayer: Lord, You see what others cannot see, and You know my heart completely. Thank You that I do not need to impress You or perform for You. Search my heart and show me where I have cared more about appearances than about You. Turn my heart toward You, and make it a heart that keeps returning to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought God your heart, not just your appearance.

days.title: A Clean Heart
days.devotion: David, the man God chose, later fell badly. He committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged for her husband's death (2 Samuel 11). When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David wrote this psalm. He made no excuses, confessing that it was against God, and God alone, that he had sinned (v. 4). Then he asked for what only God could give: that God would create a clean heart in him and make his spirit new and steady. David knew his deepest problem was not only what he had done, but what was inside him. He pleaded not to be sent away from God's presence, and asked God to give back the joy of His salvation. Sin damages our fellowship with God, but it does not have to be the end of the story. The way back begins with honest confession and rests on God's mercy (v. 1). He is able to make a heart new.
days.reflection: What do you need to confess honestly to God today, so that you can ask Him to renew your heart?
days.prayer: Merciful God, like David I need a clean heart. I will not hide or excuse my sin; I confess it to You now. Wash me, and make my spirit steady and true again. Do not send me away from Your presence. Give me back the joy of Your salvation, and hold me up by Your Spirit, so that I can walk closely with You again. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought honest confession to God and asked for a clean heart.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 51:10

days.title: The Beginning of Wisdom
days.devotion: Proverbs was gathered to teach God's people how to live well in God's world. In chapter 9, Wisdom is pictured as a woman who has prepared a feast and calls the simple to come in (vv. 1–6). At the heart of her invitation stands this verse: wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, and knowing the Holy One is understanding. To fear the LORD is not to cower before Him in terror. It is deep reverence, taking God seriously as God, and letting that shape every choice. True wisdom does not start with cleverness or experience; it starts with a right relationship to Him. Notice too that it is paired with knowing the Holy One. Wisdom is not only information about God; it grows from knowing Him. As you seek His guidance today, begin by honoring who He is.
days.reflection: What decision are you facing where honoring God first would change the way you choose?
days.prayer: Holy LORD, You are the beginning of all true wisdom. I want to take You seriously as God in every part of my life. As I face the choices before me, teach me to honor You first. Help me to know You more deeply, not just to know about You. Give me an understanding heart that grows from reverence and trust. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to begin your decisions with reverence for God.

days.title: Wounded for Us
days.devotion: Isaiah spoke, centuries before Christ, of a coming Servant of the LORD. In chapter 53 this Servant is despised and rejected, yet He suffers for others: He was wounded because of our rebellion and crushed because of our sins. The chapter is honest about our part: all of us have wandered off like sheep, each one turning to go our own way. Then comes the astonishing exchange: the LORD has put all our sin on Him. The New Testament applies these words to Jesus (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:24–25). The broken relationship between God and people would not be repaired by us finding our own way back. It would be repaired by Someone carrying our sin for us. When you wonder how you could ever be at peace with God, look here: He bore the punishment that made our peace with God.
days.reflection: Where have you been going your own way, and what does it mean to you that your sin was laid on Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You were wounded and crushed because of my sins. Like a sheep, I have gone astray and turned to my own way. Thank You for carrying what I could never carry. Thank You that my peace with God was bought by Your suffering. Seek me when I wander, my Shepherd, and keep me close to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked to the One who carried your sin.

days.title: An Everlasting Love
days.devotion: Jeremiah served God during Judah's darkest years, warning of judgment and then seeing Jerusalem fall and the people carried into exile. Yet chapters 30–33 are full of hope. Here the LORD speaks to Israel, recalling how His people met with grace in the desert (v. 2). Then He says that He has loved them with an everlasting love, and so has drawn them to Himself with faithful kindness. These words were first spoken to a broken, scattered nation, with a promise of restoration. God's love for them had not ended because of their failure. It reached back further than their sin, and so it could outlast it. The New Testament shows this same faithful love reaching us in Christ, a love from which nothing can separate God's children (Romans 8:38–39). God's love is not a feeling that comes and goes. It is steady, and it draws people back to Him.
days.reflection: When have you doubted that God's love for you could last, and how does this verse speak to that doubt?
days.prayer: LORD, You told Your scattered people that You loved them with an everlasting love. Thank You that in Christ that same faithful love has reached me. When I feel that my failures have worn out Your patience, remind me that Your love does not come and go. Draw me to Yourself with Your faithful kindness, and help me rest in it today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned your thoughts to God's everlasting love.

days.title: A New Heart
days.devotion: Ezekiel was a priest carried into exile in Babylon. He explained that the exile came because Israel had defiled the land and profaned God's holy name (vv. 17–23). Their problem ran deep: hearts hardened like stone. Yet God promised to act for the sake of His own name. He would cleanse them (v. 25) and do what they could not do for themselves. He would give them a new heart and put a new spirit within them. He would even put His own Spirit within them (v. 27). This promise was spoken to Israel, looking toward their restoration. The New Testament shows God giving new life by His Spirit to all who trust in Christ (Titus 3:5). Real change in our relationship with God does not begin with trying harder. It begins with God giving what we lack: a new heart that can love Him and follow Him.
days.reflection: Where does your heart feel hard or cold toward God, and how will you ask Him today for the change only He can give?
days.prayer: Lord God, You promised Your people a new heart and a new spirit. I cannot change my heart by myself. Where my heart has grown hard or cold toward You, soften it. Take away what is stony and give me a heart that is alive to You. Fill me with Your Spirit, and help me walk in Your ways. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked God for the change only He can give.

days.title: God With Us
days.devotion: After the prophets came centuries of waiting. Then an angel appeared to Joseph, who was engaged to Mary and had learned she was expecting a child. The angel told him the child was from the Holy Spirit and was to be named Jesus, because He would rescue His people from their sins (v. 21). Matthew then shows that this fulfilled the prophet Isaiah's words: a virgin would conceive and give birth to a son, and he would be called "Emmanuel," which means "God with us." All through the Old Testament, God had drawn near to His people: in a garden, at a burning bush, in a tabernacle. Now He came nearer than ever, as a human child. In Jesus, God did not only send a message. He came Himself. The God who has pursued people from the beginning came to be with us.
days.reflection: How would your day look different if you remembered that in Jesus, God has come to be with you?
days.prayer: Father, thank You for sending Jesus, Emmanuel, God with us. You did not stay far away or only send messages from a distance. You came Yourself to save us from our sins. Thank You that through Jesus I can know You. Help me to live today aware that You have come near, and to trust You in everything. Amen.
days.completion_message: You welcomed the truth that in Jesus, God came to be with us.

days.title: He Lived Among Us
days.devotion: John begins his Gospel with the Word, who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made (vv. 1–3). Then he writes an astonishing sentence: the Word became flesh and made His home among us. The Greek verb here, which many English Bibles render "dwelt" or "lived", is related to the word for a tent, and many commentators hear in it an echo of the tabernacle where God's glory rested among Israel. Now God's glory was seen in a person, full of grace and truth. The apostle adds that no one has ever seen God, but the only Son has shown us who He is (v. 18). If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus. In Him we see God's holiness and His kindness together. Knowing God is not guessing about a distant being. It is coming to know Jesus, who came to make the Father known.
days.reflection: What have you believed about God that does not match what you see in Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Word made flesh. You came and lived among us, full of grace and truth. Thank You for showing me what the Father is like. Where I have believed wrong things about God, correct me by Your life and Your words. Help me to know You better each day, and through You to know the Father. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked to Jesus to see what God is like.

days.title: The Father Ran
days.devotion: The religious leaders grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them (vv. 1–2). So He told three stories about lost things being found. In the third, a younger son took his inheritance, wasted it, and ended up starving and feeding pigs. He came to his senses and headed home, planning to ask to be treated as a hired servant. But while the son was still a long distance away, his father caught sight of him and his heart went out to him. He ran, embraced him and kissed him. The father was watching. He ran to his son before a word of apology was spoken. Jesus was showing what God is like toward sinners who return. The son's shame did not stop the father's welcome. If you have wandered from God, you do not need a perfect speech to come home. The Father welcomes those who return to Him.
days.reflection: What is keeping you from returning to God fully, and what would change if you pictured the Father running to welcome you home?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that You are like the father in Jesus' story. When I have wandered, You have not stopped watching for me. I come home to You today, not with a perfect speech, but with an honest heart. Thank You for Your compassion and Your welcome. Help me to live as a loved child in Your house. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned toward the Father who welcomes those who return.

days.title: Seeking the Lost
days.devotion: In Jericho lived Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector and a rich man, likely despised for working with Rome and cheating his own people. He wanted to see Jesus, but being short, he climbed a sycamore tree. When Jesus reached the spot, He looked up, called him by name, and told him to come down, because that day He must stay at his house (v. 5). The crowd grumbled, but Zacchaeus was changed. He promised to give half his goods to the poor and to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated. Jesus then summed up His mission: He, the Son of Man, had come to look for the lost and to save them. Zacchaeus thought he was the one seeking, but Jesus had come looking for him. Jesus still seeks people who seem beyond reach, and His welcome leads to real change.
days.reflection: In what way has Jesus sought you out, even when you thought you were the one searching for Him?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You came to seek out and save the lost. Thank You that You sought me, even when I thought I was the one searching. Like Zacchaeus, I want to welcome You gladly. Let Your welcome change me, and show me anything in my life that needs to be made right. Be merciful to me, a sinner. Amen.
days.completion_message: You welcomed the Jesus who came looking for you.

days.title: While We Were Still Sinners
days.devotion: In Romans, Paul explains how sinful people can be made right with God. In chapter 5 he shows what our peace with God rests on. Christ did not die for people who had already improved themselves. He died for the ungodly, when we were powerless to help ourselves (v. 6). Someone might, rarely, dare to die for a good person (v. 7). But God proves how much He loves us by this: Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Paul's word here means to show or prove. The cross is where God proves His love, and He proved it before we had changed at all. Paul goes on to say that even while we were God's enemies, we were reconciled to Him through His Son's death (v. 10). Your connection with God does not rest on how well you are doing. It rests on the love God showed at the cross.
days.reflection: On a day when you feel unworthy of God's love, how will you remind yourself of what He proved at the cross?
days.prayer: God, thank You that You proved Your love for me while I was still a sinner. You did not wait for me to become good enough. Christ died for me when I had nothing to offer. When I feel unworthy, turn my eyes back to the cross. Let my confidence rest on Your love, not on my performance. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to ground your connection with God in the love He showed at the cross.

days.title: To Bring Us to God
days.devotion: Peter wrote to believers who were suffering for doing good. To encourage them, he pointed them to Jesus, who also suffered unjustly: Christ also suffered for sins once, the just in the place of the unjust. Christ's suffering was once for all; it never needs to be repeated. He, the righteous one, took the place of the unrighteous. Then Peter gives the purpose: to bring us to God. The goal of the cross was not only to deal with our guilt but to restore a relationship. Jesus died to bring us home to God. He was put to death physically, but made alive again. Everything we have seen this month, from God calling Adam in the garden to dwelling among Israel, comes to this: through Jesus, the way back to God is open.
days.reflection: How does knowing that Jesus died to bring you to God change the way you approach Him today?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You suffered once for sins, the righteous in place of the unrighteous, to bring me to God. Thank You that the way is open, and that I can come to the Father because of You. When I am suffering or feel unworthy, remind me that You have already brought me near. I come to God today through You, with thanks. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to God through the One who died to bring you there.

days.title: He Is Risen
days.devotion: Very early on the first morning of the week, women came to Jesus' tomb with spices for His body. The stone had been rolled away, and the body was gone. Two men in shining garments stood by them and asked why they were looking among the dead for someone who was alive. He was not here; He had risen. Then they told the women to remember what He had said to them while He was still in Galilee (v. 6). Jesus had told them He would be crucified and rise again on the third day. And they remembered His words (v. 8). The resurrection means that the Jesus who died to bring us to God is alive. Following Him is not devotion to a memory or to a set of teachings alone. It is a relationship with a living Lord. Like the women, we are invited to remember His words and trust that He does what He says.
days.reflection: Where have you been relating to Jesus as a figure from the past rather than as your living Lord?
days.prayer: Risen Lord Jesus, You are not among the dead; You are alive. Thank You that You kept Your word and rose again. Forgive me when I treat You as a figure from the past. Help me to remember Your words and to trust You as my living Lord today. Let the joy of Your resurrection fill my heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned to Jesus as your living Lord.

days.title: He Will Be in You
days.devotion: On the night before the cross, Jesus sat with His disciples in the upper room. He had just told them He was going away, and their hearts were troubled. So He gave them a promise: He would ask the Father, and the Father would give them another Helper to be with them forever. Jesus uses a Greek word that English Bibles render "Comforter," "Helper" or "Advocate": one who would stand beside them as He Himself had. He is the Spirit of truth, and Jesus told them that the Spirit lived with them and would be in them. Then He added that He would not leave them as orphans; He would come to them (v. 18). After His resurrection and return to the Father, this promise was kept when the Spirit was poured out (Acts 2). The God who once dwelt in a tent among Israel now makes His home within His people. For every believer, God's presence is not far away. By His Spirit, He lives within.
days.reflection: Where do you feel most alone right now, and how would it change that place to remember that God's Spirit dwells within you?
days.prayer: Father, thank You for keeping Jesus' promise and giving the Helper, the Spirit of truth. Thank You that I am not left alone, and that Your Spirit dwells within Your people. Where I feel alone or unsure, remind me that You are with me and in me. Teach me Your truth, and help me to listen to Your Spirit and follow where You lead. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that God has given His Spirit to dwell with His people.

days.title: Together in Fellowship
days.devotion: At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon Jesus' followers, and Peter preached that the crucified Jesus had been raised and made both Lord and Christ (v. 36). About three thousand people believed (v. 41). What did their new life look like? they gave themselves steadily to four things: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. They did not follow Jesus alone. They learned together from the apostles' teaching, shared their lives, ate together and prayed together. God's plan was never only to bring individuals to Himself, but to gather a people, a family of believers. Our connection with God grows alongside our connection with His people. If you have been trying to walk with God on your own, the early church invites you into a shared life of teaching, fellowship and prayer.
days.reflection: Who could you connect with this week to grow in faith together, and what step will you take toward them?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that You have brought me into a family and not left me to follow You alone. Help me to value Your Word, the fellowship of other believers, and praying together. Show me who I can connect with this week. Make me faithful and steady, like the early church, and let my life encourage others who follow You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to seek God together with His people.

days.title: A Living Sacrifice
days.devotion: For eleven chapters Paul has explained the mercy of God: our sin, His grace, faith, the Spirit, and God's faithful purposes. Now he turns to how we live. On the basis of God's mercies, he therefore urges his brothers and sisters to present their bodies to God as a living sacrifice. The word therefore matters. Our response flows from His mercy; it does not earn it. In the Old Testament, sacrifices were offered on an altar and died. Now believers offer their whole selves, still living, to God. Paul adds that they are not to be molded by this present age, but changed from the inside as God makes their thinking new. A relationship with God is not only a feeling or a set of beliefs. It shapes how we think, choose and live. Every ordinary part of your day can be offered back to the God who has shown you such mercy.
days.reflection: What ordinary part of your daily life do you want to offer to God as a living sacrifice this week?
days.prayer: Merciful God, You have shown me more mercy than I can measure. In response, I offer myself to You: my body, my mind, my time and my choices. Keep me from being shaped by the world around me, and renew my mind so that I can know and follow Your good will. Let my ordinary days become worship. Amen.
days.completion_message: You offered your everyday life to God in response to His mercy.

days.title: God With Them Forever
days.devotion: The Bible's story began in a garden, and it ends with creation made new. John was given a vision of heaven and earth made new (v. 1). Then he heard a loud voice announce that God's dwelling, His tent, is with people. He will live among them, they will be His people, and He Himself will be with them as their God. These are words we have heard all month: at the tabernacle, through the prophets, and in Jesus, the Word who dwelt among us. What God has pursued since Eden will one day be complete. There will be no more hiding, and God Himself will dry every tear. We do not need to know every detail of the future to hold on to this hope. The God who has walked with His people through all of history will be with them forever.
days.reflection: How does the hope of being with God forever shape the way you want to walk with Him from today onward?
days.prayer: Faithful God, from the garden to the cross to the new creation, You have pursued a relationship with Your people. Thank You for the hope that one day You will dwell with us and wipe away every tear. Until that day, help me walk with You, love You and trust You. Thank You for this month with You. Keep me close to You always. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this month holding on to the hope of being with God forever.

plans.title: Walk With God Daily
plans.subtitle: Live each ordinary day with God.
plans.description: Discover how God comes to walk with His people, and learn to walk with Him in faith, light, love and wisdom each day.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants their faith to shape ordinary, everyday life, one step at a time
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep walking with God one ordinary day at a time, trusting the One who walks with you and is able to keep you steady to the end.

days.title: He Draws Near on the Road
days.devotion: On the day Jesus rose from the dead, two of His disciples walked from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. Their hopes had died with Jesus on the cross (v. 21). As they talked, Jesus Himself came near and joined them on the road. They did not recognise Him, because they were kept from seeing who He was, yet He was there, walking beside them and asking what troubled them. This Connection Path is about walking with God, and it begins here. Before we take a single step toward Him, He comes alongside us. These disciples were not looking for Him; they were walking away from Jerusalem in sadness. Still He drew near. Walking with God is not something we begin by our own effort. It is our response to a Saviour who has already come to walk with us, even on roads where we do not yet recognise Him.
days.reflection: Where in your life right now might Jesus be walking beside you, even if you have not recognised Him?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You draw near to the discouraged and walk with them. Like those two disciples, I do not always recognise You beside me. Open my eyes to see that You are with me on this road. As I begin this Connection Path, I want to walk with You, not as a performance, but as an answer to Your love. Amen.
days.completion_message: You began this Connection Path remembering that Jesus comes alongside you first.

days.title: Enoch Walked With God
days.devotion: Genesis 5 is a list of generations, and one line repeats like a drumbeat: "and he died." Then comes Enoch. Twice we are told that Enoch walked with God (vv. 22, 24). Verse 22 says he walked with God for three hundred years after his son Methuselah was born, while he raised sons and daughters. That is ordinary family life. Then suddenly he was gone, because God had taken him. Hebrews 11:5 explains that Enoch did not see death, and that by faith he pleased God. We are told very little else about him: no battles, no miracles, only a life lived in step with God, day after day. That is what makes his story so encouraging. Walking with God is not reserved for dramatic moments. It happens in homes and workplaces, through years of ordinary faithfulness, as we trust Him and keep company with Him.
days.reflection: Which ordinary part of your daily life most needs to be lived consciously in step with God?
days.prayer: Lord, I want my life, like Enoch's, to be described as walking with You. Not only on special days, but in my home, my work and my daily routines. Thank You that walking with You begins with trusting You, not with great achievements. Keep me close to You, day after day and year after year, so that my life pleases You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to walk with God in the ordinary places of your life.

days.title: Walk Before Me
days.devotion: Years earlier God had promised Abram a son and a great family (Genesis 12:2; 15:4–6). But Abram and Sarai had tried to bring about the promise their own way through Hagar (Genesis 16). Now Abram is ninety-nine, and the promise still seems impossible. Then the LORD appeared to Abram, introduced Himself as God Almighty, and told him to walk before Him and be blameless. God begins with who He is: the Almighty, able to do what Abram cannot. Only then does He call Abram to walk before Him, living openly in His sight. The Hebrew word behind "blameless" does not mean sinless. It means whole and sincere, without a divided heart. And Abram's call came wrapped in grace, because God went on to renew His covenant with him (v. 2). Our walk with God also rests on His power and His promises, not on our own strength or past record.
days.reflection: Where are you trying to make things happen in your own strength instead of walking before the Almighty God?
days.prayer: Almighty God, You are able to do what I cannot. Like Abram, I have sometimes tried to bring about Your promises my own way. Forgive me. Today I want to walk before You, living openly in Your sight with an undivided heart. Thank You that my walk rests on who You are and on Your faithful promises. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to walk before the Almighty God with an undivided heart.

days.title: Newness of Life
days.devotion: In Romans 5 Paul declares that wherever sin grew, grace overflowed even more (5:20). Someone might ask, then, whether we should keep on sinning so that grace can increase. Paul answers with an emphatic no (6:2). Why? Because those who belong to Christ have been united with Him in His death and resurrection. Baptism pictures this union: we have been buried with Christ in His death, so that just as the Father's glory raised Him from the dead, we too may walk in a life that is entirely new. Notice the order. First comes what God has done: He has joined us to Christ, who died and rose again. Then comes how we live: we walk in newness of life. Our daily walk is not an attempt to become new; it is living out the new life God has already given us in Christ. Sin is no longer our master.
days.reflection: What old habit or attitude are you still living with as though it were your master, and how does belonging to Christ change that?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that in Christ my old life has died and I have been given new life. I confess that I still slip back into old ways of thinking and living. Help me remember who I am in Jesus. By the same glory that raised Him from the dead, help me to walk in newness of life today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that your walk with God flows from the new life He has given you.

days.title: Walking Together
days.devotion: Amos preached to Israel in a time of prosperity and spiritual drift. God reminded them of His grace: of all the peoples on earth, Israel alone was the family He had known in this close, chosen way (v. 2). Yet they were living far from His ways. Their special relationship with God did not excuse their sin; it made them more accountable (v. 2). Then Amos asks a series of plain questions, beginning with this one: can two walk together without first coming to an agreement? Two travellers do not end up on the same road by accident; they go together because they have agreed to meet. Israel claimed to belong to God but was walking a different way. For us, the question invites honest self-examination. God does not ask us to earn His company, but walking with Him does mean going His way. Where our path has drifted from His, He calls us to turn and walk with Him again.
days.reflection: In what area of your life are you walking in a different direction from God, and what would it mean to come into agreement with Him there?
days.prayer: Holy God, You chose me and drew me to Yourself by grace. I want to walk with You, not merely to say that I belong to You. Show me where my path has drifted from Yours. Give me a heart that agrees with You, and turn my steps back to Your way wherever I have wandered. Amen.
days.completion_message: You examined your path honestly and chose to walk in agreement with God.

days.title: Not Knowing Where
days.devotion: Hebrews 11 describes people who trusted God's word before they saw it fulfilled, among them Abraham. When God called him to leave his country and his father's house for a land He would show him later (Genesis 12:1), God did not hand him a map. Hebrews says that when God called him to go to the land that would one day be his inheritance, he obeyed and set out without knowing his destination. His walk began with God's call and promise, not his own plan. What he knew was not the road but the One who called him. Even in the land, he lived in tents, because he was looking ahead to a city with lasting foundations, designed and built by God (v. 10). Walking with God often means taking the next step He shows us without seeing the whole journey, trusting His promise more than our need to know.
days.reflection: Where is God asking you to take a next step before you can see how things will turn out?
days.prayer: Faithful God, You called Abraham to go out without knowing where he was going, and he trusted Your promise. I often want to see the whole road before I take a step. Help me to trust You more than my need to know. Show me the next step, and give me the faith to take it, looking to You as the One who leads me home. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to take your next step trusting God, even without seeing the whole road.

days.title: What the Lord Requires
days.devotion: Deuteronomy 10 comes after Israel's great failure with the golden calf. Moses reminds the people that God forgave them, gave them the tablets of the law again, and kept leading them toward the promised land (vv. 1–11). Then he asks Israel what the LORD their God asks of them now. The answer is not a long list of sacrifices, but a heart turned toward Him: to fear Him, to walk in all of His ways, to love Him and serve Him with their whole heart and soul. Even His commands were given for their good (v. 13). And behind it all stands grace: the LORD delighted in their forefathers and chose to love them (v. 15). God's love came first; Israel's walk was to be the response. The same is true for us. We walk in His ways not to win His love, but because in Christ we have already received it.
days.reflection: Of these four, fearing God, walking in His ways, loving Him or serving Him, which do you most want to grow in this week?
days.prayer: LORD my God, thank You that You set Your love on Your people and did not give up on them even after they failed. You have been patient with me too. I want to answer Your love by walking in Your ways. Teach me to fear You rightly, to love You with all my heart, and to serve You gladly today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You responded to God's love by choosing to walk in His ways.

days.title: Walk Humbly With Your God
days.devotion: Micah 6 is set like a courtroom. God brings a case against His people and reminds them of all He has done: He had brought them up from Egypt (v. 4). The people respond by asking what they should bring to God: burnt offerings, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, even their firstborn (vv. 6–7)? They assume God wants something impressive. Micah's answer is simple and searching: God has already shown them what is good. What He asks is that they do what is just, love mercy, and walk humbly with their God. God wanted their lives, not extravagant gifts. Justice toward others, a love of mercy, and a humble walk with Him belong together. To walk humbly is to go through life aware that we depend on God and need His mercy ourselves. That humility then shapes how we treat others.
days.reflection: Where in your daily relationships do you most need to show justice, mercy or humility this week?
days.prayer: LORD, You have shown me what is good. I do not need to impress You with great offerings; You have already redeemed me. Help me to act justly in my dealings, to love mercy as You have shown mercy to me, and to walk humbly with You today. Keep me from pride, and let my walk with You shape how I treat others. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose justice, mercy and humility as the shape of your walk with God.

days.title: A Lamp to My Feet
days.devotion: Psalm 119 celebrates God's word in almost every verse. Verse 105 uses a picture familiar to ancient travellers: the psalmist calls God's word a lamp for his feet and a light shining on his path. In a world without street lights, a small oil lamp at night showed only the next few steps, not the whole road ahead. That is often how God guides us. His word does not usually reveal every detail of our future, but it gives enough light for faithful next steps: how to speak, what to value, what to avoid, whom to trust. The writer adds that he has solemnly vowed to keep God's righteous rulings (v. 106), and admits that he is suffering greatly (v. 107). He needed light in a hard season, and he looked to God's word for it. As we walk with God day by day, Scripture is the light we carry.
days.reflection: What next step in your life do you need God's word to light up, and where in Scripture could you look for that light?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for Your word, which gives light to my feet and my path. I do not need to see the whole road if I can trust You with the next step. Open Scripture to me as I read it. Give me light for the choices in front of me today, and help me walk in what You show me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to let God's word light your next steps.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 119:105

days.title: This Is the Way
days.devotion: Isaiah 30 begins with a rebuke. Judah had gone down to Egypt for help against Assyria without first seeking God's counsel (v. 2). God's word to them had been that in returning to Him and resting in Him they would be saved, yet the chapter records that they were unwilling (v. 15). Even here grace breaks through: the LORD waits, longing to show them grace (v. 18). God promises that after their affliction He will guide them again: they will hear a word behind them pointing out the way to walk, whenever they turn to the right or to the left. This promise was first spoken to Judah, and it is not a promise of an audible voice for every decision. But it reveals God's heart: He is patient with wandering people and delights to guide those who return to Him. Through His word He still leads His people in His way.
days.reflection: What have you been leaning on instead of God, and what would returning to Him look like this week?
days.prayer: Gracious LORD, thank You that You wait to be gracious to me, even when I have leaned on other things instead of You. I return to You now. In returning and rest, let me find my strength in You. Guide me when I turn to the right hand or to the left, and help me to hear and follow Your way. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned back to God and asked Him to guide your way.

days.title: Walking in the Light
days.devotion: John begins his letter with a clear message: God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all (v. 5). Some people claimed to know God while living in sin, but John says that if we claim fellowship with Him while walking in darkness, we are lying (v. 6). Then comes good news: when we walk in the light, just as He Himself is in the light, we share fellowship with one another, and the blood of God's Son, Jesus, keeps cleansing us from all sin. Walking in the light does not mean being sinless; verse 8 says that claim would be self-deception. It means living honestly before God, not hiding. For those who walk this way, there is ongoing cleansing. The light is not a place of fear but of forgiveness. We can bring everything into the open with God, because He is faithful and just and will forgive our sins (v. 9).
days.reflection: What have you been keeping in the dark that you need to bring honestly into God's light today?
days.prayer: Father, You are light, and there is no darkness in You at all. I do not want to hide from You. I bring into Your light the things I have kept in the dark. Thank You that the blood of Jesus cleanses me from all sin, and that You are faithful and just to forgive. Help me walk honestly with You and with others today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to walk in the light and bring your life honestly before God.

days.title: Children of Light
days.devotion: Paul reminds the Ephesian believers of the great change God has made in them. He does not only say they were once in darkness, but that they once were darkness. Darkness described who they were. But now, Paul says, they are light in the Lord. Their new identity is not their own achievement; it is theirs "in the Lord." Then comes the call to walk as children of light. Children resemble their parents, and those who have been made light are to live in a way that shows it. Verse 9 describes what that looks like: goodness, righteousness and truth. Verse 10 adds that we are to discern what the Lord approves, learning in daily life what pleases Him. Our walk does not create our identity; it displays it. We do not walk in the light to become children of light; we walk in it because, in Christ, we already are.
days.reflection: Where in your daily life do you most need to live like who you already are in Christ?
days.prayer: Lord, I was once darkness, but now You have made me light in You. Thank You for this new identity that I did not earn. Help me to walk today as a child of light, in goodness, righteousness and truth. In the choices I make, teach me what pleases You. Let my life show whose child I am. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to walk today as a child of light.

days.title: Walk in Love
days.devotion: Paul has just urged believers to be kind and forgiving, just as God in Christ has forgiven them (4:32). He continues by calling them, as God's dearly loved children, to be imitators of Him; Paul's Greek word describes someone who copies another's example. Children learn by copying the parents they love, and we, as God's dearly loved children, are to learn His ways. How? By walking in love, following the pattern of Christ, who loved us and gave Himself for us. The pattern of our love is the self-giving love of Christ, offered to God like a fragrant sacrifice. Notice that the call rests on being loved first. We are dearly loved children before we are asked to walk in love. Walking in love means letting Christ's sacrifice shape everyday choices: patience with a difficult person, forgiveness for a wrong, putting someone else's need before our own comfort. We give because we have first received.
days.reflection: Who in your life is hardest to love right now, and what is one way you can walk in Christ's love toward them today?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that I am Your dear child, loved and forgiven for Christ's sake. Help me to imitate You. Teach me to walk in love as Jesus loved me and gave Himself for me. Today, especially toward the person I find hardest to love, give me patience, kindness and a willingness to forgive. Let my love be a fragrant offering to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to walk in love toward others as Christ has loved you.

days.title: Walk in the Spirit
days.devotion: The Galatian churches were being told they had to keep the law of Moses to be right with God. Paul insists that Christ has set them free so that they might live in freedom, and they must stand firm in it (5:1). But he also warns them not to use that liberty as an opening for the flesh (5:13). How then can freed people live a holy life? Not by going back under the law, but by the Spirit: if they walk in step with the Spirit, they will not give in to the cravings of the flesh. Paul is honest that there is a real struggle within the believer: the desires of the flesh pull against the Spirit, while the Spirit opposes the flesh (v. 17). The answer is not grim self-effort. It is to walk step by step with the Holy Spirit whom God has given, relying on Him and yielding to Him. As we do, the pull of the flesh loses its hold.
days.reflection: Where do you feel the pull of the flesh most strongly, and how can you rely on the Spirit rather than willpower there today?
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, thank You that I do not have to fight sin in my own strength. You know where the pull of my flesh is strongest. Today I want to walk with You, step by step. Help me to listen to You, depend on You and yield to You when temptation comes. Lead me in a freedom that honours Christ. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to rely on the Spirit rather than on your own strength.

days.title: Brighter and Brighter
days.devotion: In Proverbs 4 a father urges his son to hold on tightly to instruction (v. 13) and to avoid the path of the wicked (v. 14). Then he sets two roads side by side. The path of the righteous, he says, is like the first light of morning, which keeps growing brighter until full day. The picture is of dawn: first a faint glow, then growing light, until the full brightness of midday. By contrast, those on the wicked road walk in darkness and cannot even see what trips them up (v. 19). The righteous are those who live by God's ways; their path is not a sudden leap but steady growth. This is a general truth about the way of wisdom, not a promise that every day will feel brighter. Yet it encourages anyone walking with God. You may feel you are only at the first light of dawn. Keep walking; the light grows.
days.reflection: In what area of your walk with God would you like to see the light grow over the coming months?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that the path of those who walk in Your ways grows brighter, like the dawn. Some days I feel I have only a little light. Keep me from the way of darkness, and help me hold fast to Your instruction. Let my walk with You grow steadily, day by day, until the light is full. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to keep walking the path that grows brighter with God.

days.title: Walk Wisely
days.devotion: Paul continues his teaching on how believers are to walk, and now he calls for care: he urges them to take great care how they walk, living as wise people and not as fools. Paul's word for this careful walking pictures someone looking all around, picking their way along a difficult path. Then he adds that they should make the most of their time, since the days are evil. The Greek expression means to buy up the opportunities we are given rather than letting them slip away. Paul does not mean anxious busyness. In verse 17 he links wisdom with understanding what the Lord wants. Walking wisely means living attentively, noticing the opportunities God gives each day to do good, to speak truth, to show kindness and to grow in Him, in a world that pulls us in other directions. Every ordinary day holds moments that can be used for God.
days.reflection: What opportunity to do good might you miss today if you do not walk carefully and attentively?
days.prayer: Lord, teach me to walk wisely. Open my eyes to the opportunities You give me today, and keep me from wasting time on what does not matter. I do not want to rush carelessly through my day. Give me understanding of Your will, and help me use my hours well, for You and for the people around me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked God to help you walk wisely and use your time well.

days.title: Worthy of the Lord
days.devotion: This verse is part of a prayer. Paul had heard of the Colossians' faith and love (v. 4), and from that day he had not stopped praying for them (v. 9). He asks that God would give them a full knowledge of His will, and the purpose is practical: that they would walk in a way worthy of the Lord, pleasing Him fully, fruitful in all kinds of good work, and growing in their knowledge of God. To walk worthy is not to earn a place with God. Verses 12–14 remind them that the Father has already rescued them out of the realm of darkness and given them redemption through the blood of Christ. To walk worthy is to live in a way that fits the Lord we belong to. Paul's prayer also shows that this walk depends on God, for strength comes from His glorious might (v. 11). We can pray these words for ourselves and for others.
days.reflection: Who could you pray this verse for today, and which part of it do you most need for yourself?
days.prayer: Father, fill me with the knowledge of Your will. Help me walk in a way that fits the Lord I belong to: pleasing You, fruitful in good works and growing in knowing You. Strengthen me with Your glorious power for patience and joy. And I pray the same for the people I love, that their walk with You would grow. Amen.
days.completion_message: You prayed to walk in a way worthy of the Lord, for yourself and for others.

days.title: Walking as Jesus Walked
days.devotion: John writes so that believers can have assurance and not be deceived. Some claimed to know God, but their lives showed no change. John gives a test: whoever says they abide in Him should walk as Jesus walked. To abide in Christ is to remain in living union with Him, and that union shows in how we live. Jesus walked in love for the Father and obedience to Him, with compassion for the weak and honesty toward the proud. Earlier John reminded his readers that if anyone sins, we have Jesus Christ, the Righteous One, as our advocate before the Father (v. 1). So this verse is not meant to crush us with an impossible standard. It gives us a direction. We are not saved by copying Jesus, but those who belong to Him grow, step by step, to live more like Him.
days.reflection: Looking at how Jesus lived, which part of His walk would you most like to see grow in your own life?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to walk as You walked. Thank You that You are my advocate when I fail, and that my hope rests on You, not on my performance. Let my life show more of Your love, Your obedience to the Father and Your compassion for others. Keep me abiding in You, and shape my steps to be more like Yours. Amen.
days.completion_message: You set your direction toward walking as Jesus walked.

days.title: The Way of the Blessed
days.devotion: Psalm 1 stands at the doorway of the whole book of Psalms and describes two ways to live. The blessed person does not walk by the advice of the ungodly, nor linger on the road sinners travel, nor take a seat among scoffers. Notice the movement: walking, then standing, then sitting. Taking advice from those who ignore God can slowly lead to settling down among those who mock Him. The blessed person's life is shaped by something else: a delight in the LORD's law, meditating on it day and night. The psalm pictures this person as a fruitful tree planted beside streams of water (v. 3). Walking with God involves daily choices about whose voices we listen to. The strongest protection is not only avoiding bad counsel, but delighting in God's word so that it becomes the counsel we trust.
days.reflection: Whose counsel or influence most shapes your thinking right now, and how can you give God's word a greater place?
days.prayer: LORD, I want to walk in Your way. Guard me from the counsel of those who ignore You, and from slowly settling into a scornful spirit. Give me a real delight in Your word. Help me meditate on it through the day and night, so that my life is like a tree rooted beside the water, fruitful in its season. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose God's word as the counsel that will shape your walk.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 1:1–2

days.title: Upheld When You Stumble
days.devotion: Psalm 37 is wisdom from David as an older man (v. 25). Its theme is trusting God when the wicked seem to prosper: do not fret because of evildoers (v. 1). In verses 23–24 he speaks of God's care for those who trust Him: the LORD makes firm the steps of a good person, and He delights in that person's way. God is not distant from the path of His people. Then comes an honest word: even if they fall, they will not be left lying flat, for the LORD's hand supports them. David does not pretend that the godly never stumble. They may fall into trouble, or fail. But they are not thrown down for good, because the LORD holds them by the hand. For anyone walking with God, this is deep encouragement. A stumble is not the end of the walk. The One who orders our steps also lifts us up to walk on.
days.reflection: Where have you stumbled recently, and what would it look like to take God's hand and keep walking?
days.prayer: LORD, thank You that You order the steps of those who trust You and delight in their way. You know where I have stumbled. I do not want to stay down in discouragement. Take my hand and lift me up again. Help me keep walking with You, trusting that my standing depends on Your hand holding me, not on my hand holding You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to get up after stumbling and keep walking with God.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 37:23–24

days.title: Kept to the End
days.devotion: Jude writes a short, urgent letter to believers surrounded by false teachers who were turning the grace of God into an excuse for immorality (v. 4). He calls them to hold fast and keep themselves in God's love (v. 21). Yet Jude does not end by placing all the weight on them. He closes with praise to the One who is able to keep them from stumbling and to bring them faultless and full of joy into the presence of His glory. This is where our walk with God finally rests. We are called to walk faithfully, but the One who keeps us is God Himself. He is able to keep us from stumbling and one day to present us faultless before Him, with great joy. As this Connection Path ends, you can keep walking with God each day with confidence, not in your own strength, but in the Saviour who holds you to the end.
days.reflection: As you finish this Connection Path, what one step will help you keep walking with God each ordinary day?
