days.prayer: God our Saviour, You are able to keep me from falling. To You belong glory, majesty, dominion and power. Thank You that my walk with You began with Your grace and will be completed by Your power. Keep me in Your love. Help me keep walking with You, one ordinary day at a time, until I stand before Your glory with great joy. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by entrusting your walk to the One who is able to keep you.

plans.title: The Lord's Prayer
plans.subtitle: Learn to pray as Jesus taught.
plans.description: Walk slowly through the prayer Jesus gave His disciples, one part each day.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants to learn to pray, or to pray these familiar words with fresh understanding
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May the words Jesus taught keep shaping your own prayers as you come each day to your Father in heaven.

days.title: Our Father
days.devotion: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus warns against two wrong ways of praying: praying to be seen by others (v. 5), and piling up empty, repeated words as though God must be worn down by sheer length (v. 7). Then He gives the reason we need neither: our Father already knows what we need before we ask Him. Only after this does He tell them how to pray. The Lord's Prayer is a pattern to learn from, not a formula to recite for effect. And it begins with a relationship. Through Jesus, His followers are invited to call God "Our Father." Prayer does not start with us trying to get God's attention; it starts with coming to a Father who already knows and cares. The word "our" also reminds us that we pray as part of a family, alongside all who belong to Him.
days.reflection: How would your prayers change if you began each one remembering that God already knows what you need?
days.prayer: Our Father, thank You that I do not have to impress You or wear You down with many words. You know what I need before I ask. Teach me to come to You simply and honestly, as Your child. Thank You that through Jesus I can call You Father, and that I pray alongside all Your family. Lord, teach me to pray. Amen.
days.completion_message: You came to God today as your Father, simply and honestly.

commentary: Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer, Lesson 4 ("After this manner pray" – Matthew 6:9)

days.title: Hallowed Be Your Name
days.devotion: Today we stay with the same verse and turn to its next phrases. Having called God "Our Father," Jesus adds that He is in heaven. The Father who is near is also the holy, exalted God. Then comes the first request, that God's name be hallowed. To hallow means to treat as holy, to honour and set apart. In Scripture God's name stands for who He is and all He has revealed of Himself. So the prayer begins not with our needs at all. It asks that God would be known, honoured and treated as holy, in the world and in our own lives. This shapes every request that follows. Before we bring our lists, we lift our eyes to Him. Nearness and reverence belong together: we come as children, and we come to a holy Father whose glory matters more than anything we ask.
days.reflection: In what part of your daily life do you most want God's name to be honoured through the way you live?
days.prayer: Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. You are near to me, and You are also holy and high above all. Forgive me for the times I have rushed to You with only my own needs in view. Let Your name be honoured in my home, my work and my words today. Not to me, Lord, but to Your name be the glory. Amen.
days.completion_message: You lifted your eyes to honour God's holy name before bringing your needs.

commentary: Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer, Lesson 4 ("After this manner pray" – Matthew 6:9)

days.title: Your Kingdom Come
days.devotion: From the start of His ministry Jesus proclaimed that the kingdom of heaven had come near (Matthew 4:17). God's kingdom is His rule, already breaking in through Jesus and one day to be seen in full. So when He teaches us to pray "Your kingdom come," we are asking God to bring His good reign more and more into this broken world, and one day to complete it. The next line shows what that looks like: that God's will be done on earth just as it is done in heaven. In heaven, God's will is done gladly and completely. We pray for that same willing obedience here, starting in our own hearts. This is not a passive prayer of resignation. It is an act of surrender and hope, like Jesus in Gethsemane, who asked that the Father's will, not His own, be done (Luke 22:42). Our plans are placed beneath His.
days.reflection: Which of your own plans do you need to place under God's will today?
days.prayer: Father, Your kingdom come, Your will be done in my life as it is in heaven. I bring You the plans I hold most tightly, and I place them under Your rule. Where my will pulls against Yours, give me a willing heart. Let Your good reign be seen in how I love and serve today, and fill me with hope for the day Your kingdom comes in full. Not my will but Yours. Amen.
days.completion_message: You placed your own plans under God's will today.

days.title: Our Daily Bread
days.devotion: After lifting our eyes to God's name, kingdom and will, Jesus turns to our ordinary needs, teaching us to ask for our "daily bread." For His first hearers, bread was the basic food of each day. The request is humble and specific. It asks for what we need, for today. It recalls Israel in the wilderness, where God sent manna morning by morning and the people gathered what they needed for each day (Exodus 16:4). Asking for daily bread teaches daily dependence. Even when our cupboards are full, everything we have comes from God's hand. This prayer also loosens the grip of anxiety about tomorrow; later in the same chapter Jesus tells us not to worry about tomorrow (v. 34). And Jesus teaches us to say "us" and "our." We pray for the needs of others as well as our own.
days.reflection: What need, large or small, do you want to bring to God today, trusting Him with it for just this day?
days.prayer: Father, give us the bread we need for today. Everything I have comes from Your hand, even the things I take for granted. I bring You the needs I carry today, and I trust You with them one day at a time. Free me from worrying about tomorrow. Make me grateful for what You provide, and open my eyes to the needs of others around me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought today's needs to your Father and chose to trust Him for this day.

days.title: Forgive Us Our Debts
days.devotion: Jesus teaches us to call our sins "debts." Sin is something we owe to God and can never repay ourselves. Just as we need bread every day, we need forgiveness every day, and so Jesus teaches us to ask for it. God's forgiveness is a gift of grace, not a wage we earn by forgiving others. Yet Jesus ties the two closely together: we ask to be forgiven as we also forgive those who owe us. Right after the prayer He returns to the point (vv. 14–15), and later He tells of a servant forgiven a huge debt who refused to forgive a small one (Matthew 18:21–35). A heart that has truly received mercy cannot comfortably hold on to bitterness. Forgiving others does not mean pretending that wrong was not wrong. It means releasing the debt into God's hands, as He has released ours. Receiving and giving forgiveness belong together.
days.reflection: Is there someone whose debt against you God is asking you to release today?
days.prayer: Merciful Father, forgive me my debts. I owe You more than I could ever repay, and You have been patient with me. Thank You for the mercy You give through Jesus. Now help me to forgive those who have wronged me. I name them before You. I cannot do this in my own strength, so soften my heart and help me let go of what I have been holding on to. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked for God's mercy and chose to release someone else's debt.

days.title: Deliver Us From Evil
days.devotion: Today we look at the first part of verse 13: the request that God not lead us into temptation but rescue us from evil. This does not mean God tempts anyone to sin; James is clear that God tempts no one (James 1:13). The word can also carry the sense of testing or trial. The request is an honest admission of weakness. We ask our Father to keep us from situations where we would fall, and to rescue us when evil presses in. Jesus prayed for His disciples in the same way, asking the Father to keep them from evil (John 17:15). We are not strong enough to stand alone, and this prayer does not pretend we are. Yet Paul reminds us that God is faithful, and that when temptation comes He will also open a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). Humble dependence is where our strength begins.
days.reflection: Where do you feel most vulnerable to temptation right now, and how can you ask God for help there today?
days.prayer: Father, do not lead me into temptation, but rescue me from evil. You know where I am weak, and I will not pretend to be stronger than I am. Guard my heart and my steps today. When temptation comes, show me the way of escape and give me the will to take it. Keep me from evil, as Jesus prayed for His disciples. Amen.
days.completion_message: You admitted your weakness and asked God to guard you from evil.

days.title: Yours Is the Kingdom
days.devotion: We stay with verse 13 for its closing words. Many English Bibles place them in a footnote, because some of the earliest manuscripts do not include them, but Christians have prayed them from very early times. The prayer ends where it began, with God: the kingdom, the power and the glory are His for ever, and it closes with a final Amen. After all our asking, we return to praise. These words echo David's praise, when he declared that the greatness, the power and the glory belong to the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:11). The little word "For" gives the reason behind every request. We ask for God's kingdom because the kingdom is His. We ask for bread, forgiveness and deliverance because the power to give them is His. And we pray it all for His glory, not our own. "Amen" is a word of trust and agreement. Every prayer, however weak, can end in confident praise.
days.reflection: What request are you carrying that you can end today with praise, trusting it to God's kingdom, power and glory?
days.prayer: Father, the kingdom, the power and the glory are Yours for ever. Thank You for teaching me to pray this week. Everything I have asked rests on who You are. I trust my requests to Your rule and Your strength, and I want my life to bring glory to You, not to me. May Your glorious name be praised for ever and ever. Amen.
days.completion_message: You ended this week of prayer by giving God the kingdom, the power and the glory.

plans.title: The Shepherd's Psalm
plans.subtitle: Rest in the Shepherd's care.
plans.description: Walk through Psalm 23 verse by verse and meet the Shepherd who leads, restores and stays with His people.
plans.best_for: Anyone who is weary, anxious or walking through a hard season and needs to rest in the Shepherd's care
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep following the Good Shepherd, trusting His care in green pastures and dark valleys alike.

days.title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
days.devotion: Before he was king, David was a young shepherd who kept his father's sheep (1 Samuel 16:11) and defended them from the lion and the bear (1 Samuel 17:34–35). He knew what a flock needed and how helpless sheep are on their own. So when he called the LORD his shepherd, he was saying that the covenant God of Israel cared for him the way he had cared for his sheep, and far better. Notice the word "my." This is personal trust, not a distant idea. From that trust flows his confession that he will not be in want. David does not mean he would have everything he wished for. He means that with the LORD as his Shepherd, he would lack nothing he truly needed. Our peace does not begin with our circumstances, but with knowing whose care we are under.
days.reflection: What would change in how you face this week if you truly believed that, with the LORD as your Shepherd, you lack nothing you need?
days.prayer: LORD, You are my Shepherd. Thank You that I am not left to look after myself. You know my needs better than I do. When I feel I am lacking, teach me to trust Your care. Quiet my fears about what I do not have, and help me rest in the truth that I belong to You. I am Yours, and You will lead me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to trust the LORD as your own Shepherd today.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 23:1

days.title: Green Pastures, Still Waters
days.devotion: In the dry hills of Judea, green grass and calm water did not simply appear. A shepherd had to know where to find them and lead his flock there. A hungry or frightened flock does not settle; sheep lying down at rest are a sign of a shepherd's good care. David pictures the LORD doing this for him: He makes him lie down in green pastures and leads him beside quiet waters. The Shepherd provides both nourishment and rest, and He leads gently. Sometimes He makes us lie down, slowing us when we would keep running. Rest is not wasted time in God's sight; it is part of His provision. The quiet waters are not a place we reach by striving, but a place He leads us to as we follow Him. Peace is found in staying close to the Shepherd.
days.reflection: Where in your life is God inviting you to stop and rest instead of pushing on in your own strength?
days.prayer: Good Shepherd, thank You for green pastures and still waters. You know how often I keep running when I need to stop. Lead me to the rest I need, and help me not to resist it. Feed my soul with Your word and quiet my restless heart. I want to follow You at Your pace, not mine. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked the Shepherd to lead you to rest today.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 23:2

days.title: He Restores My Soul
days.devotion: Sheep wander, and they grow weary. David, who knew his own failures well, also knew the Shepherd who brings His sheep back, the One who restores his soul. The phrase can speak both of refreshing a tired life and of turning a straying heart back home. Then David says the LORD guides him along right paths. A shepherd leads along the right tracks, the paths that truly lead somewhere safe. God guides His people in ways that are right and good. And the reason is striking: it is for the sake of His name. The Shepherd restores and leads us not because we deserve it, but because His own name and faithfulness are at stake. That is firm ground for hope. When you feel worn out, or know you have drifted, you can come back, not on the strength of your own record, but on the strength of His name.
days.reflection: Where do you feel weary or drifted, and what would it look like to let the Shepherd bring you back today?
days.prayer: Lord, restore my soul. You know where I am tired and where I have wandered from You. Bring me back, not because I have earned it, but for Your name's sake. Lead me in paths of righteousness, and give me a heart willing to follow. Give me back the joy of Your salvation. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked the Shepherd to restore your soul and turned back to His paths.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 23:3

days.title: Through the Dark Valley
days.devotion: The psalm now moves from the pasture into a deep, dark ravine, a valley of deathly shadow. The phrase pictures a place of deep darkness and danger, where death itself can feel close. David does not say the Shepherd keeps him from every valley. He says he walks through it. Sheep sometimes had to pass through such places to reach new pasture. And here the psalm changes voice. David stops speaking about the LORD and speaks to Him: You are with me. In the darkest place, the Shepherd is closest. The text does not describe them, but commentators usually explain the rod as a shepherd's club for defending the flock and the staff as a crook for guiding the sheep. Both meant the shepherd was near and protecting. His refusal to fear evil is not a denial that the valley is real, but trust in the One who walks through it with us.
days.reflection: What dark valley are you walking through right now, and how can you speak to God directly about it today?
days.prayer: Lord, You are with me. I bring You the dark valley I am walking through, and I will not pretend it is not hard. Thank You that You do not leave me to walk it alone. Let Your rod protect me and Your staff guide me. When fear rises, remind me that You are closer than the darkness. Even when I am afraid, I will trust You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You spoke to God honestly about your valley and trusted Him to walk it with you.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 23:4

days.title: A Table Prepared
days.devotion: The picture now shifts from shepherd to host. Commentators often point out that in the ancient Near East a host was expected to protect a guest at his table. David says the LORD spreads a table for him in full view of his enemies. David had real enemies, and the danger had not disappeared. Yet God honoured and provided for him right in front of them. Anointing his head with oil describes a gesture of welcome, refreshment and honour for a guest. And his overflowing cup speaks of generosity far beyond need. God's care is not grudging or minimal. Even when trouble is still near, He can give His people a place at His table and more than enough of His goodness. Peace here is not the absence of enemies, but the presence of a generous Host.
days.reflection: Where are you facing pressure or opposition right now, and what good gifts from God can you still see around you in it?
days.prayer: Lord, You prepare a table for me even when trouble is near. Thank You for Your generous care that runs over. Forgive me for fixing my eyes only on what is against me. Open my eyes to the good gifts You set before me today. Keep me calm in the middle of pressure, and help me receive Your kindness with a thankful heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked past the pressure to notice the table God has set for you.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 23:5

days.title: Goodness and Mercy
days.devotion: David ends with confident hope: goodness and mercy will surely follow him all the days of his life. The Hebrew word many English Bibles render "follow" is often used elsewhere for pursuing. God's goodness and His steadfast, covenant love come after His people through every season, not only the bright ones. The psalm then reaches its home: David will dwell in the LORD's house for ever. For David, the house of the LORD was the place of God's presence among His people. His deepest longing was not simply for safe pasture but for God Himself (see Psalm 27:4). For those who belong to Christ, this hope reaches beyond this life to being with Him for ever. Whatever lies ahead, the sheep of this Shepherd are followed by mercy and are on their way home.
days.reflection: Looking back over your life, where can you see God's goodness and mercy following you, even when you did not notice it at the time?
days.prayer: Faithful Lord, thank You that Your goodness and mercy follow me every day of my life. Looking back, I see how Your kindness came after me even when I did not notice. Give me that same confidence for the days ahead. More than anything, I want to dwell with You. One thing I ask: to be near You all my days. Amen.
days.completion_message: You traced God's goodness and mercy following you through your life.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 23:6

days.title: The Good Shepherd
days.devotion: About a thousand years after David, Jesus stood in Jerusalem and declared that He is the good shepherd. Many of His hearers knew the shepherd psalms, and they knew God had promised to shepherd His people Himself (Ezekiel 34:11–15). Jesus was taking that role. Then He said what no ordinary shepherd would: the good shepherd gives up his own life for his sheep. A hired hand runs when the wolf comes (v. 12), but Jesus lays down His life for His flock. This is how He leads us to green pastures and through dark valleys: by first going to the cross for us. He adds that as the good shepherd He knows His sheep, and they know Him (v. 14). The LORD who was David's Shepherd is made known to us in Jesus, who knows each of His sheep by name and gave Himself for them.
days.reflection: How does knowing that Jesus gave His life for you change the way you trust Him with the week ahead?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Good Shepherd. You laid down Your life for me, and You know me by name. Thank You that the Shepherd of Psalm 23 has come near in You. I want to hear Your voice and follow You. In green pastures and in dark valleys, keep me close to You, and let me rest in Your love. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by trusting Jesus, the Good Shepherd who gave His life for you.

plans.title: Abide in Him
plans.subtitle: Live connected to the Vine.
plans.description: Walk through Jesus' words about the vine and the branches, and learn what it means to remain in Him.
plans.best_for: Believers who feel spiritually dry or stretched thin and long for a life rooted in Christ
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep abiding in Christ, the true Vine, drawing your life from Him day by day.

days.title: The True Vine
days.devotion: Jesus spoke these words on the night before the cross. He had shared the Passover meal with His disciples and was preparing them for His departure (John 13:1). In the Old Testament, Israel was pictured as a vine God had planted, yet it often failed to bear good fruit (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1–7). Now Jesus calls Himself the true vine. He is everything Israel was meant to be, and the source of life for all who belong to Him. And His Father is the vinedresser, the farmer who tends the vineyard. On the eve of leaving them, Jesus does not hand His friends a program for keeping their faith alive. He points them to Himself. The Christian life grows out of this: not trying harder on our own, but living in union with Christ, under the Father's careful hand.
days.reflection: Where have you been trying to grow spiritually in your own strength instead of drawing your life from Christ?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the true Vine, and my life comes from You. Forgive me for trying to grow in my own strength. Thank You that the Father tends my life with care. Draw me into a deeper union with You this week, and teach me what it means to live from You and not merely for You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You turned to Jesus as the true Vine and the source of your life.

commentary: Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ, ch. 4 ("As the Branch in the Vine") and ch. 6 ("God Himself has united you to Him")

days.title: The Father's Pruning
days.devotion: Jesus describes the Father's work in two ways. First, He takes away every branch in Him that bears no fruit. This is a sobering word, and Christians have understood its details in different ways. What is clear is that a branch with no fruit shows no living flow from the vine, and Jesus wants His hearers to take that seriously rather than presume. But He speaks just as much about fruitful branches: the Father prunes each one so that it will bear still more fruit. A vinedresser cuts back healthy branches not to harm them, but so their strength goes into fruit. God's pruning can feel painful, coming through hardship, correction or loss, yet it comes from a Father who cares. Then Jesus reassures the disciples in front of Him: they are already clean because of the word He has spoken to them. His word had already done its cleansing work in them.
days.reflection: What difficulty in your life right now might God be using to prune you for greater fruitfulness?
days.prayer: Father, You are the gardener of my life. I confess that pruning is hard, and I do not always understand it. Help me trust that Your hand is careful and kind. Cut away whatever keeps me from bearing fruit for You. Thank You that Your word has made me clean through Jesus. Search me, O God, and lead me in the way everlasting. Amen.
days.completion_message: You trusted the Father's hand in the pruning places of your life.

days.title: Abide in Me
days.devotion: The key word of this passage is the one many English Bibles render "abide" or "remain." It means to remain, to stay, to make one's home. Jesus calls His disciples to abide in Him, and He promises to abide in them. This is both an invitation and a promise. He has already joined His disciples to Himself; now He calls them to go on living from that union. The picture is simple: a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it stays joined to the vine. A branch does not strain to produce grapes. It stays connected, and the life of the vine flows through it. Abiding is not a special feeling or a technique. It is a settled dependence on Jesus, day by day, expressed through His word, prayer, trust and obedience. Our part is not to manufacture fruit, but to remain close to the One who gives life. The fruit is His work in us.
days.reflection: What is one simple way you can stay consciously connected to Jesus through the ordinary hours of today?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to abide in You, and I thank You for Your promise to abide in me. I cannot bear fruit on my own. Teach me to stay close to You through the busy hours of this day, in Your word, in prayer and in trust. When I drift, draw me back. Let Your life flow through mine. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to stay close to Jesus instead of striving on your own.

commentary: Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ, ch. 4 ("As the Branch in the Vine")

days.title: Without Me, Nothing
days.devotion: Jesus repeats the picture and makes it personal: He is the vine, and they are the branches. Then come a wonderful promise and a humbling truth. The one who abides bears much fruit, the kind of fruit that shows Christ's life at work: love, faithfulness and a changed character. But apart from Him, they can do nothing. We may be busy and even successful, yet nothing of lasting spiritual worth grows apart from Him. Verse 6 is a solemn warning. A branch that does not remain in the vine withers, and in a vineyard such branches were gathered and burned. Christians have understood this warning in different ways, but its purpose here is plain: Jesus urges His disciples not to treat their connection to Him lightly. The warning is meant to drive us not into despair, but back to the Vine, where there is life.
days.reflection: In which area of your life are you most tempted to act as if you can manage without Jesus?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Vine, and I am a branch. Without You I can do nothing that lasts. Forgive me for the times I have acted as though I could manage on my own. I take Your warning seriously, and I run to You, not away from You. Keep me joined to You, and let Your life bring forth fruit in me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You admitted your need and returned to Jesus as your source.

days.title: His Words in You
days.devotion: Now Jesus adds something new: He speaks of His disciples abiding in Him and His words abiding in them. Abiding in Christ includes letting His words take up residence in our hearts, shaping our thinking and our desires. Then comes a remarkable promise: they may ask for whatever they desire, and it will be done for them. This is not a promise that every wish will be granted. It is spoken to those whose lives are rooted in Christ and filled with His words. As His words fill us, our asking begins to reflect His heart. John later writes that God hears us when we ask according to His will (1 John 5:14). And the goal is clear in verse 8: the Father is glorified when His disciples bear much fruit. Prayer that grows out of abiding seeks the Father's glory, and fruit that honours Him is the mark of true disciples.
days.reflection: Which of Jesus' words do you want to let shape your prayers this week?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, let Your words make their home in me. Shape my thoughts and my desires until my prayers begin to sound like Yours. Teach me to ask according to Your will, and give me faith to trust You with the answers. Fill me with the knowledge of Your will, and let my life bear fruit that brings glory to the Father, not to myself. Amen.
days.completion_message: You let Jesus' words shape what you asked of God today.

commentary: Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ, ch. 21 ("So will you have Power in Prayer" – John 15:7)

days.title: Continue in My Love
days.devotion: Here Jesus shows the heart of abiding: He has loved His disciples just as the Father has loved Him. The love between the Father and the Son is the measure of Christ's love for His disciples. He spoke these words only hours before laying down His life for them (v. 13). Then He tells them to remain in His love. We do not create this love or earn it; we are called to remain in it, to live in what has already been given. Verse 10 shows how: those who keep His commands will abide in His love. Obedience is not the price of His love. Jesus Himself obeyed the Father as a Son who was already loved. In the same way, our obedience is how we stay at home in a love we have already received. Love comes first; loving obedience follows.
days.reflection: What step of obedience is Jesus asking of you, and how can you take it today as someone already loved?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You love me as the Father has loved You. I can hardly take that in. Thank You that I do not have to earn Your love. Help me to remain in it. Show me where I have been resisting You, and give me a glad heart to obey, not to win Your love, but because I already have it. Keep me in Your love. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to obey as someone already loved by Jesus.

commentary: Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ, ch. 22 ("And in His Love") and ch. 24 ("Obeying His Commandments" – John 15:10)

days.title: Your Joy Made Full
days.devotion: Jesus explains why He has spoken about the vine, the pruning, abiding, prayer and love: so that His joy would be in them, and their joy would be complete. It is striking that He speaks of joy on the night of His betrayal, with the cross only hours away. His joy was not the absence of trouble, but the deep gladness of living in the Father's love and doing His will. That is the joy He wants to share with His disciples, a joy that comes from Him and can remain even when circumstances do not change. Abiding is not a heavy burden laid on us; it is the way into Christ's own joy. As you finish this Connection Path, remember that the aim of abiding is not only fruit, but fullness of joy in Him. The branch that stays close to the Vine shares its life, and its gladness too.
days.reflection: What is one habit of abiding in Christ that you want to keep after this Connection Path ends?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for speaking these words so that Your joy might be in me. Even when life is hard, let Your joy remain. Keep me abiding in You, with Your words in my heart and Your love as my home. Let my joy be full because it is found in You. God of hope, fill me with all joy and peace as I trust in You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by choosing to keep abiding in Christ, the source of full joy.

commentary: Andrew Murray, Abide in Christ, ch. 25 ("That your Joy may be full" – John 15:11)

plans.title: Rest for the Weary
plans.subtitle: Come to Jesus and rest.
plans.description: Hear Jesus' invitation to the weary and discover the rest God gives His people across Scripture.
plans.best_for: Anyone who feels tired, burdened or worn out, in body or in soul
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep coming to Jesus with every burden, and find in Him the rest your soul was made for.

days.title: Come to Me
days.devotion: Jesus speaks these words just after rebuking the cities that had seen His mighty works and still would not repent (vv. 20–24). He then thanks the Father for revealing His truth to little children (v. 25), and says that only the Son can make the Father known (v. 27). Out of that authority comes a warm invitation: all who are weary and carrying heavy loads may come to Him, and He will give them rest. Many who heard Him were weighed down not only by hard lives but by the heavy load of rules that religious teachers laid on people's shoulders (Matthew 23:4). Jesus does not hand them a better system to carry. He offers Himself. A yoke still means walking with Him and learning from Him, but His yoke is easy, because He is gentle and humble of heart. Rest does not begin with a method. It begins with a Person, and with coming to Him.
days.reflection: What burden are you carrying right now that you need to bring to Jesus instead of carrying alone?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You call the weary and the heavily burdened, and today that includes me. I have tried to carry so much on my own, and some of it was never mine to carry. I come to You now. Teach me to walk beside You and to learn from You, because You are gentle and humble of heart. Give my soul the rest You promised. Amen.
days.completion_message: You answered Jesus' invitation and came to Him with your burden.

days.title: Rest Is a Gift
days.devotion: As Jesus walked through the fields on the sabbath, His hungry disciples picked some ears of grain. The Pharisees accused them of breaking the sabbath (vv. 23–24). Jesus reminded them how David once ate the holy bread when he and his men were in need (vv. 25–26), and then said that the sabbath was made to serve people, not people to serve the sabbath. God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3) and gave Israel a day of rest as a kindness, reminding them that they were no longer slaves in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Pharisees had turned that gift into another heavy load. Jesus adds that the Son of Man has authority over the sabbath itself. Christians hold different convictions about how to keep a day of rest, but all can receive its heart: rest is God's gift, not a reward we earn. Stopping is a way of trusting that He holds the world while we lay our work down.
days.reflection: What makes it hard for you to stop and rest, and what might that reveal about where you are placing your trust?
days.prayer: Lord of the sabbath, thank You that rest is Your gift to me, not a reward I have to earn. Forgive me for the times I have treated stopping as weakness, or turned even rest into another task. Help me to lay my work down and trust You to hold what I cannot. Teach me to receive Your good gifts with a thankful and restful heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to see rest as God's gift rather than something to earn.

days.title: Under the Broom Tree
days.devotion: Elijah had just seen God answer by fire on Mount Carmel. Yet when Queen Jezebel threatened his life, he ran for the wilderness, sat under a broom tree and told God he had had enough (v. 4). He was worn out, afraid and discouraged. Notice how God first responded. There was no lecture. An angel touched him and told him to get up and eat. Elijah found bread and water, ate, and slept again. Then the angel came a second time with the same care, adding that the journey ahead was too much for him. God knew Elijah's limits and met his body's needs before He spoke to him about anything else at Horeb (v. 9). Weariness can make everything look darker than it is. Sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is to receive God's ordinary care: food, sleep, and the help of others. If your tiredness has become despair, do not carry it alone.
days.reflection: Where are you running on empty right now, and what simple care might God be offering you through rest, food, or other people?
days.prayer: Father, You saw Elijah under the broom tree, and You see me when I am worn out and discouraged. Thank You that You did not scold him, but fed him and let him sleep. I bring You my tiredness and my limits today. Help me to receive the care You provide, even through ordinary things and ordinary people, and give me strength for the journey ahead. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your tiredness honestly to God and asked Him to care for you.

days.title: My Soul Waits for God
days.devotion: David wrote this psalm while people were plotting to pull him down from his position, speaking kindly to his face but cursing him in their hearts (vv. 3–4). Yet he begins with calm confidence: his soul waits for God in silence, because his salvation comes from Him. The Hebrew here speaks of silence, a soul that has stopped its restless struggling and is resting on God alone. Notice the emphasis: God alone is his rock and his salvation. David's rest did not come from his enemies giving up, but from knowing Who held him. Later he speaks to his own soul, telling it to wait for God alone (v. 5). Even David had to call his heart back to rest. Then he invites others to pour out their hearts before Him (v. 8). Our souls often look for rest in approval, success or control. True rest comes as we lean our whole weight on God.
days.reflection: Besides God, what are you most tempted to rely on for your sense of security right now?
days.prayer: Lord, You alone are my rock and my salvation. My soul is so often restless, looking to people, results, or my own control to feel secure. Today I choose to wait on You. I pour out my heart before You, with all its worries. Be my defence and my refuge, so that I am not badly shaken. My hope comes from You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You called your soul to wait quietly on God alone.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 62:1–2

days.title: Strength for the Faint
days.devotion: Isaiah 40 opens with God's call to comfort His people (v. 1). It speaks to God's people who would later sit in exile and feel forgotten, complaining that their way was hidden from the LORD (v. 27). God answers by pointing them to Himself: the everlasting Creator never grows faint or weary (v. 28). Then comes the promise: He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of those who have none. Even the young and strong eventually run out, but those who wait on the LORD will find their strength renewed. To wait on the LORD is to look to Him in hope and trust rather than to our own reserves. For Israel, this promised strength for the long road home. For us, it points to a principle that runs through Scripture: God does not promise that we will never feel tired, but He gives strength to those who keep looking to Him when their own is gone.
days.reflection: Where do you feel your own strength running out, and how can you look to God in that place today?
days.prayer: Everlasting God, You never faint and You are never weary. I confess that I often am. When I feel forgotten or overlooked, remind me that my way is not hidden from You. I have little strength of my own today, so I look to You. Give power to the faint, and renew my strength as I wait on You in hope. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked to the everlasting God for strength when your own ran low.

days.title: Return to Your Rest
days.devotion: The writer of Psalm 116 had been close to death, surrounded by its terrors (v. 3). He called on the LORD, and the LORD rescued him; when he was brought low, God came to his help (v. 6). Then he turns and speaks to himself, telling his soul to return to its rest, because the LORD has been good to it. His soul had been shaken and anxious, and now he calls it home. Notice the reason he gives. It is not that life has suddenly become easy, but that the LORD has been good to him. Remembering God's past kindness is one of the ways our restless hearts find their way back to rest in Him. When fear rises again, we can do what the psalmist did: recall how the LORD has helped us, and tell our souls to settle on Him once more.
days.reflection: What is one specific way God has been kind to you in the past that you can remember when your soul feels restless?
days.prayer: Gracious Lord, You have been so good to me. When I was brought low, You helped me, even in ways I did not see at the time. Today I remember Your kindness, and I tell my soul to return to its rest in You. When worry pulls me away again, bring Your faithfulness back to my mind, and let me walk before You in peace. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered God's kindness and called your soul back to rest in Him.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 116:7

days.title: A Rest That Remains
days.devotion: The letter to the Hebrews was written to believers tempted to drift away from Christ. In chapters 3 and 4 the writer recalls Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the promised land because of unbelief (v. 6). Even Canaan was not the final rest, for God later spoke of "another day" (v. 8). So he concludes that God's people still have a rest waiting for them. This rest is like God's own rest after creation (v. 4). The one who enters it rests from his own works. That does not mean doing nothing. It means no longer relying on our own efforts to make ourselves right with God, and trusting instead in what Christ has done. Those who have believed do enter that rest (v. 3), and its fullness is still to come. This is where this Connection Path began: with Jesus, who said, "Come to me." The deepest rest is found in Him.
days.reflection: In what area of your life are you still trying to earn God's approval instead of resting in what Christ has done?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that there is a rest for Your people, and that it is found in You. I confess that I still try to prove myself, as if Your work were not enough. Today I cease from my own works and trust in Yours. Keep my heart from unbelief, and hold me in Your rest until I share its fullness with You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to rest in what Christ has done rather than in your own efforts.

plans.title: Peace in the Storm
plans.subtitle: God is with you in trouble.
plans.description: Find peace in God's presence and rule when life is hard, even before the storm has passed.
plans.best_for: Anyone going through a hard season who needs to know God is with them in it
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep finding your peace in Jesus, who is with you in every storm and has overcome the world.

days.title: Jesus in the Boat
days.devotion: At the end of a long day of teaching, Jesus told His disciples to cross over to the other side (v. 35). They were in the storm because they had followed Him. The wind rose, the waves filled the boat, and Jesus was asleep on a cushion. Terrified, they woke Him, asking if He did not care that they were perishing. He rose, rebuked the wind, and told the sea to be quiet and still. Then He asked them why they were so afraid. Their question was not whether a storm could come, but whether Jesus cared. The answer was already in the boat with them. They were left asking who this man could be, since even wind and waves obey Him (v. 41). Jesus does not always calm our storms when we want Him to. But no storm is outside His rule, and being in one never means He does not care.
days.reflection: What storm are you facing right now, and what would change if you remembered that Jesus is with you in it?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, sometimes I ask the same question Your disciples asked: do You not care? Forgive me when I measure Your love by how quickly the storm passes. You are with me, and even the wind and the waves obey You. I bring You the storm I am in today. Calm it if that is Your will, and calm my fearful heart as I trust You in it. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought your storm to Jesus and trusted that He cares.

days.title: Lying Down in Peace
days.devotion: Psalm 4 is an evening prayer from a time of distress. David begins by asking God to answer when he calls (v. 1). People were turning his honour into shame and spreading lies about him (v. 2), and many around him were asking who would ever show them anything good (v. 6). Nothing in the psalm says his troubles had all gone away by nightfall. Yet he ends with quiet confidence: he will lie down and sleep in peace, for the LORD alone keeps him safe. His peace did not rest on having solved his problems, but on the LORD who kept him. Earlier he encouraged others to reflect quietly on their beds and be still (v. 4). Night is often when worries grow loudest. It is also a good time to hand them over to the One who does not sleep, and to lie down trusting Him.
days.reflection: What worry tends to keep you awake at night, and how can you hand it over to God before you sleep tonight?
days.prayer: LORD, You alone keep me safe. When night comes and my worries grow loud, help me to remember that You are awake and watching over me. I hand over to You the things I cannot fix tonight. Lift up the light of Your face upon me, put gladness in my heart, and let me lie down in peace and sleep. Amen.
days.completion_message: You handed your night-time worries to the God who keeps you.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 4:8

days.title: A Mind Fixed on God
days.devotion: Isaiah 26 is a song God's people would one day sing in Judah, celebrating the salvation He would bring: they have a strong city, with God's salvation as its walls and ramparts (v. 1). In the middle of that song comes this promise: God will keep in perfect peace the one whose mind leans on Him, because that person trusts in Him. In Hebrew the phrase "perfect peace" simply repeats the word peace, pointing to a full and settled peace. The word many English Bibles render "stayed" or "steadfast" pictures a mind that leans on God and is held up by Him. This is not the power of positive thinking. The peace comes from the One we trust, not from our effort to feel calm. That is why Isaiah goes on to call God's people to trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD Himself is their everlasting strength. In hard seasons our thoughts wander toward fear. Each time, we can bring them back to lean on Him.
days.reflection: Where do your thoughts most often run when you are afraid, and what truth about God can you lean your mind on instead?
days.prayer: LORD, You are my everlasting strength. My mind runs so quickly to fear and to every thing that could go wrong. Today I lean my thoughts on You. Keep me in Your perfect peace, not because I have made myself calm, but because I trust in You. When my mind wanders again, draw it gently back to rest on You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to lean your mind on God and trust Him.

days.title: Through the Waters
days.devotion: These words were spoken to Israel, a people facing God's discipline and the prospect of exile (42:24–25). Yet God begins with tenderness: they need not fear, for He has redeemed them; He has called them by name, and they are His. Then He promises that when they pass through the waters, He will be with them. Notice the word "when," not "if." God did not promise Israel they would never face waters or fire. He promised His presence in them, and that these things would not destroy them. The waters would have reminded Israel of the Red Sea and the Jordan, where God had brought them through before. This promise was first given to Israel, but it shows us God's heart toward those He has redeemed. In Christ, He has called you by name too. His presence does not always keep hard things away, but He does not leave His people to face them alone.
days.reflection: What "waters" or "fire" are you passing through right now, and how does knowing you belong to God change how you face them?
days.prayer: Holy One, You created me, You redeemed me in Christ, and You call me Your own. I am passing through hard waters right now, and I am afraid. Thank You that You do not leave Your people alone in them. Be with me in what I am facing. Keep me from being overwhelmed, and help me remember that I belong to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You faced your hard place remembering that you belong to God.

days.title: His Peace, Not the World's
days.devotion: Jesus spoke these words at the Last Supper, on the night before His death. He had just told His disciples that He was going away (v. 28), that one of them would betray Him, and that Peter would deny Him (13:21, 38). Their hearts were troubled. Into that moment He says that He is leaving them peace, His own peace, and that He does not give as the world gives. The world's peace usually depends on circumstances going well, and it can only wish us well. Jesus gives His own peace, the peace of the Son who fully trusts the Father, and He gives it as a gift. He also promised the Holy Spirit, whom the Father would send to help them (v. 26). Within hours He would face the cross, yet His peace held. So He can tell us not to let our hearts be troubled or afraid. His peace is given, not manufactured.
days.reflection: Where have you been looking for the kind of peace the world gives, and what would it look like to receive Christ's peace instead?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You give Your own peace, not the fragile peace the world offers. I have looked for calm in circumstances going my way, and it has not lasted. Today I receive Your peace as a gift. Send Your Holy Spirit to steady my heart. Where my heart is troubled and afraid, let Your peace hold me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to look to Christ for His peace rather than to the world.

days.title: Pressed but Not Crushed
days.devotion: Paul wrote to the Corinthians about the real cost of serving Christ. He did not pretend life was easy. He says the gospel is a treasure carried in ordinary clay jars, so that it is plain the extraordinary power comes from God and not from us (v. 7). Then he describes his life honestly: hard-pressed from every direction but not crushed, confused but not despairing. He was pressed, confused, attacked and knocked down, yet not abandoned and not destroyed. Paul holds both halves of the sentence together. The trouble is real, and so is God's sustaining power. His weakness only made it clearer that the strength belonged to God. Because of this, he could say that they do not lose heart (v. 16). You do not have to deny how hard things are in order to trust God. You can name the trouble and still say, "but not."
days.reflection: If you wrote your own honest version of Paul's words, what would your "pressed... but not" sentence say today?
days.prayer: Father, I am pressed and perplexed in ways You already know. I will not pretend otherwise before You. Yet I thank You that I am not forsaken and not destroyed. I am only a clay jar, but Your power is at work in me. Let Your strength be seen in my weakness, and keep me from losing heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You named your troubles honestly and held on to God's "but not."

days.title: Take Heart
days.devotion: These are the last words Jesus spoke to His disciples before He prayed for them and went out to be arrested. He had just told them that they would scatter and leave Him alone, though He was not alone, because the Father was with Him (v. 32). Then He sums up everything He had said: He has told them these things so that in Him they may have peace. Notice where peace is found: "in me," not in the world. He is honest: in the world they will have trouble. Trouble is not a sign that something has gone wrong with our faith. But He does not stop there: they are to take heart, because He has overcome the world. He spoke of His victory before the cross, as though it were already won. As this Connection Path ends, this is the peace to carry into every storm: Jesus is with you, and He has already overcome.
days.reflection: What trouble do you need to face this week with the reminder that Jesus has overcome the world?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You told me plainly that in this world I will have trouble, and I do. But You have overcome the world. Thank You that my peace is found in You and not in my circumstances. Help me to take heart today, not because every storm is gone, but because You are with me and You reign. Keep me in Your peace. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to take heart in Jesus, who has overcome the world.

plans.title: Faith Over Fear
plans.subtitle: Meet your fears with God's promises.
plans.description: Discover what God said to fearful people in Scripture, and learn to bring your own fears to Him in trust.
plans.best_for: Anyone who struggles with fear or anxiety and wants to meet it with trust in God
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. Fear may still knock at the door; when it does, may you keep turning to the God who is with you, who holds you, and who has the final word.

days.title: When I Am Afraid
days.devotion: David wrote Psalm 56 when the Philistines seized him in Gath (see the psalm's title). He was far from home and surrounded by enemies who, he says, were ready to trample him all day long (v. 2). Notice what he does not say. He does not claim that he is never afraid. He says that whenever he is afraid, he will put his trust in God. Fear came, and David admitted it. Faith was not the absence of fear; it was where he turned when fear arrived. Then he adds that, having put his trust in God, he will not be afraid of what mere flesh can do to him. The same man who was afraid chose to trust, and his trust began to loosen fear's grip. As this Connection Path begins, there is no shame in admitting your fears. The question is where you will take them.
days.reflection: What fear have you been carrying quietly, and what would it look like to turn to God with it today?
days.prayer: Lord, I am honest with You: there are things that make me afraid. Thank You that David was not ashamed to admit his fear, and that I do not have to hide mine from You. When I am afraid, I choose to trust in You. Help me to hold on to Your word and to remember that no person or circumstance is greater than You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You admitted your fear to God and chose to trust Him with it.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 56:3

days.title: I Am With You
days.devotion: Isaiah 41 is addressed to Israel. God reminds His people who they are: Israel is His servant, Jacob the one He has chosen (v. 8). The nations around them were in turmoil and afraid (vv. 5–6), and Israel had reason to fear too. Into that fear God speaks: they need not fear, because He is with them; they need not be dismayed, because He is their God. Every reason He gives is about Himself: His presence, His relationship to them, His help. He promises to strengthen them, to help them, and to uphold them. This promise was first spoken to Israel as God's chosen servant, not as a guarantee that hard things would never happen. Yet it reveals God's heart toward His people, and in Christ we are His people too. The answer to fear is not a change of mood but the nearness of God.
days.reflection: Which of God's words here, "with you," "your God," "strengthen," "help" or "uphold," do you most need to hold on to this week, and why?
days.prayer: Lord, You spoke to Israel as Your chosen servant and told them not to fear, because You were with them. Thank You that in Christ I belong to You too. When I feel dismayed, remind me that You are my God. Strengthen me, help me, and uphold me with Your righteous right hand. Amen.
days.completion_message: You heard God's words to His people and brought your fear under them.

days.title: He Goes Before You
days.devotion: Moses was 120 years old and about to die (v. 2). He would not lead Israel into the Promised Land; Joshua would. In front of all Israel, Moses called Joshua and charged him (v. 7). Joshua was about to face walled cities and strong enemies without the leader he had followed for forty years. Then Moses gave him this word: the LORD Himself goes ahead of him and will be with him; He will not fail him or abandon him, so Joshua need not be afraid or dismayed. Joshua's courage was not built on his own ability. It rested on the fact that God was already ahead of him, and would stay with him. This word was given to Joshua for a specific task, yet it shows us how God leads His people. When you face a new and unknown season, you do not step into it alone.
days.reflection: What new or unknown situation are you facing, and how does knowing God goes before His people change how you approach it?
days.prayer: LORD, like Joshua I sometimes face things that feel too big for me. Thank You that You go before Your people and do not forsake them. I bring to You the unknown things ahead of me. Help me to walk into them with courage, not because I am strong, but because You are faithful. Amen.
days.completion_message: You brought the unknown road ahead to the God who goes before His people.

days.title: Be Strong and Courageous
days.devotion: Moses was dead, and now God spoke directly to Joshua (v. 1). The task was huge: to lead the people across the Jordan and into Canaan. Three times God tells him to be strong and courageous (vv. 6, 7, 9). Joshua was not being told to feel brave on his own. God grounds the command in two things. First, His word: Joshua was to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth and meditate on it "day and night" (v. 8). Second, His presence: the LORD his God would be with him wherever he went. God's reminder that the command is His own tells Joshua that the task and the courage both came from God. This was Joshua's calling, not a promise of success in every venture we choose. But the principle stands: courage grows as we fill our minds with God's word and remember His presence.
days.reflection: What task has God placed before you that needs courage, and how can His Word feed that courage this week?
days.prayer: Lord, You told Joshua to be strong and courageous because You were with him. I face things that need courage, and I often feel weak. Fill my mind with Your Word so that my courage rests on what You have said. Help me to remember that You are with Your people wherever they go. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to draw courage from God's Word and His presence.

days.title: Whom Shall I Fear?
days.devotion: David wrote Psalm 27 with enemies around him. He speaks of evildoers who came to devour him and of an army that might encamp against him (vv. 2–3). The danger was real. Yet he begins with three names for God: the LORD is his light, his salvation, and the strength of his life. Light shows the way when everything is dark. Salvation means rescue. Strength is what holds us up when we cannot stand. Then come his questions: whom should he fear, and who could make him afraid? These are not a denial that there are dangers. They are a comparison. When David set every threat beside the LORD, the threats looked smaller. Later in the psalm he still asks for help and says to wait on the LORD (v. 14). Faith over fear starts by looking at God first.
days.reflection: What fear looks biggest to you right now, and how does it look when you set it beside who the LORD is?
days.prayer: LORD, You are my light when things are dark, my salvation when I need rescue, and the strength of my life when I cannot stand. I set my fears beside You, and I see that You are greater. Help me to look at You first, before I look at my problems. Teach me to wait on You with courage. Amen.
days.completion_message: You set your fears beside the greatness of the LORD.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 27:1

days.title: Under His Shadow
days.devotion: Psalm 91 celebrates the safety of those who make God their home: the one who makes the Most High a dwelling place will find rest beneath the Almighty's shadow. The psalmist then makes it personal, declaring that the LORD is his refuge and fortress, his God, the one he trusts. The rest of the psalm uses vivid pictures of protection. But we need to read them carefully. When Satan quoted this psalm to Jesus and urged Him to throw Himself from the temple, Jesus refused to treat it as a guarantee to be tested (Matthew 4:6–7). Faithful believers in Scripture still suffered and died. The psalm's promise is that God is truly our refuge, and nothing can touch us outside His care or separate us from Him. Our safety is in Him, not in escaping every harm.
days.reflection: What would it look like for you to make God your refuge today, rather than looking for safety in avoiding every possible harm?
days.prayer: Most High God, You are my refuge and fortress, my God, and I trust in You. I do not ask You to prove Yourself by keeping every hard thing away, but I ask You to be my dwelling place in all of it. Keep me under Your shadow, and let my heart rest in Your care, whatever comes. Amen.
days.completion_message: You named the LORD as your refuge and chose to dwell with Him.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 91:1–2

days.title: The LORD Is for Me
days.devotion: Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving for rescue. The singer had been in real danger: all the nations surrounded him (v. 10), and he was pushed so hard that he was falling (v. 13). But he remembers how he cried to the LORD in his distress, and the LORD answered and brought him out into a broad, open place (v. 5). Out of that experience he says that the LORD is for him, so he will not fear; what can mere people do to him? He is not claiming people could never hurt him; they had tried. He is saying that with the LORD for him, no one has the final say over his life. So he concludes that taking refuge in the LORD is better than relying on people (v. 8). Hebrews 13:6 later applies these words to all believers. Our courage rests on whose side God is on.
days.reflection: Whose opinion or power do you fear most right now, and how does knowing the LORD is for you change how you see them?
days.prayer: LORD, when I am in distress, I call upon You. Thank You that You are on the side of those who trust You. I confess that I often fear what people can say or do to me. Help me to put my confidence in You and not in people. Bring me out into a broad place, and let my courage rest on You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You called on the LORD and chose to trust Him over your fear of people.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 118:6

days.title: More Than Many Sparrows
days.devotion: Jesus spoke these words as He sent out His twelve disciples. He did not promise them an easy road. He warned that they would be hated, arrested and even killed (vv. 17–22). In verse 28 He tells them not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. So when He speaks of sparrows, He is not promising they would never suffer. He is telling them that nothing would happen outside their Father's knowledge and care. Sparrows were so cheap that two sold for a single small coin, yet, Jesus says, not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father. Even every hair on your head has been counted. Then Jesus concludes: they need not be afraid, for they are of greater value than many sparrows. You are known in detail and valued by your Father.
days.reflection: Where do you feel overlooked or unimportant, and what would it mean to remember that your Father knows and values you there?
days.prayer: Father, You see every sparrow, and You know the number of hairs on my head. Thank You that nothing in my life happens outside Your knowledge and care. When I feel small or forgotten, remind me that I am of great value to You. Help me to live without fear because I am held by You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that your Father knows you in detail and values you.

days.title: Do Not Fear, Little Flock
days.devotion: In Luke 12 Jesus is teaching His disciples about worry. He tells them not to be anxious about food or clothing, because their Father knows that they need these things (v. 30). Instead, they are to seek God's kingdom (v. 31). Then He speaks very tenderly: His little flock need not be afraid, because it is their Father's delight to give them the kingdom. His disciples were few and weak, a "little flock" in a hostile world. But they had a Shepherd, and a Father who delighted to give them His kingdom. Notice that the kingdom is a gift, not a reward earned by being fearless. God is not reluctant or stingy toward His children. Worry often assumes we must secure our own future. Jesus reminds us that our Father has already given His people the greatest gift of all.
days.reflection: What worry about your future could you hand over today, remembering that your Father delights to give His kingdom?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that it is Your good pleasure to give Your kingdom to Your little flock. I am often anxious about what I need and what tomorrow will bring. You already know my needs. Help me to seek Your kingdom first and to rest in Your generous heart toward me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to rest in the Father's delight in giving His kingdom to His flock.

days.title: Only Believe
days.devotion: Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, had come to Jesus because his little daughter was dying (v. 23). On the way, Jesus stopped to heal a woman, and the delay must have felt unbearable. Then messengers arrived: his daughter had died, so why trouble the Teacher any longer? (v. 35). Every hope seemed gone. Immediately Jesus told Jairus not to be afraid, but only to believe. Jesus went to the house and raised the girl to life. This was a specific miracle in a specific home, and we should not read it as a promise that every sick loved one will be healed in this life. But Jesus' word to Jairus still speaks: when the news is at its worst, keep trusting Him. Fear says it is too late. Jesus says, stay with Me. He has power even over death.
days.reflection: Where has bad news or waiting made you want to stop trusting Jesus, and how can you keep bringing it to Him today?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, when Jairus heard the worst news, You told him not to be afraid but to believe. There are situations in my life where I feel it may be too late. I bring them to You. I do not ask You to follow my plan, but I choose to keep trusting You, because You have power even over death. Amen.
days.completion_message: You kept trusting Jesus even where the news seemed too hard.

days.title: Delivered from All My Fears
days.devotion: Psalm 34 comes from the same frightening time as Psalm 56. David had fled to the Philistine city of Gath and, afraid for his life, pretended to be mad before the king (see the psalm's title and 1 Samuel 21:10–15). He escaped, and afterward he wrote this song of praise. At its heart is his testimony: he sought the LORD, who heard him and delivered him from all his fears. Notice the order. David had fears, many of them. He did not overcome them by trying harder to be brave. He sought the LORD, and the LORD heard him. Deliverance came from God's side. David then invites others to join him in magnifying the LORD (v. 3). Seeking God is not a technique that makes fear vanish on demand, but it is the path David shows us.
days.reflection: Which of your fears have you been trying to manage alone, and how can you seek the LORD about it today?
days.prayer: LORD, like David I have fears that I cannot shake on my own. Today I seek You. Thank You that You hear those who call on You. I bring You each fear by name, and I ask You to deliver me from them in Your way and Your time. Let my life become a reason for others to magnify You with me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You sought the LORD and brought your fears to Him by name.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 34:4

days.title: Power, Love and a Sound Mind
days.devotion: Paul wrote to Timothy from prison. Timothy was young, perhaps timid by nature, and facing opposition as he led the church in Ephesus. Paul reminds him to stir up again the gift God had given him (v. 6). Then he says that God did not give us a spirit of fear, but one of power, love and a sound mind, a phrase some Bibles render "self-discipline" or "self-control." In context, Paul is encouraging Timothy not to shrink back from serving Christ or be ashamed of testifying about our Lord (v. 8). Paul does not scold Timothy for feeling afraid; he points him to what God has given. The Spirit gives power to act, love for others, and a sound, disciplined mind. When fear tells us to shrink back, we can ask God to stir up what He has already given, and take the next faithful step.
days.reflection: Where has fear been causing you to shrink back from something God has called you to do?
days.prayer: Lord, You have not given me a spirit of fear, but a spirit of power, love and a sound mind. You know the places where I shrink back. Stir up in me what You have given by Your Spirit. Give me power to act, love for the people in front of me, and clear thinking where fear clouds my mind. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked God to stir up His gifts where fear had held you back.

days.title: Perfect Love Casts Out Fear
days.devotion: John has been writing about God's love. "God is love" (v. 16), and His love reaches its full purpose in us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment (v. 17). That is the fear John has in mind: fear of God's judgment, the dread of punishment. He says that love leaves no room for fear; perfect love drives fear out, because fear has to do with punishment. The Greek word here, rendered "torment" in some Bibles, carries the idea of punishment. If we think God is waiting to punish us, we will always be afraid of Him. But God's love, shown in sending His Son for our sins (v. 10), removes that dread. This is not a rebuke to anyone who feels afraid. It is an invitation: the more deeply we know how God loves us in Christ, the less room fear of rejection has in our hearts.
days.reflection: In what ways do you still fear God's punishment, and how does His love in Christ speak to that fear?
days.prayer: Father, You have loved me in Christ and sent Your Son for my sins. Forgive me for sometimes seeing You as waiting to punish me. Let Your perfect love drive out my fear of judgment. Help me to know Your love more deeply, so that I can come to You with confidence instead of dread. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You let God's love in Christ speak to your fear of judgment.

days.title: The First and the Last
days.devotion: John was an old man, exiled on the island of Patmos because of the word of God (v. 9). Churches he loved were facing persecution. Then he saw the risen Jesus in His glory, and fell at His feet like a dead man. Even the beloved disciple was overwhelmed. But Jesus placed His right hand on him and told him not to be afraid, for He is the First and the Last. Then He gave His reasons: He is the Living One; He was dead, and now He is alive forever and ever. And He holds the keys of death and of the realm of the dead. The deepest fear of all is death, and Jesus has passed through it and come out victorious. He holds the keys. Every fear we have faced in this Connection Path meets its final answer here: the risen Christ is Lord over all things, even the last enemy.
days.reflection: What fear do you need to place under the rule of the risen Jesus as you finish this Connection Path?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the first and the last. You were dead, and You are alive forever and ever, and You hold the keys of death. Thank You that no fear has the final word over my life. When I am afraid, lay Your right hand on me and remind me who You are. I put my trust in You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by bringing your fears to the risen Lord who holds the keys.

plans.title: The Fruit of the Spirit
plans.subtitle: Grow in the life of the Spirit.
plans.description: Explore each part of the fruit of the Spirit and learn to walk with the Spirit who grows it in you.
plans.best_for: Anyone who wants to grow in Christlike character and learn to walk by the Spirit day by day
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. The fruit of the Spirit is not a list to achieve but a life He grows. May you keep walking in step with Him, trusting Him to finish the good work He has begun in you.

days.title: One Fruit, Grown by the Spirit
days.devotion: Paul wrote Galatians to believers who were being told they must add law-keeping to faith in Christ. He insists they were called to freedom (v. 13), but that freedom is not a licence to live for self. He sets two ways of living side by side. First, the works of the flesh (v. 19): a long list of what human nature produces on its own. Then, the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Some Bibles use older names for several of these, such as longsuffering (patience), meekness (gentleness) and temperance (self-control). Notice the contrast between works and fruit. Works are manufactured; fruit is grown. And Paul says "fruit," not "fruits." Many commentators take this to mean one Christlike character with many sides, grown together rather than collected one by one. We cannot produce it by effort alone. The Holy Spirit grows it in those who belong to Christ, as we yield to Him.
days.reflection: Which part of the fruit of the Spirit do you most long to see grow in your life right now, and why?
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, thank You that the fruit of a Christlike life is Your work in me, not something I must manufacture by my own effort. I confess that I often try to change myself in my own strength. Over these days, grow Your fruit in me: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Teach me to yield to You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You began this Connection Path by asking the Spirit to grow His fruit in you.

days.title: Filled with the Spirit
days.devotion: Before we look at each part of the fruit, we need to see where it comes from. In Ephesians 5 Paul urges believers to watch carefully how they live, not foolishly but wisely (v. 15). Then he makes a striking contrast: instead of getting drunk on wine, which leads to reckless living, believers are to be filled with the Spirit. Wine can take control of a person and lead to ruin. Paul calls believers to live under a different influence: the Holy Spirit. The command is written in a way that describes something ongoing and received: keep on being filled. It is not a single dramatic moment we must achieve, but a daily yielding to the Spirit God has already given us. Paul shows what it looks like in ordinary life: singing to the Lord, giving thanks, and submitting to one another (vv. 19–21). The fruit grows as He fills us.
days.reflection: What tends to fill and control your mind and heart most days, and how can you make more room for the Spirit's influence?
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, thank You that You live in those who belong to Christ. So many other things try to fill and control me. Today I yield to You. Keep filling me, day by day, so that my life is shaped by Your influence. Fill my heart with thanks and my words with praise to the Lord. Amen.
days.completion_message: You yielded yourself to be filled with the Spirit today.

days.title: Love
days.devotion: Love comes first in Paul's list, and every other quality grows from it. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians 13 to a church rich in gifts but divided by pride and rivalry. He tells them that gifts without love are worth nothing (vv. 1–3). Then he describes what love does: it is patient and kind, and it is not envious. Paul's word for love here means self-giving love. It does not seek its own way, is not quick to anger and keeps no account of wrongs; it bears with everything, and keeps on believing, hoping and enduring through it all. Read slowly, this portrait describes Jesus perfectly, and it shows how far short we fall. That is why love must be the Spirit's fruit. As Paul writes elsewhere, the Holy Spirit pours God's love into our hearts (Romans 5:5). We love as we receive His love first.
days.reflection: Which line of this description of love is hardest for you to live out, and toward whom?
days.prayer: Father, thank You for loving me with a patient, kind, enduring love in Jesus. When I read this description, I see how far my love falls short. Pour Your love into my heart by Your Holy Spirit. Help me to be patient and kind, not envious or easily provoked, especially toward the person I find it hardest to love. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked the Spirit to grow His self-giving love in you.

days.title: Joy
days.devotion: Habakkuk lived as Judah faced invasion by Babylon. God had told him the enemy was coming, and the prophet trembled at the news (v. 16). He knew that invading armies could strip the land bare. So he imagines the worst: the fig tree without blossom, no grapes on the vines, the olive crop failing. No crops, no flocks, no herds. For a farming people, this meant losing everything. Then comes one of the boldest lines in Scripture: even so, he will rejoice in the LORD and be joyful in the God who saves him. Habakkuk's joy was not a cheerful mood or pretending things were fine. It was gladness in God Himself, who would still be his Saviour when everything else was gone. This is the joy the Spirit grows in us: rooted in God, not in circumstances.
days.reflection: What would it look like for you to rejoice in God Himself this week, even in an area where things are not going well?
days.prayer: LORD, like Habakkuk I face things that make my heart tremble, and some good things in my life feel empty right now. Yet I choose to rejoice in You, the God of my salvation. Holy Spirit, grow in me a joy that is rooted in God and not in my circumstances. Let my gladness in You be my strength. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to rejoice in the God of your salvation, whatever your circumstances.

days.title: Peace
days.devotion: Paul wrote to the Colossians about the new life believers have in Christ. In chapter 3 he describes a community clothed with Christ's character, bearing with and forgiving one another (vv. 12–14). Then he tells them to let the peace of Christ rule in their hearts (some Bibles read "of God"), the peace to which they were called as one body. The Greek word behind "rule" was used of an umpire deciding a contest. When our hearts are pulled in different directions by anger, worry or rivalry, the peace of God is to have the deciding voice. Notice that this peace is both personal and shared. We are called to it as one body, with other believers. The Spirit grows a settled peace that begins with being at peace with God through Christ, and spreads into our relationships. And Paul adds three simple words: "and be thankful."
days.reflection: Where is something other than the peace of God making the decisions in your heart right now?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that through Jesus I have peace with You. Let Your peace rule in my heart today, like an umpire with the final say. When anger, worry or rivalry pull at me, bring me back to Your peace. Help me to live at peace with the people around me, and give me a thankful heart. Amen.
days.completion_message: You invited the peace of God to rule in your heart.

days.title: Patience
days.devotion: This patience, which some Bibles call longsuffering, is directed toward people: a long fuse, slow to anger, willing to bear with others over time.
