In Ephesians 1–3 Paul has described all that God has done for us in Christ. Now, writing as a prisoner for the Lord, he urges believers to live in a way that matches the calling God has given them. Notice the order: God's calling first, our response second. We do not become patient in order to be called; we are called and loved, and now we live in a way that fits that calling. What does it look like? Humility and gentleness in every way, patience, and bearing with one another lovingly. Bearing with others means putting up with one another's weaknesses, and doing it "in love." God has been endlessly patient with us. The Spirit grows patience in us as we remember His patience and extend it to others.
days.reflection: Who in your life is testing your patience right now, and how does remembering God's patience with you change how you see them?
days.prayer: Father, You called me and have been so patient with me. I confess that I am often quick to become frustrated with others. Help me to walk worthy of Your calling, with humility, gentleness and patience. Teach me to bear with the people who test my patience, in love. Grow this fruit in me by Your Spirit. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to bear with others in love, as one called by God.

days.title: Kindness
days.devotion: Kindness, the fifth quality in Paul's list in Galatians 5:22, translates a Greek word that a few older Bibles render "gentleness" there; it is not the same word as the gentleness (sometimes called meekness) of Day 10. It describes a warm, generous goodwill toward others. In Ephesians 4, Paul describes the new life of those who belong to Christ. He tells them to put away every kind of bitterness, fury, anger, loud quarrelling and slander (v. 31). Then he gives the positive picture: they are to be kind and tenderhearted toward each other, forgiving one another. Once again, the reason is grace: they are to forgive just as God has forgiven them in Christ. Kindness is not weakness or mere politeness. It is the tender warmth of a heart that has been treated kindly by God. The Spirit grows this fruit as He softens what has become hard in us, replacing bitterness with tenderness toward others.
days.reflection: Where has bitterness or harshness crept into your words or attitudes, and how could you show kindness there this week?
days.prayer: Father, You have been so kind to me in Christ. Forgive me for the bitterness and harshness that sometimes come out in my words and attitudes. Holy Spirit, soften what has become hard in me. Make me kind, tenderhearted and forgiving, just as You have forgiven me in Christ. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked the Spirit to make you kind and tenderhearted.

days.title: Goodness
days.devotion: In Romans 12 Paul describes what life looks like when we offer ourselves to God in response to His mercy (v. 1). Near the end of the chapter he turns to how we treat those who wrong us: never pay back evil with evil (v. 17), and never take revenge (v. 19), leaving justice to God. Instead, if an enemy is hungry, feed him (v. 20). Then comes the summary: do not let evil defeat you, but defeat evil with good. Goodness is more than avoiding wrong. It is active, practical doing of good, even toward those who do not deserve it. It reflects the heart of God, who sends sunshine on evil and good people alike (Matthew 5:45). When we are wronged, our natural response is to strike back. The Spirit grows a different response: goodness that refuses to let evil have the last word.
days.reflection: Is there someone who has wronged you, and what is one good thing you could do for them instead of repaying them?
days.prayer: Lord, You have been good to me when I did not deserve it. When I am wronged, I want to strike back, but You call me to overcome evil with good. Give me grace to leave justice in Your hands. Holy Spirit, grow in me a goodness that acts, even toward the people who have hurt me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to answer evil with good.

days.title: Faithfulness
days.devotion: In Galatians 5:22 the Greek word Paul uses, which some Bibles render "faith," carries the sense of faithfulness: being trustworthy and dependable. Jesus spoke of it after a parable about a steward who handled his master's goods (vv. 1–8). He said that whoever is faithful in very little will also be faithful in much. Faithfulness is not proven in grand moments, but in small, daily ones: keeping your word, finishing what you started, handling money honestly, showing up for people when it is inconvenient. Jesus says the little things reveal the heart. This fruit grows from God's own character. Scripture says, "God is faithful" (1 Corinthians 1:9). He has kept every promise to us. As the Spirit makes us more like Christ, we become people others can rely on, reflecting the faithfulness of the God who has never failed us.
days.reflection: What small, everyday responsibility is God asking you to be faithful in right now?
days.prayer: Faithful God, You have never broken a promise to me. I want to reflect Your faithfulness in my life. Forgive me for the small ways I have been careless or unreliable. Holy Spirit, make me faithful in little things: in my words, my work, my money and my relationships. Help me to be someone others can trust. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked God to make you faithful in the small things.

days.title: Gentleness
days.devotion: Just after listing the fruit of the Spirit, Paul shows what it looks like in real church life. Paul says that if a believer is caught in some wrongdoing, those who are spiritual should restore that person with a gentle spirit. Gentleness, which some Bibles call meekness, is not weakness. It is strength held under God's control, a gentle humility that does not need to crush others to feel right. Here it is shown in how we treat someone who has fallen. The goal is to "restore." The same Greek word is used of fishermen mending their nets in Matthew 4:21, and in medical writing for setting a broken bone. And Paul adds a warning: each should keep watch on themselves, or they too may be tempted. Gentleness remembers that we too depend on grace. Jesus described Himself as gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29). The Spirit grows this same humble gentleness in us.
days.reflection: Is there someone who has stumbled whom you need to approach with gentleness instead of judgment?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are gentle and humble in heart, and You have been gentle with me in my failures. Forgive me for the times I have been harsh or proud toward others who stumbled. Holy Spirit, give me a spirit of gentleness. Help me to restore rather than condemn, remembering that I also depend on Your grace. Amen.
days.completion_message: You asked for a spirit of gentleness toward those who stumble.

days.title: Self-Control
days.devotion: Self-control in Galatians 5:23, which some Bibles call temperance, means mastery over our desires, rather than being mastered by them. In Titus 2, Paul has been describing how believers of every age should live (vv. 1–10). Then he gives the reason and the power behind it: God's grace has appeared, and it brings salvation to all people. Grace does not only forgive; it trains us. It teaches us to turn away from godlessness and worldly cravings, and to live with self-control, integrity and devotion to God here and now. Notice that self-control is not the way to earn grace. It is something grace teaches. God's kindness in Christ gives us a new reason and a new power to say no to what harms us. The Spirit grows self-control not by harsh willpower alone, but by filling us with a greater love and hope (v. 13).
days.reflection: What desire or habit most tends to control you, and how might God's grace be teaching you to say no to it?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your grace has appeared and brought me salvation. I confess the areas where I am mastered by my desires. Let Your grace teach me to say no to what harms me and yes to what honours You. Holy Spirit, grow self-control in me, and fill me with a greater love for Jesus than for anything that pulls me away. Amen.
days.completion_message: You let God's grace teach you the way of self-control.

days.title: Keep in Step with the Spirit
days.devotion: Right after the list of fruit, Paul says that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, together with its cravings and desires. This is something that has already happened. When we came to belong to Christ, the old self-ruled life lost its right to rule us. Then Paul draws the conclusion: if the Spirit is the source of our life, we should also follow the Spirit. The Spirit has given us new life; now we are to live in line with it. The word Paul uses here, which some Bibles render "walk" and others "keep in step," means to keep in line or keep in step, like people walking in rank behind a leader. The Spirit sets the pace and direction; we follow. This is how the fruit grows: not by striving to produce it, but by keeping in step with the One who produces it, day by day.
days.reflection: What is one area where you have been running ahead of, or lagging behind, the Spirit's leading?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that I belong to You, and that the old life no longer has the right to rule me. Holy Spirit, You have given me new life. Help me to keep in step with You today. Where I have been running ahead or lagging behind, bring me back into line with Your leading. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to keep in step with the Spirit who gives you life.

days.title: God at Work in You
days.devotion: Paul had just described how Christ humbled Himself and became obedient to death on a cross (vv. 5–8). Now he tells the Philippians how to live in response: they are to work out their salvation with fear and trembling. He is not telling them to earn salvation. They already belong to Christ. He is calling them to live out, in everyday life, the salvation God has given. And he gives the reason they can: it is God who is at work in them, giving them both the desire and the ability to do what pleases Him. This is the secret of the fruit of the Spirit. We do make real choices and real effort, yet underneath our effort is God's work. He shapes even our desires and gives the power to act. Our growth rests on His working, and it pleases Him.
days.reflection: Where do you need to trust that God is at work in you, even when your growth feels slow?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that You are at work in me, giving me both the desire and the power to do what pleases You. Forgive me for thinking that my growth depends only on my own effort. Help me to work out what You have worked in, with reverence and trust. Shape my desires and strengthen my will by Your Spirit. Amen.
days.completion_message: You trusted that God Himself is at work in you.

days.title: Filled with Fruit
days.devotion: Paul wrote to the Philippians from prison, and he began by telling them how he prayed for them. He was confident that the God who began a good work in them would see it through to the end (v. 6). Then he prays that their love would keep overflowing more and more, together with knowledge and discernment, so that their lives would be full of the righteous fruit that Jesus Christ produces, bringing glory and praise to God. Notice where this fruit comes from: it comes through Jesus Christ. And notice where it leads: to God's glory, not our own. As this Connection Path ends, this is the hope. God has begun His work in you, and He will finish it. The fruit of the Spirit will keep growing, not because you are strong, but because He is faithful.
days.reflection: Which part of the fruit of the Spirit will you keep asking God to grow in you after this Connection Path ends?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that You have begun a good work in me, and You will complete it. I pray that my love would abound more and more, and that my life would be filled with the fruit that comes through Jesus Christ. Let it all be for Your glory and praise, not mine. Keep me walking with Your Spirit. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path by entrusting your growth to the God who completes His work.

plans.title: Who God Says You Are
plans.subtitle: Your identity in Christ.
plans.description: Let your sense of who you are rest on what God says about those who belong to Christ, not on performance, failure or the opinions of others.
plans.best_for: Anyone whose sense of worth rises and falls with success, failure or what others think
plans.completion_message: You've finished this Connection Path. May you keep listening to what God says about you in Christ: loved, forgiven, made new and sent, all as a gift of His grace.

days.title: Made and Known
days.devotion: Psalm 139 is David's prayer of wonder at how fully God knows him. It opens with David telling the Lord that He has searched him and known him (v. 1). God knows when he sits down and rises up, and there is nowhere David can go from His presence (vv. 2, 7). Then David looks back to the very beginning. Before anyone else knew him, God was forming him in his mother's womb. His response is praise: he praises God because he has been made in an awe-inspiring and wonderful way, and he knows that God's works are wonderful. David is not boasting about himself; he is marvelling at the God who made him. Your story did not begin with your achievements or your failures, or with what others have said about you. It began with God's careful work. Over these three weeks we will listen to what God says about those who belong to Christ. It starts here, with the God who made you and knows you completely.
days.reflection: Whose opinion, or which success or failure, has shaped the way you see yourself more than God's word has?
days.prayer: Lord, You have searched me and known me. You formed me before anyone else knew my name. I praise You, because You made me in an awe-inspiring and wonderful way, and Your works are wonderful. Forgive me for letting other voices tell me who I am. As I begin this Connection Path, open my ears to hear what You say, and help me to believe it. Amen.
days.completion_message: You began by praising the God who made you and knows you completely.

commentary: C. H. Spurgeon, The Treasury of David, Psalm 139:14

days.title: Welcomed as His Child
days.devotion: John opens his Gospel by telling us who Jesus is: the Word who was with God and was God, and who became flesh and lived among us (v. 14). Yet many turned Him away; even His own people did not receive Him (v. 11). Then comes a wonderful turn: everyone who receives Him, trusting in His name, is given the right to become a child of God. Becoming God's child is not something we achieve by family line, effort or human decision. It is given. Verse 13 says that such children owe their birth not to ancestry, human desire or anyone's decision, but to God Himself. The door is open to anyone who receives Christ and trusts in Him. If you have welcomed Him, you are God's child. If you are still unsure, this verse is an invitation: He offers this new standing to all who receive Him.
days.reflection: What would change in how you face this week if you truly believed you were God's child by His gift, not by your effort?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that Jesus came into the world, full of grace and truth. I receive Him, and I trust in His name. Thank You that being Your child is Your gift and not my achievement. Where I am unsure, help me to take You at Your word. Let me live today as one who has been welcomed into Your family. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You heard again God's welcome to become His child.

days.title: What Great Love
days.devotion: John writes to believers who needed assurance. False teachers had unsettled them, and they may have wondered whether they truly belonged to God. So John stops and invites them to look at how great a love the Father has given us: He calls us His children. This love has been given freely. It was not earned or paid back. And the name God gives His people is not servant or stranger, but children. In the next verse he says it again with certainty: dear friends, we are God's children now (v. 2). Not someday, if you improve, but now. John adds that the world may not recognise this, because it did not recognise Jesus either. Others may misunderstand you or overlook you. That does not change what the Father has called you. Your identity rests on His love, and He does not take back what He has given.
days.reflection: When you feel overlooked or misunderstood by others, how can you remind yourself of the name the Father has given you?
days.prayer: Father, how great is the love You have given me, that I should be called Your child. I did not earn it and I cannot repay it. Thank You that I am Your child now, not only when I become better. When others misunderstand me or pass me by, let Your love be the voice I trust. Help me to rest in the name You have given me. Amen.
days.completion_message: You looked at the Father's love and the name He has given you.

days.title: Adopted, Not Afraid
days.devotion: In Romans 8 Paul describes the life of those who belong to Christ and have His Spirit. He contrasts two ways of relating to God. One is a spirit that makes us slaves to fear again: the anxious life of a slave who is never sure whether he has done enough. The other is the Spirit who makes us God's adopted children, by whom we cry out, "Abba, Father." Commentators note that in the Roman world Paul's readers knew, adoption gave a child the full standing of a family member. "Abba" is the Aramaic word for "father," the same word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). God has not merely tolerated us; He has made us His own. And we are not left to convince ourselves of it: God's Spirit joins with our own spirit to assure us that we are His children. Fear says you must keep proving yourself. The Spirit reminds you that you already belong.
days.reflection: In what area of your life do you still relate to God with fear, as if you had to earn your place with Him?
days.prayer: Abba, Father, thank You that You have not given me a spirit that makes me a slave to fear. You have adopted me as Your own through Jesus. Where I still live like an anxious servant, trying to prove myself, set me free. Let Your Spirit remind my heart that I am Your child. Teach me to come to You with the trust of a child who knows he is loved. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to come to God as a child, not as a fearful servant.

days.title: Welcomed in the Beloved Son
days.devotion: Paul opens Ephesians with a long burst of praise for every spiritual blessing that is ours in Christ in the heavenly realms (v. 3). In the middle of it he says why God has done all this: so that the glory of His grace would be praised, the grace He has freely poured out on us in the Beloved. The Beloved is Jesus, the Son in whom the Father delights. Paul's word means that God has lavished His favour on us and welcomed us in Him. Notice that acceptance is something God has done, not something we have produced. It rests on grace from start to finish, so that the glory goes to Him and not to us. Many of us spend years looking for acceptance: from parents, friends, employers or the crowd. That hunger is real, and people's approval can be won and lost in a day. In Christ, God has already given what we are searching for. You do not need to perform to be welcomed by Him.
days.reflection: Whose approval have you been working hardest to win, and what would it look like to rest in God's acceptance instead?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that You have poured out Your grace on me and welcomed me in Your beloved Son. I confess that I often chase the approval of others and feel lost without it. Let Your grace be enough for me. When I am tempted to perform for acceptance, remind me that in Christ I am already welcomed. May my life bring praise to Your glorious grace. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to rest in the acceptance God has given you in Christ.

days.title: He Rejoices Over His People
days.devotion: Zephaniah warned Judah and Jerusalem of judgment for their sin. But the book ends with a promise for the day after that judgment, when God would gather a humble remnant who would take refuge in the Lord's name (v. 12). To that restored Jerusalem He says not to be afraid (v. 16), and then promises that the Lord their God is in their midst, a mighty one who saves. He will be glad over them with joy, He will be quiet in His love, and He will celebrate over them with songs of joy. This promise was first spoken to Israel. Yet it shows us something true about God's heart: He does not merely put up with the people He saves. He delights in them. In Christ, believers are brought near to this same God. When you think of how God sees His redeemed people, do not picture a disappointed frown. Scripture shows the joy of a Saviour who delights to save.
days.reflection: How do you usually picture God's face when He looks at you, and how does this verse invite you to see it differently?
days.prayer: Mighty God, You spoke joy over Your people in Jerusalem after days of judgment. Thank You that You are a God who delights to save. I often imagine You looking at me with disappointment. Teach me to see Your heart as Scripture shows it. Quiet my fears with Your love, and help me to trust in Your name as Your humble people did. Amen.
days.completion_message: You let Scripture reshape the way you picture God's heart toward His people.

days.title: Nothing Can Separate You
days.devotion: Paul ends Romans 8 with a series of questions. If God is for us, who can stand against us (v. 31)? Who can cut us off from Christ's love (v. 35)? He lists real dangers Christians faced: trouble, persecution, hunger, the sword. He does not promise that these will never come. Instead he says that even in all these things we win an overwhelming victory through the One who loved us (v. 37). Then comes his settled conviction: nothing in life or death, in the present or the future, will ever be able to cut us off from God's love, which is ours in Christ Jesus our Lord. Notice where this love is found: in Christ Jesus. Your belonging does not depend on how strong you feel, how well you perform, or what happens to you. It rests on His love, and that love holds you fast.
days.reflection: What fear or circumstance has made you wonder whether God still loves you, and how does this passage answer it?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that nothing in life or in death can separate me from Your love. You know the things that shake me and make me doubt. I bring them to You now. When I feel weak or afraid, remind me that my belonging rests on Your love and not on my strength. Hold me fast, and help me to rest secure in You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You ended this week holding on to a love that nothing can break.

days.title: Redeemed and Forgiven
days.devotion: Paul continues his praise for what God has given us in Christ. Now he names two gifts: in Christ we are redeemed through His blood and our sins are forgiven, in keeping with the riches of God's grace. To redeem is to buy back or set free by paying a price. The price was not paid by us; it was the blood of Christ. And the result is forgiveness: our sins sent away and no longer held against us. Paul says we "have" these things. They are not a hope for later, but a present possession for those in Christ. Their measure is the richness of His grace, not the size of our sin or the strength of our regret. Many believers live as though they are still on probation, waiting to see if they are really forgiven. God says otherwise. Your forgiveness is as secure as the grace that gave it.
days.reflection: Is there a sin you still carry as if it had never been forgiven, and what would it mean to trust God's word about it today?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that in Jesus I have redemption through His blood and the forgiveness of my sins. I confess that I still carry some things as if You had not forgiven them. Today I bring them to You and trust the riches of Your grace. Free me from living like someone on probation. Let me walk as one who is truly forgiven. In Jesus' name, Amen.
days.completion_message: You trusted God's word that in Christ you are redeemed and forgiven.

days.title: No Condemnation
days.devotion: In Romans 7 Paul is painfully honest about his struggle with sin. He cries out at how wretched he is, and then answers with thanks to God for the rescue that comes through Jesus Christ (7:24–25). Then Romans 8 opens with this verdict: for those who are in Christ Jesus, there is now no condemnation. Condemnation is a judge's sentence of guilt. For those in Christ, that sentence has been dealt with, because God condemned sin in the flesh of His own Son (v. 3). Paul does not say there is no struggle, but there is no condemnation. The accusing voice that says you are a failure, beyond hope or not good enough for God is not the last word. Later in the chapter Paul asks who is in a position to condemn, and points to Christ Jesus, the One who died (v. 34). Conviction from the Spirit leads us back to God; condemnation drives us away. In Christ, you can come to Him.
days.reflection: What accusing thought about yourself do you most need to answer with the truth of "no condemnation"?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that there is now no condemnation for those who are in You. You took the judgment I deserved. When accusing thoughts tell me I am a failure, help me to answer them with Your word. Where I need to change, let Your Spirit convict me and draw me back to You, not drive me away. I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.
days.completion_message: You answered the voice of condemnation with the truth of what Christ has done.

days.title: Made Righteous in Him
days.devotion: Paul has been explaining the heart of his message: God has reconciled us to Himself by means of Christ (v. 18). Here he shows how. God made Christ, who never knew sin, to be sin on our behalf. Jesus had no sin of His own. On the cross He stood in our place and bore the judgment our sin deserved. And the purpose is astonishing: that in union with Him we would become God's righteousness. This is sometimes called the great exchange. Christ took what was ours, and in Him we receive a right standing with God that we could never produce. Notice the words "in him." Our righteousness before God is not a score we build up by good days and lose by bad ones. It is found in Christ and received by faith. On the days when you feel you have nothing to offer God, you can stand in what Christ has given.
days.reflection: On a day when you feel you have failed, how will you remind yourself where your standing with God really comes from?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You knew no sin, yet You were made sin for me. Thank You for bearing what I deserved, so that I could be made right with God in You. Forgive me for trying to build my own righteousness from good days and losing heart on bad ones. Let me stand in what You have given. I receive it with gratitude. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to stand in the righteousness Christ gives, not in your own record.

days.title: A New Creation
days.devotion: Just before this verse Paul says he no longer judges people by outward and worldly standards (v. 16). Christ's death and resurrection have changed how he sees everyone, and how he sees himself. Then he declares that anyone who is in Christ is a new creation. What was old has passed away; see, something new has come into being. Being in Christ is not a small improvement on the old life. It is a new beginning that God Himself brings about; as verse 18 says, all of it comes from God. This does not mean every old habit disappears overnight. Growth takes time. But your past, your failures and the labels others have put on you are no longer the deepest truth about you. God does not define you by what you were. In Christ you are a new creation, and He is at work to make that newness visible.
days.reflection: What old label, from your past or from other people, do you need to stop letting define you?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that in Christ I am a new creation. The old has passed away, and You are making all things new. I bring You the labels I still carry from my past and from others. Help me to let them go. Where old habits still cling to me, keep working in me with patience, and help me to see myself as You see me in Jesus. Amen.
days.completion_message: You set down an old label and took hold of what God calls you in Christ.

days.title: Christ Lives in Me
days.devotion: The Galatian believers were being told that faith in Christ was not enough; they also needed to keep the law of Moses to be right with God. Paul answers with his own testimony: he has been crucified with Christ; he is still alive, yet the life is not really his own, for Christ lives in him. When Christ died, Paul's old life under sin and the law came to an end. Now he lives a new life, and its source is Christ Himself. How does he live it? By trusting in God's Son, the One who, in Paul's words, loved me and gave His life for me. Notice how personal that is: loved me, gave His life for me. The Christian life is not a new performance to keep God pleased. It is trusting the One who loved you first, and letting His life work in yours. As Paul says next, he will not cancel out the grace of God (v. 21).
days.reflection: Where are you trying to live the Christian life in your own strength, instead of trusting Christ who loved you and gave Himself for you?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You loved me and gave Yourself for me. Thank You that my old life has been crucified with You, and now You live in me. Forgive me for trying to live for You in my own strength, as if it all depended on me. Teach me to live by faith in You each day. Let Your life be seen in mine. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to live today by faith in God's Son, who loved you.

days.title: No Longer a Servant
days.devotion: Paul is still writing to believers who were being pulled back into living by the law. He explains that before Christ came, people were like young heirs under guardians, in bondage (vv. 1–3). But God sent His Son to redeem them, so that we might receive adoption as sons (vv. 4–5). Now he says that because they are sons, God has sent His Son's Spirit into their hearts, the Spirit who cries out, "Abba, Father." Notice the order: the Spirit is given because we are already His children, not to make us earn it. Then Paul concludes that each of them is no longer a slave but a son, and since a son, also an heir. Paul's word here is "son": in that culture sons were normally the heirs, and Paul uses the word for all believers, women and men alike (3:28). You are not a hired servant hoping for wages. You are a child and an heir.
days.reflection: In what way are you still relating to God like a servant earning wages, rather than a child who is an heir?
days.prayer: Abba, Father, thank You for sending Your Son to redeem me and Your Spirit to live in my heart. I am no longer a servant working for Your approval, but Your child and an heir through Christ. Where I still try to earn what You have freely given, set me free. Help me to stand fast in this freedom and to live as Your child today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to live as God's child and heir, not as a servant earning wages.

days.title: Hidden With Christ
days.devotion: The Colossian church was being pressured by teachers who judged them by rules about food, festivals and special experiences (2:16–18). Paul reminds them where their true life is. They have been raised with Christ (3:1), so they are to set their minds on things above. Then he says that they have died, and their life is kept hidden with Christ in God. Their old life has ended, and their new life is kept safe with Christ in God. Being hidden speaks of security, and also of something not yet fully seen. Verse 4 adds that one day, when Christ, who is their life, appears, they will appear with Him in glory. This means your real life is not finally measured by the judgments of others or by what can be seen today. People may not see who you are in Christ. God does, and your life is safe with Him.
days.reflection: Whose judgments of you have felt heavier than the truth that your life is hidden with Christ in God?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that my life is hidden with Christ in You. When others judge me, and when I cannot see much change in myself, remind me that my true life is safe with You. Lift my thoughts to things above, where Christ is. Help me to live today from that security, waiting for the day when He appears. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered that your life is hidden with Christ in God.

days.title: His Handiwork
days.devotion: Paul has just said that salvation is entirely God's gift: we have been saved by grace, through faith. It does not originate with us; it is God's gift, and it does not come from our works, so no one has grounds to boast (vv. 8–9). Now he adds what follows: God has made us, creating us in Christ Jesus for good works that He planned ahead of time as the path we should walk in. The order matters. We are not saved by good works, but we are saved for them. The Greek word Paul uses, often translated "workmanship" or "handiwork," speaks of something God has made with care. You are not a project you must complete by yourself, but a work in His hands. And the good works He has for you are not a ladder to climb toward God. They are a path He has already prepared, for you to walk in with Him. Your purpose flows from His grace, not the other way around.
days.reflection: What is one good work in front of you this week that you can do as a response to grace, rather than to prove yourself?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that I am saved by grace through faith, and not by my works. Thank You that I am Your handiwork, made in Christ Jesus for good works You have prepared. Free me from doing good to earn Your favour. Help me to see the path You have set before me this week, and to walk in it gladly with You. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to see yourself as God's handiwork and walk in the good He has prepared.

days.title: Not Your Own
days.devotion: Some in Corinth thought that what they did with their bodies did not matter to God. Paul answers with a truth about who they are: the body is a temple where the Holy Spirit dwells, the Spirit God has given them. Then he adds that they do not belong to themselves, because they were bought at a price. The price was Christ's own life. This is not meant to make you feel owned in a cold way. It means you are valued. Someone paid dearly for you, and God's Spirit has made His home in you. So Paul concludes that they are to bring glory to God in the way they use their bodies. Our choices matter, not because God's love is conditional, but because we belong to Him. When the world tells you that your worth depends on your appearance or your usefulness, remember the price that was paid. You are precious to God, and your whole life can honour Him.
days.reflection: What is one practical choice about how you use your body, time or energy that would honour the One who bought you?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that I am not my own, because You bought me with a price. Thank You that Your Holy Spirit lives in me. When I feel worthless, remind me how much I cost You. When I am tempted to live only for myself, remind me that I belong to You. Help me to glorify You in my body today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You remembered the price paid for you and chose to honour God with your life.

days.title: Chosen, Holy and Beloved
days.devotion: Having reminded the Colossians that their life is hidden with Christ, Paul now describes how that new life looks among other people. He begins with who they are before he tells them what to do: they are God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved. Chosen means God has picked them out as His own. Holy means set apart for God. Beloved means dearly loved. These are gifts they have received in Christ, not rewards for good behaviour. Only after this does Paul list what to "put on": mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Then he adds forgiveness, just as the Lord forgave them (v. 13). Our identity comes first; our way of treating others flows from it. People who know they are loved by God are freer to be kind, patient and forgiving, because they are not fighting for their own worth. Today you can clothe yourself in Christ's character because you are already His.
days.reflection: Which relationship would change if you treated that person out of the security of being chosen and loved by God?
days.prayer: Father, thank You that in Christ I am chosen, holy and dearly loved. I did not earn these names; You gave them. Because I am Yours, help me to put on mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Show me where I need to forgive as Christ forgave me. Let my security in Your love make me gentle with others today. Amen.
days.completion_message: You let God's names for you shape the way you treat others.

days.title: You Belong to the Body
days.devotion: The church in Corinth was divided, and some believers compared their gifts with others. Paul pictures the church as a human body. The foot might say that because it is not a hand, it does not belong to the body (v. 15), yet it still belongs. God has placed every part just as He chose (v. 18), and even the parts that seem weaker are essential (v. 22). Then Paul makes it personal: together they are Christ's body, and each one is a member of it. Every believer belongs to Christ's body, and each one has a place. Your identity in Christ is not only private. You are joined to other believers, and you need them as they need you. When you feel you have little to offer, or that others are more gifted, remember that God placed you where you are on purpose. The body is not complete without you.
days.reflection: Where have you been comparing yourself with other believers, and how can you take your place in Christ's body this week?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that I am part of Your body and that You have given me a place in it. Forgive me for comparing myself with others or thinking I am not needed. Help me to value the believers around me and to serve them with what You have given me. Let me care for others as a member of Your body. Amen.
days.completion_message: You took your place in the body of Christ instead of comparing yourself with others.

days.title: A Chosen People With a Purpose
days.devotion: Peter writes to scattered believers who were often misunderstood and mistreated by their neighbours. He tells them that Jesus Himself was rejected by people but chosen by God and precious to Him (v. 4). Then he speaks to them with titles once given to Israel: they are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people God claims as His own possession. And these names come with a purpose: that they would declare the praises of the One who called them out of darkness into His wonderful light. Verse 10 reminds them that once they were not a people, but now they are God's people. Our identity is not only for our comfort. God has brought us into His light so that others may see His goodness through us. Even when others reject you, you are chosen and precious to God, and called to point beyond yourself to Him.
days.reflection: Where in your everyday life can you show the goodness of the God who called you into His light?
days.prayer: Lord, thank You that You called me out of darkness into Your wonderful light. Once I was not Yours, and now I belong to You and have received mercy. When others reject or overlook me, remind me that I am chosen and precious to You. Let my life declare Your praises, so that people around me may see Your goodness. Amen.
days.completion_message: You embraced your calling to declare the praises of the One who called you.

days.title: The Light of the World
days.devotion: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus speaks to His disciples. He has just described the blessed life of those who belong to His kingdom (vv. 3–12). Then He tells them who they are: light for the whole world. He does not tell them to try to become light; He says they are. Light is not meant to be hidden, any more than a city on a hilltop can be concealed. No one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket. So Jesus tells them to let their light shine before others, so that people see their good deeds and give glory to their Father in heaven. The light is not about drawing attention to ourselves. It is about living in such a way that people see the goodness of God. You may feel small or unremarkable. Jesus still says you are light, and He sends you into the places where you live and work.
days.reflection: Where are you tempted to hide your light, and what is one way you can let it shine there this week?
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You call Your followers the light of the world. I often feel small and hesitant, and sometimes I hide. Give me courage to let Your light shine where You have placed me. Let my words and good works point people to my Father in heaven, not to myself. Amen.
days.completion_message: You chose to let your light shine where God has placed you.

days.title: He Will Finish What He Began
days.devotion: Paul writes to the Philippian church from prison, and his letter begins with thanksgiving. He remembers their partnership in the gospel from the very first day up to the present (v. 5). Then he says he is fully convinced that the God who started a good work in them will keep at it and bring it to its finish on the day of Jesus Christ. Paul's confidence is not in the Philippians' strength, but in God. The One who began the work is the One who will complete it. This is a fitting place to end. Over these weeks we have heard what God says about those in Christ: known, loved, adopted, forgiven, made new, chosen and sent. You may not feel like all of these things yet. But your identity was never your own project. God began it by His grace, He is at work in you now, and He is faithful to finish what He started.
days.reflection: Which truth from this Connection Path about who you are in Christ do you most want to carry with you into the weeks ahead?
days.prayer: Faithful God, thank You that You began a good work in me, and You will bring it to completion on the day Jesus Christ returns. Thank You for all You have said about who I am in Him. When I doubt, remind me that my identity rests on Your grace and not on my performance. Keep working in me, and help me to trust You to finish what You started. Amen.
days.completion_message: You finished this Connection Path trusting God to complete the good work He began in you.
